author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 1 review of #32 (B04): in the outbox, `attempts` is only consulted by `Fail`. A row whose processing kills or hangs its worker never reaches `Fail`, so its lease just expires and it is taken over again, forever, holding every later version of its entity behind it.

The drain must therefore check the attempt count **at claim time**: a row claimed for the Nth time beyond the ladder's length is parked as a dead letter (reason: something like "attempts exhausted without a recorded failure") before any work is done on it.

Add to this item's acceptance: a row whose worker dies on every attempt ends up dead-lettered, and the next version of its entity is then delivered.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 3 review of #31 (B03), for the worker drain:

- **`tenancy.Bind` does not narrow a helper-role transaction.** Permissive RLS policies are OR-ed, so inside `RoleTx(worker)` a `Bind` changes nothing: the worker's `USING (true)` policy still shows every tenant (reproduced on 200,000 rows). Per-tenant work after a claim must be a **second transaction under `TenantTx`**, as the application role, never a `Bind` inside the helper role. B04's outbox already works this way; the drain must too. Add to acceptance: a test that the drain never reads a payload in a worker-role transaction.
- Cost of the pattern, measured: `SET LOCAL ROLE` is 0.030 ms and `set_config` 0.034 ms of server time, two extra round trips, about 1 ms at 0.5 ms RTT, under 1 percent of the 200 ms budget. They could be one pgx batch. Not worth doing unless a profile says so.
- **Pool sizing.** The pool is at pgx defaults: `max(4, NumCPU)` connections, shared by all drain goroutines. On a small container that is 4. Tunable with `pool_max_conns` in the URL (works today) but documented nowhere. Size the drain pool against it and document it.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
Two more from the delta review of #31, for the drain:

- `store.Tx`, `TenantTx` and `RoleTx` scrub connection-level errors so that no part of the database URL can reach a log. That includes errors returned by the transaction function itself: a caller's own sentinel joined with a `*net.OpError` comes back relabelled as a database connection error, and `errors.Is(err, sentinel)` is false. This is deliberate (fail closed on the secret) and documented. The consequence for the drain: **never do network I/O inside a transaction function** (hydration, sink delivery). It is already architecture principle 6; now it also silently changes your error.
- `tenancy.Bind` refuses a `RoleTx` transaction (`ErrCrossTenantTx`). The guard is against accidents, not against effort: wrapping the transaction in another struct, or using `tx.Conn()`, drops the marker. Do not wrap a `RoleTx` transaction.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 3 fix of #32 (B04). The outbox API changed, and this item builds on it:

- Failures are reported with a `Cause`, never with text: `outbox.NewCause(Class).WithStatus(n).WithCode(s)`, passed to `Fail(ctx, c, ladder, cause)` or `MarkDead(ctx, c, cause)`. There is deliberately no way to pass an error string from a remote system, because `err.Error()` of a `*url.Error` quotes the request URL, query-string API key included, and `last_error` is a plain column. A new kind of failure means adding a `Class`. `WithCode` stops accidents, not a caller who passes a bare secret as the code: pass only provider or sink error codes.
- `Claimed` is read-only: `ID()`, `Tenant()`, `Attempt()`.
- `Accept` refuses an ordering key over 512 bytes with `ErrBadOrderingKey`. That is poison, not a server error: park it and answer 2xx, never 5xx (a provider would retry-storm).
- `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` now take the per-key advisory lock and promote the next row, so they wait for an open `Accept` or `Replay` of the same key. Keep accepting transactions short, and never do network I/O inside one.
- The claim is a stored head marker (`docs/adr/0010-outbox-head-marker.md`). Never insert into `outbox` except through `Accept`: a row written without the marker into a key with no head is never delivered.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text: From the review of the claim redesign in #32, for sizing the drain: the redesigned write path (per-key lock, head marker, promotion on finish) is about 20 percent slower than before, measured at 2,630 deliveries per second against 3,300 with 8 acceptors and 8 workers on 1 KB bodies. A fleet restart where 10,000 leases expire in the same second shows no cliff (2.7 to 3.5 ms per poll at batch 100). Claim cost is about 1 buffer per row to find plus about 25 per row for the UPDATE, so batch 100 is about 2,500 buffers.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
From the round 1 review of #48 (B07), a throughput ceiling this item inherits and cannot change on its own.

The hub sets the outbox ordering key to `{provider}:{subscription id}`, not per entity, because the hub never parses a delivery and so cannot name the entity inside it. The FIFO guarantee still holds (an entity is a subset of a subscription, and `outbox_one_head` is keyed on `(tenant_id, ordering_key)`), but **one subscription's deliveries drain serially**. The reviewer measured the consequence: about **6.7 deliveries per second per subscription at a 150 ms sink round trip, whatever the worker count**. A busy ClickUp workspace is one subscription.

Two ways out when this becomes the limit, neither this item's alone: B08's normalizer knows the entity, so the ordering key could be narrowed once a delivery is parsed (it would have to be set on the outbox row before the drain claims it, so it belongs to whatever writes the row); or the drain could pipeline within one key while keeping versions of one entity ordered. Measure before choosing.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
Carried from the round 1 review of #49 (B08), which is where `internal/pipeline` takes entity advisory locks.

**1. The advisory-lock order across modules is written down nowhere.** B10 will hold the outbox ordering-key lock and then take entity locks inside the same transaction, and both live in the same single advisory-lock namespace (`pg_advisory_xact_lock` over a 64-bit key, with no classid split). `internal/pipeline` sorts the entity keys of one delivery so that two deliveries carrying the same entities can queue rather than deadlock, and `internal/outbox` takes the ordering-key lock before it assigns a seq, but nothing states the order BETWEEN the two, and a worker that ever took an entity lock before an ordering-key lock (a reconciliation pass, say) could deadlock against the ordinary drain. Whatever B10 does, the rule belongs in a comment where both are visible, and probably in ADR 12 decision 1 beside the entity-lock paragraph.

**2. A smaller residual in the same place.** The entity locks of one delivery are sorted by `external_id`, but the lock identity is `hashtextextended(tenant || chr(31) || provider || chr(31) || external_id, 0)`. A pair of 64-bit collisions across two tenants could invert the order for two transactions and deadlock. The probability is not worth acting on for its own sake, but if B10 touches the lock helper, sorting by the hash value rather than by the external id removes the argument entirely.

**3. Two things about `pipeline.Prepare` that B10 is the first caller to meet**, from the same review:
- `Prepare` does not check that `tx` is bound to `tenant`. If they disagree, the ledger insert is refused by row-level security as a plain retryable error rather than a dead letter, and the ladder burns its attempts on a programming error.
- `Prepare` returns the counters it had reached beside every error, with `Records` nil (this changed in the round 1 fixes). B10 should log `Prepared` on the error path too, not only on success: that is where `ScopeReturned` and `VersionUnordered` are, and they are the counts ADR 4 decision 7 and ADR 12 decision 1 ask an operator to watch.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text:
Carried from the review of #49 (B08), which added the per-entity advisory lock this item owns the
key for.

`internal/pipeline/queries.sql` used to say, under `LockEntity`, that "two entities whose lock
strings hash alike only wait for each other, which is harmless". That is not quite true, and the
reason matters for the lock key #10 settles.

The locks of one delivery are sorted by **external id** and taken over `hashtextextended(...)`, a
64 bit hash. A collision therefore breaks the order the sorting exists to create. With external ids
`A < B < C` in string order and `hash(A) = hash(C) = h1`, `hash(B) = h2`:

- a delivery carrying `{A, B}` takes `h1` then `h2`;
- a delivery carrying `{B, C}` takes `h2` then `h1`.

That is a deadlock, not a wait, and Postgres aborts one of them. At 64 bits it will not happen, and
the retry ladder would carry the aborted transaction if it did, so there was nothing to do in B08.
The line is corrected there and now says so.

**Sorting by the hash rather than by the external id is what makes the sentence true**, and that is
already this item's proposal for the lock key. Worth doing it for this reason as well as the others,
and worth keeping the two in one place: the thing sorted and the thing locked have to be the same
value, or the sort guarantees nothing.
title: Comment on issue #10

author: gablooge
text: From B05 (#43), for the ClickUp normalizer: `version` must move on every reported change, a move included (ADR 4). A ClickUp task moved to another list changes the record's scope; check what ClickUp's `date_updated` does on a move and on a move back, record a real payload of each (scrubbed), and make the golden files cover them. A provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}` (the tunnel's routing rule) and, more narrowly, `[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}` to be a scope id segment (ADR 3).
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text: From the review of #43, for the ClickUp normalizer (and every later one): a provider may emit a leap second (`23:59:60`). The record format refuses it (Go's `time` cannot hold it), so clamp second 60 to 59 when parsing provider times, with a test. Otherwise the event becomes a normalizer failure: a visible dead letter, not a lost event, but avoidable.
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text:
From the round 1 fix of #43 (the record format), for this normalizer and every later one: **the format refuses, it never repairs.** `Seal` now fails on a record whose identifier fields or `author.display` contain control, invisible or bidirectional-formatting characters, and whose `title` is not a single line (a tab, a line break or any other control character is refused). Real data has these: a display name with a pasted zero-width space, a task name with a tab, a folded email subject. A provider that does not clean them first turns a real event into a dead letter.

So this item must add the cleaning helper in `internal/record`, next to the rules it mirrors (it was deliberately not added in B05, where it would have had no caller): one function per field class that removes or replaces exactly what the format refuses, with a table test tying it to the validation rules, so that a cleaned value always passes and the two cannot drift. Every normalizer calls it before `Seal`. Decide what cleaning does to a `title` line break (a space) and say it in the guide. Check the round 2 review of #43 for whether the format's contract changes on this point.
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text: From the round 2 review of #43: forgetting to clean must be HARD, not easy. Today nothing in the repository cleans, and a fixture with a clean name passes. So, with the cleaning helpers asked for above (for `author.display` and `title` ONLY, never for identifiers), add a **hostile fixture to the provider conformance harness** that every normalizer must turn into a record that `Seal` accepts: a display name with a zero-width space, one with a right-to-left mark, one with a soft hyphen, a title with a tab, a title with a line break, a title that is only whitespace. A provider that skips cleaning then fails its own tests, not production.
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text: See the correction on #16: a sender-controlled identifier needs its own injective encoding or a hash; the scope id escaper refuses control bytes and is not the tool for it. ClickUp ids are provider-minted, so this item is unlikely to need it, but the cleaning helpers must not be applied to identifiers under any circumstances.
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text:
A constraint on ClickUp registration, decided in #48 (B07) and recorded as **ADR 11, decision 5**.

**The hub parks a delivery that more than one subscription verifies, including two subscriptions of the SAME tenant.** The tenant is unambiguous in that case, but the subscription is not, and the ordering key is `{provider key}:{subscription id}` (ADR 11, decision 3). Choosing one of two rows is choosing a queue on no evidence, and the choice cannot be made stable: pick the lowest id and it holds only while both rows do, so deleting or re-registering the chosen row sends an entity's later versions into the other queue while an earlier version is still in flight. The row is also where the `resource` this item hydrates against lives.

**Why it matters here.** ClickUp issues one webhook secret per workspace. A registration design that writes one subscription row per list, each carrying the workspace id and that one secret, produces two or more verifying rows on the first delivery, and **every delivery of that workspace parks forever** as `unattributable: ambiguous owner`.

**The shape that avoids it:** at most one subscription row per (provider, workspace) per tenant, with any finer scoping (which lists, which spaces) carried inside that row rather than as a second row. Two rows of one tenant on one workspace with *different* secrets resolve correctly and are fine.

Whether the `subscriptions` table should enforce this with a unique index is left open, because it needs the real registration shape: B11 and B14 to settle.

The park is at least actionable now. The log line reads `more than one subscription's secret verified one delivery, so it is parked and not routed` and carries `subscriptions` and `tenants`, so it says which rows collided and whether the collision is inside one tenant.
title: Comment on issue #11

author: gablooge
text: Credentials for the live ClickUp check are now available on the maintainer's machine: `~/.config/sluiceway/clickup.env` (`CLICKUP_TOKEN`). See "Credentials for live verification" in `CLAUDE.md` (arrives with #34) for the rules. Still needed from the maintainer for this item: a public tunnel (cloudflared or ngrok) so ClickUp can reach the local `/ingress/clickup`, and a test space or list where a comment may be posted.
title: Comment on issue #12

author: gablooge
text:
The public webhook tunnel now exists and was tested end to end on 2026-09-19.

- URL: a Cloudflare Tunnel on the maintainer's machine. The hostname is deliberately not written down in this repository, because publishing it invites traffic to a developer machine; it is in `~/.config/lawang/tunnel.env` as `LAWANG_TUNNEL_HOSTNAME`.
- Start it on demand (the token travels in the env file, never on a command line):

```sh
docker run --rm --name sluiceway-tunnel \
  --env-file ~/.config/lawang/cloudflare-tunnel.env \
  cloudflare/cloudflared:2026.9.1 tunnel --no-autoupdate run
```

- Cloudflare forwards ONLY `^/ingress/[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}$` to `http://host.docker.internal:8080` and answers 404 itself for everything else. Checked from the public internet: `/ingress/ping` 200, a POST to `/ingress/clickup` arrives, and `/healthz`, `/v1/...`, `/ingress/../x`, `/ingress/%2e%2e/x`, `/ingress/a/../../x`, `/ingress/a/b`, `/ingress/` and `/INGRESS/x` all get 404. With the container stopped the hostname answers 502.
- A first attempt with a plain `^/ingress/` prefix let `/ingress/../secret.txt` through to a server that normalizes paths. Do not loosen the rule.
- Consequences for the code: the service must listen on port 8080 where the Docker host can reach it (the default `:8080` works); a provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}` (put that in the provider registry, with a test); the ingress handler must still treat every request as hostile, since the tunnel is only a second line.
- Wanted from the item that first uses it: a `make tunnel` target with exactly the command above, and a line in the setup guide saying to stop the container and deregister the webhooks afterwards.

Rules for the credentials: "Credentials for live verification" in `CLAUDE.md` (arrives with #34).
title: Comment on issue #12

author: gablooge
text:
**Correction to my earlier note on this issue.** I wrote that a provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, taken from the first tunnel routing rule. That contradicts ADR 3 (from #43), which freezes the provider segment of a scope id as `[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}`: lowercase letter first, no hyphen, at most 32 characters. **ADR 3 wins.** A registry that accepted `ms-graph` would produce records that all fail in `Seal`.

The tunnel now enforces the same grammar: Cloudflare forwards only `^/ingress/[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$`. Retested from the public internet on 2026-09-19: `/ingress/clickup` and `/ingress/ms_graph` arrive; `/ingress/ms-graph`, `/ingress/9lives`, `/ingress/Slack`, a 33 character key, `/ingress/../x` and `/healthz` all get 404 at Cloudflare.

For the provider registry: validate a key against ADR 3's grammar at registration, by calling the function in `internal/record` that owns the rule and not by copying the pattern, with a test.
title: Comment on issue #12

author: gablooge
text:
From #7 (PR #48), so that this item does not have to rediscover it.

B07 added a `secret` column to `subscriptions`: the secret a provider signs its deliveries with, which the accept path needs **before** it knows whose delivery this is, so `Vault.Fetch(ctx, tenant, provider)` cannot serve it. ADR 11, decision 1, is the record of that, including why it is a different credential from the API tokens this item puts in the vault.

When this item encrypts that column, these are all of the places that touch it:

- **Readers: the two candidate queries in `internal/hub/queries.sql`,** `CandidatesByWorkspace` and `CandidatesBySubscription`, and the one function that runs them, `hub.candidates`. Both are needed now: B07's first round used one query or the other, and the review found that this attributed a delivery to the wrong tenant, so the candidate set is now the union of one probe per key the delivery carries. Decrypting therefore happens in one place, `hub.candidates`, over the rows either query returns.
- **Writer: `UpsertSubscription`,** run by `hub.Subscriptions.Register`.
- **Nothing else.** `UpsertSubscription` deliberately does **not** return the column (the first round did, and the review pointed out it made ADR 11's claim false and sent the value on towards B14's operator API). `Register` hands back the secret its own caller passed in. `lawang_resolver` is granted `SELECT` on the column and nothing may write it.

Two constraints on whatever interface this item builds for it:

1. It must work **before the tenant is known**. That is the whole reason the column exists, so it cannot be keyed by tenant the way `Vault.Fetch` is.
2. It runs once per delivery on the accept path, inside the resolver transaction, which targets 200 ms end to end and currently costs two index probes of 3 buffers each. A decryption that needs a network call per candidate would change that, and the resolver transaction must not be held across network I/O.

The table also has `CONSTRAINT subscriptions_secret_is_not_empty CHECK (octet_length(secret) > 0)`, and `hub.newCandidate` refuses a candidate whose secret is empty, so whatever ciphertext this item stores must still be non-empty.
title: Comment on issue #13

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 3 review of #32 (B04), for the operator API:

- `outbox.Replay` returns `ErrNotFound` both for "no such row" and for "the row is not dead". The API needs to tell them apart (404 versus 409), so the outbox needs a second sentinel.
- `outbox.Row` is an alias of a generated sqlc type whose tenant is a plain `string`, while `Claimed.Tenant` is a `tenancy.ID`. Do not let the generated type leak into the API's response shape.
- A per-tenant dead-letter listing has no index yet. Add one with the endpoint, and check it with EXPLAIN on a large table.
title: Comment on issue #14

author: gablooge
text:
## From B06's review (#47): `POST /v1` will answer `no such provider`

Carried here so it is decided where the `/v1/` mount is written, not rediscovered from a support question.

`net/http.ServeMux` answers 307 from `/x` to `/x/` when `/x/` is registered and `/x` is not, and a 307 on the webhook path turns a delivery into a 401 that reads as a forgery. So `ingress.New` owns the routing table and registers `/x` itself, with the 404 body every refusal before the hub uses: `no such provider\n`. That body is shared on purpose, because a request refused for its path shape must not reveal whether the provider behind it exists.

The consequence for this item: as soon as the operator API is given to `ingress.New` as a `Route` with `Path: "/v1/"`, a request for `/v1` with no trailing slash will answer **404 `no such provider`**. That is correct for `/ingress/...` and misleading for `/v1`: an operator reading it looks for a provider registry problem when the only thing wrong is a missing slash.

Two ways out, both cheap, neither decided here:

1. Register `/v1` as a `Route` of the operator API's own, answering whatever the API answers for an unknown path. `ingress.New` then sees an exact match for `/v1`, asks for no route of its own and leaves the caller's alone. This is already tested as `the caller covers the root` in `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`.
2. Let the guard route answer, and accept the body. Fine if the operator API is never reached by hand.

Option 1 is the one to prefer unless there is a reason not to, and it needs no change in `internal/ingress`.

Two things about `Route` that matter when this is wired: a route under `/ingress/` is refused at start (the webhook endpoint owns that prefix), and `New` decides whether it needs a route of its own by asking a copy of the routing table rather than by reading pattern strings, so a collection route and a subtree under it (`/v1/{resource}` plus `/v1/tenants/`) is a shape it handles rather than one it breaks.
title: Comment on issue #14

author: gablooge
text:
Three things from #7 (PR #48) that land on this item when it exposes subscriptions over `/v1` and `lawang connect`.

**1. A caller-supplied id leaks across tenants, in principle.** (Review note 4.) `hub.Subscriptions.Register` takes an optional `ID`, and `subscriptions.id` is a **global** primary key, not `(tenant_id, id)`. So a unique violation tells a caller that some other tenant already holds that id. ULIDs make it unexploitable in practice, and the id has to stay global because it is half of the outbox ordering key, but an API that lets an operator choose an id should decide what it does about this: mint the id itself and ignore what was sent, or answer the same way for "taken by you" and "taken by someone else".

**2. Do not echo the secret.** `Register` returns a `provider.Subscription` whose `Secret` is the value the **caller passed in**, not one read back out of the table: `UpsertSubscription` deliberately does not return that column, so that `hub.candidates` stays the only reader of it and B13 has one place to encrypt. The type redacts the secret in every print and `slog` form, but an API that serializes the struct itself would not go through those, so the response shape wants to leave the field out.

**3. `Register` refuses fourteen things, each with a message that names a field and never a value.** They are all `hub.ErrInvalidSubscription`, so an API can map the lot to 400 and pass the message through without leaking a secret that was pasted into the wrong field. The refusals are exactly "this row could never resolve any delivery", and in particular a row with only a workspace id, or only a registration id, is **accepted**: the candidate lookup asks every row either key could select (ADR 11, decision 4).
title: Comment on issue #14

author: gablooge
text:
Small carry-over from the review of #48 (B07).

`hub.Subscriptions.Register`'s doc comment says the returned subscription "carries the caller's own secret ... see the field", but `provider.Subscription.Secret`'s own doc says nothing about it, so the pointer leads nowhere. One sentence on the field would land it where this item reads it.

Worth knowing while you are there, from the same review: `Register` takes a caller-supplied `ID` and the subscriptions primary key is global, so a unique violation tells a caller that some other tenant already holds that id. ULIDs make it unexploitable in practice, but this item is where `Register` is exposed, so it is this item's to decide.

Also, from ADR 11 decision 5: whether the table should refuse a second subscription row for the same (provider, workspace) within one tenant needs the real registration shape, so it is shared between this item and #11. Two such rows with one secret park every delivery of that workspace forever.
title: Comment on issue #14

author: gablooge
text: From the round 2 review of #47 (B06), for Slack: `provider.Request` carries `Method`, `URL`, `Header` and `Body`, but **no receive timestamp**. Slack's replay window compares `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp` against the time the request arrived, and HubSpot v3 does the same with its own header. Reading the clock inside `Verify` works but makes the check untestable without faking time globally, so the timestamp belongs on the request. `provider.Request` is a struct, so adding a field later costs one field rather than every implementation. #47 decides whether to add it now or here; check what it settled before building the replay window.
title: Comment on issue #15

author: gablooge
text:
From B06's round 2 review (#47): **`provider.Request` has no receive timestamp, and this is the item that should add it.**

Slack's v0 scheme wants a replay window (its guidance is to refuse a delivery whose `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp` is more than five minutes old), and HubSpot v3 wants one too (B18). The decision in B06 was to leave the field out for now rather than add one nothing reads, since `Request` is a struct and a field added later costs no implementation anything, unlike the interface widening that had to happen before B07, B11 and B15.

What to do here: add `ReceivedAt time.Time` (or a clock on the hub) when the window is implemented, and have the edge fill it. The reason it must not be `time.Now()` inside `Verify` is testability: a window checked against a clock the provider reads itself cannot be tested without smuggling a clock into the provider package, so the "just expired" and "just inside" cases never get a test. Whatever shape it takes, the timestamp is the receiver's own clock and never a value from the delivery, and the comparison goes into the same `Verify` that already returns a plain false for everything.
title: Comment on issue #15

author: gablooge
text: From B05 (#43), for Outlook (and #17, Teams): the scope id (ADR 3) percent-encodes every byte of a container id outside `A-Za-z0-9._~-`, and the whole id is capped at 512 bytes. That limit was reasoned, not measured. Microsoft Graph ids are long base64 with `=`, `+` and `/`, each of which becomes three bytes. Before writing the normalizer, measure real mailbox, folder, team and channel ids from the test tenant and confirm the encoded scope id fits, with room. If it does not, that is a format change and must happen before v0.1 freezes it.
title: Comment on issue #16

author: gablooge
text: From the round 2 review of #43, for Outlook: an identifier a SENDER controls must never reach a record raw. If this normalizer builds `edges.reply_parent` or an `external_id` from a mail header (`In-Reply-To`, `References`, `internetMessageId`), a stranger can put characters in it that the record format refuses, and their mail dead-letters itself, or worse, every reply to it does. Identifiers are NEVER cleaned (removing a character merges two different ids into one). Either use Graph's own opaque ids, which are printable ASCII, or escape or hash the header value injectively. Add a test with a hostile `Message-ID`.
title: Comment on issue #16

author: gablooge
text: Correction from the delta review of #43 to the note above about mail-header identifiers: do not reuse the scope id's percent escaping for them. That escaper is unexported, and it REFUSES control bytes (below 0x20, and 0x7F), which is exactly what a hostile `Message-ID` contains. A header-derived identifier needs its own injective encoding that escapes control bytes too, or a hash, and must stay within `MaxExternalID` (1,024 characters) after escaping triples some bytes. Prefer Graph's own opaque ids wherever they exist.

From the round 1 review of #47 (B06): the `provider.Verify` interface as first written took only the body, the headers and the secret, which **cannot carry this item**. HubSpot's v3 signature covers the request method and the full request URI as well as the body and a timestamp. Rather than widen the interface after three providers have implemented it, #47 widens it now.

The part that matters here: the URI a sender signs is the **public** one it posted to, which behind a tunnel or any proxy is not what the Go server sees. It is taken from configuration, never from `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` or `Host`, because a sender that chooses part of the signed input can make a signature verify over content of their own choosing. When this item is built, check the exact v3 recipe against HubSpot's current documentation (the order of method, URI, body and timestamp, and the timestamp freshness window), and add a test that a signature computed over a different URI is refused.

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the review cycle on #32 (B04): `Accept` now takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock per (tenant, ordering key) before its INSERT, so that within one key the queue order equals the commit order.

Consequence for reconciliation: a reconcile chunk that accepts **several ordering keys in one transaction** holds several of those locks until commit. Two such transactions that take keys in different orders can deadlock (Postgres detects it and aborts one with 40P01).

So for this item: either accept one key per transaction, or sort the keys of a chunk into a stable order before accepting them, and in either case treat 40P01 as retryable. Add to the acceptance: two reconcile passes over overlapping keys running at once both finish.

author: gablooge
text: Carried over from the round 3 review of #32 (B04), for retention: a retention sweep by `finished_at` has no index yet, so add one with the sweep and check it with EXPLAIN on a table with millions of finished rows. Delete in bounded chunks, never inside one long transaction. Also note the HOT update finding: lease and state updates on the outbox are almost never HOT at the default fillfactor (0 of 10,000 measured), so the table bloats under load; measure autovacuum behaviour and consider a lower fillfactor here.
title: Comment on issue #25

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the review of the claim redesign in #32 (B04), for hardening and operations. The claim is now O(batch), with one cost that is this item's to manage:

- **Dead index entries between vacuums.** Every lease, retry and finish leaves a dead entry at the front of the index the claim walks. Measured with autovacuum off: a batch of 10 costs 302 buffers fresh, then about 11 more per 1,000 lease-and-finish cycles (2,511 buffers, 3.9 ms after 200,000 cycles). It does not recover without a vacuum; a VACUUM restores 302 buffers and 0.44 ms. Default autovacuum fires at 20 percent of the TABLE, so with a large delivered history it fires late: at 5.1M rows that is about 5,900 buffers and 9 ms per poll just before it fires, and it scales with retention. Set per-table storage parameters on `outbox` (a low `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`, or a fixed `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold`) so vacuum frequency does not depend on how much history is retained, and measure it.
- **A held snapshot stops the cleanup.** 50,000 cycles under a held snapshot cost 50,871 buffers and 10.4 ms per poll. `pg_dump`, a replication slot, or a forgotten `psql` transaction does this routinely. Add a metric for claim latency and for the oldest open transaction.
- **Head invariant at runtime.** Nothing checks at runtime that every key with unfinished rows has exactly one head. A key without a head is never delivered and raises no error. #32 adds a targeted detection query and documents the repair statement; this item should run it on a sweep, export a metric (stranded keys), and alert.
- Retention also bounds all of the above: a smaller table vacuums sooner.
title: Comment on issue #25

author: gablooge
text:
From the delta review of #32, for the stranded-key sweep in this item:

- `StrandedKeys` (tenant-scoped, in `internal/outbox/queries.sql`) carries `AND NOT u.is_head`, which the `NOT EXISTS` already implies, and which forces a heap visit per row. Measured on a scattered heap: 52 to 60 ms and 94,805 buffers with it, 27 to 30 ms and 54,629 buffers without, same result, and index-only capable. Drop it when building the sweep, and correct the query's comment, which describes a per-row probe plan where the planner actually chooses a merge anti join. Cost is O(unfinished rows of the tenant), never the history; no new index is worth its write-path cost.
- The repair statement exists twice, in ADR 10 and as the `repairKey` constant in the tests, with nothing tying them together. When the sweep gains a repair mode, make one source.
- `StrandedKeys` returns sender-derived ordering keys, which may contain control characters other than NUL. Log them quoted (`%q`), never raw.
- It needs a decision recorded in ADR 10: call it per tenant, or give the sweep a role of its own with `SELECT (tenant_id, ordering_key, state, is_head)` and a policy. The worker role deliberately reads neither `state` nor `ordering_key`.
title: Comment on issue #25

author: gablooge
text:
From the review of #7 (PR #48), two things that belong here rather than there.

**1. A row quota, or an age cap, on the sentinel tenant.**

`/ingress/{provider}` answers anyone, with no credential, and a delivery nobody can be shown to own is parked under `_parked` and answered 2xx. That is correct and it is what this item re-resolves, but it means a stranger can create parked rows at will. The reviewer measured it: twenty unauthenticated POSTs of distinct unparseable bodies produced twenty rows, and the edge's body cap is 1 MiB. Dedupe does not help, because the delivery id is `blake3(provider, raw_body)` and distinct bodies are free to produce.

B07 closed the part that could be closed without a policy decision: a delivery parked as `unattributable: unreadable delivery` now stores a note (its length and the delivery id its bytes had, about 100 bytes) instead of the body, because no sweep can ever re-resolve those bytes and nothing will read them again. See `outbox.Park` and ADR 11, decision 2.

What is left is the two reasons this item **does** re-resolve, `unattributable: no owner` and `unattributable: ambiguous owner`. Those must keep the body, because re-resolving means routing the delivery once the subscription that owns it exists. A "no owner" park is also reachable by a stranger: any body the provider can parse, naming a workspace nobody has connected, parks with its full payload. So the question for this item, or for retention:

- a row count or a byte budget per provider on the sentinel tenant, refusing or evicting past it, and
- an age cap, so an unresolved park that no registration has claimed after some window is deleted rather than swept forever.

Both are policy, both need a number, and neither should be guessed in the item that only writes the rows.

**2. A counter for a `Verify` that never returns.**

Also from the same review, note 2. When a provider's `Verify` does not return, `hub.verifyOne` gives up on it at the accept path's deadline and answers 503, but the goroutine stays until `Verify` returns, holding its own copy of the body. At the 1 MiB cap that is one goroutine and up to 1 MiB per delivery for as long as the provider bug lasts. The copy is what makes it safe rather than a race, so the code is right as built; what is missing is a way to see it, which is a counter when metrics land here.
title: Comment on issue #25

author: gablooge
text:
From the second review of #48 (B07), a measurement to carry here beside the note already on this issue.

**`ParkNoOwner` keeps every byte, and a stranger produces it with no credential.** The reviewer sent twenty unauthenticated POSTs of well formed 4 KiB bodies naming workspaces nobody had registered, and got **twenty rows holding 83,990 bytes** of the payloads, all `dead_reason = "unattributable: no owner"`. The delivery id is a hash of the body, so every distinct body is another row.

That is correct as built, and it is the reason this sweep exists: B25 re-resolves those rows from exactly those bytes, so dropping them would make the sweep impossible. `ParkUnreadable` is the one park whose bytes are dropped, because no later registration can ever make them resolvable. The narrowing is real (the body now has to be one the provider package can parse) but the shape of the exposure is unchanged.

**What is left for this item to decide:** whether the re-resolvable park reasons need a row quota per provider, an age cap before retention, or a byte budget, and what happens when one is reached. A sweep that never gives up and a table that grows without a bound are the two halves of the same question.

In #48 the wording that claimed `ParkUnreadable` is the only park a stranger produces at will has been softened in `outbox.go`, in `hub.park` and in ADR 11, so nothing in the tree argues that this residual does not exist.

author: gablooge
text: From the delta review of #32, for the operator docs (or a preflight check, decide here): the outbox validates ordering keys with Go's UTF-8 rule, which matches Postgres's rule exactly on a UTF8 database (1,376,512 byte sequences compared, 0 differ). On a database created with another encoding (LATIN1, for example) a perfectly valid CJK or emoji key fails with SQLSTATE 22P05, indistinguishable from an outage, and nothing checks `server_encoding`. Either document "the database must be UTF8" in the setup guide, or have `store`'s preflight refuse any other `server_encoding`. The preflight is cheap and fails closed, so prefer it.

author: gablooge
text: From the review of #43, for the guide to writing a sink: warn that Python's `jsonschema` silently skips `format: date-time` unless a format checker AND the `rfc3339-validator` package are installed, so "format assertion on" can check nothing. The schema therefore also guards `occurred_at` with a pattern, which is the real guard in most validators; only calendar-impossible dates (February 30) need format assertion. Also state the document rules a sink may rely on (UTF-8, no unpaired surrogates), the body size a sink should accept, and that a scope id is an opaque value that must be percent-encoded again before it goes into a URL.
title: Comment on issue #28

author: gablooge
text:
From the delta review of #48 (B07), for the provider-authoring guide: **how far a provider package is trusted, written down, because a type name filter cannot carry the whole argument.**

`internal/hub` logs the dynamic type of a value a provider's `Verify` panicked with, and only when that name is short (128 bytes) and made of the characters a plainly written type name uses. That exists because a type name is **not** a compile-time constant: `reflect.StructOf` takes arbitrary bytes in a struct tag and `%T` prints them, so a `Verify` holding a tenant's signing secret can panic with a value whose type name *is* the secret. The reviewer demonstrated it, and then attacked the fix with 13 run-time constructions (struct tag, struct field name, pointer, slice, map, array and func wrappers, `chan`, generic instantiation, 100-deep `SliceOf`, the 128-byte boundary exactly). Everything that can carry a byte of TEXT of its own was refused.

**The residual, which is deliberately not fixed in code.** An array length is digits, and digits pass the filter. `reflect.PointerTo(reflect.ArrayOf(n, byteType))` prints `*[126664548954996]uint8`, which is logged, and that number is `s3cr3t` read as a base-256 integer. A nil pointer to the array costs nothing to build, and `reflect`'s address-space check caps the channel at roughly 47 bits, so about six bytes of a secret per panicking delivery. Banning digits would not close it, only narrow it again: the channel is the provider package's own choice of what to panic with, not the character set of a type name. `typeNameForLog`'s comment in `internal/hub/hub.go` now names this residual, so the next reader does not take the character set for a boundary.

**Why it lands here.** The real boundary is a trust statement, not a filter, and this item is where it gets written for people who will author providers:

- A provider package runs in the same process and is handed the tenant's signing secret. It could log that secret itself. Lawang's log filter narrows the trivial route into *Lawang's* log line, at error level, in every backup of it; it does not make a hostile provider package safe, and nothing can.
- So the guide should say plainly what a provider package is trusted with, that a third-party provider package is a supply-chain decision the operator makes, and what the rules are for one: never log or panic with anything derived from a secret, a body or a delivery key, and `Verify` returns `false` rather than panicking.
- Worth pairing with #26's isolation suite, which already greps captured logs for token material. That test catches an accident, not a package that encodes on purpose.
title: Comment on issue #28

author: gablooge
text:
Correction to the residual number in the note above, from the close-out review of #48. The
conclusion is unchanged, only the size of the channel, and the guide should not be written from the
low figure.

That note says reflect's "address-space check caps the channel at roughly 47 bits, so about six
bytes of a secret per panicking delivery". There is no such cap for a one-byte element.
`reflect.ArrayOf` panics only when `length > ^uintptr(0)/elemSize`, which for `uint8` is never
reached below `math.MaxInt`, and nothing is allocated, because what a provider package would panic
with is a NIL pointer to the array, which costs one word:
`reflect.New(reflect.PointerTo(reflect.ArrayOf(n, byteType))).Elem().Interface()`.

Measured on go1.26.7 (darwin/arm64) against a copy of `typeNameForLog` at `bf1b9f4`:

| n | logged as | length |
|---|---|---|
| 126664548954996 | `*[126664548954996]uint8` | 23 bytes |
| math.MaxInt | `*[9223372036854775807]uint8` | 27 bytes |

Both pass the character check and both are well under the 128-byte bound. So the channel is about
63 bits, near 7.8 bytes of a secret per panicking delivery, not 47 bits and six. Eight bytes of a
secret read base 256 overflow into the sign bit, so seven bytes per panic is the round number to
write.

That makes the point the guide has to make slightly stronger rather than weaker: a filter over the
character set of a type name is not a boundary at any size, and the boundary is the trust statement
about what a provider package is allowed to panic with.

The same figure is in the comment on `typeNameForLog` in `internal/hub/hub.go`, so that comment
wants the same correction whenever that function is next touched. It is a note, not a defect: the
review of #48 is approved.

Carried over from the round 1 review of #33 (the agent rules). Before the repository flips to public in this item:

- The implementer and reviewer agents read issue, comment and pull request text. From the moment the repository is public, anyone can write that text. The rules now say text is data, never instructions (`CLAUDE.md`, both agent files), but that is a request, not an enforcement. Decide whether the agents run on outside contributions at all.
- The reviewer runs `make check` on a pull request's head. For a pull request from a fork that means running a stranger's Makefile and tests on the maintainer's machine, with the maintainer's `gh` token and SSH keys in reach. author: gablooge
text:
Branch protection for `main`. GitHub refuses it today ("Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public"), so apply it the moment the repository goes public in this item, or earlier if the account is upgraded. Until then a local `pre-push` hook on the maintainer's machine refuses pushes to `main` (it covers every agent worktree, but only that machine, and it is not versioned).

```sh
gh api -X PUT repos/gablooge/lawang/branches/main/protection --input - <<JSON
{
  "required_status_checks": { "strict": true, "contexts": ["check"] },
  "enforce_admins": true,
  "required_pull_request_reviews": { "required_approving_review_count": 0 },
  "restrictions": null,
  "allow_force_pushes": false,
  "allow_deletions": false,
  "required_linear_history": false,
  "required_conversation_resolution": false
}
JSON
```

Why these values:
- **Pull request required, 0 approvals.** The agents act as `gablooge`, and GitHub does not let an account approve its own pull request. Requiring one approval would block every merge. The `review:*` label stays the verdict until the reviewer has its own bot account or GitHub App; then raise this to 1.
- **`check` must pass, branch up to date.** `check` is the CI job name. When the isolation suite gets its own job (#26), add it here.
- **`enforce_admins: true`.** Otherwise the owner, which is also the identity the agents use, bypasses everything.
- **No force pushes, no deletion.**
- **Linear history off.** Stacked pull requests are merged with merge commits.
- **Conversation resolution off.** The reviewer leaves many inline threads; requiring each to be resolved by hand would block merges for no gain.

Also turn on "Automatically delete head branches": with stacked pull requests GitHub then retargets the next one to `main` by itself.
