author: gablooge
text:
Built in #43 (commit 89a22ba, CI green). The checklist line is demonstrated there, against the schema compiled with and without format assertion.

**What was done**

- `internal/record`: Go types for the envelope, `Validate`, `Seal` (the only way to a record id), strict `MarshalJSON` and `UnmarshalJSON`, `ScopeID` and `ParseScopeID`, and the JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) as `internal/record/record.v1.schema.json`, embedded.
- ADR 3 (scope id format) and ADR 4 (format v1). Architecture sections 1, 5, 6, 8 and 12, the roadmap table, the ADR index, the backlog and the README are updated.
- The Go side and the schema refuse the same things, held together by about 250 documents, 46 Go values, 1,500 random records and a fuzz target. 19 mutations were run and each one failed a test.

**What differs from the proposal in architecture section 6**

1. A `format` field (`"sluiceway.record/v1"`) carries the version. The proposal had none.
2. `meta.raw_ref` is dropped: it pointed into a raw payload store the design does not have. `meta` may be absent and is not part of a record's content.
3. `delete` is part of the schema now, with its shape defined (a tombstone with empty `title` and `text`), because `op` is a closed set and a value that is only reserved could never be added without a new format version. v0.1 never sends one.
4. `visibility` is closed. Every other object ignores unknown fields. Field names are lowercase only.
5. **The scope is hashed into the record id**, which changes the recipe of B02 (`ids.RecordID` takes the scope, golden vectors regenerated and re-verified with Python `blake3`). A record that moves to another scope is then a new record even when the provider's version did not change with the move. With the old recipe the ledger would skip it and the sink would keep the old scope, silently.
6. The scope id's first segment is the internal provider key, never the wire name, so `source` and the scope need not match. The container id is percent-escaped into one canonical spelling. The tenant is not part of it.
7. Meanings made exact: `version` is opaque to a sink and its monotonicity is the normalizer's promise, which the format cannot check. `edges.reply_parent` is an `external_id`, not a record id. `author.id` is the raw provider user id, and access is never decided on it. `occurred_at` is always UTC with `Z`, years 1000 to 9999.
8. A record carries its scope and never the scope's members. The README and goal 2 of the architecture said otherwise and are corrected. The membership message and the person identifier are left to B23 and B24 on purpose (issue #36).

**Left for the maintainer and for later items**

- The schema `$id` (`https://gablooge.github.io/sluiceway/schema/record/v1.json`) is a name under a host the maintainer controls. It freezes with v0.1.0, so it needs a confirmation or a replacement before then.
- The five kinds freeze with v0.1.0. B18 (HubSpot) is the last item that can add one without a new format version.
- B09: the strict stub has to add the two checks no schema can make (a record that supersedes itself, a field name used twice in one object), and compare content without `meta`.
- B08 and B11: a normalizer must move `version` on every change the provider reports, a move included. Moving from A to B and back to A with an unchanged provider version still yields the first id again. ADR 4 documents that and does not solve it.
- B16 and B17: check the 512 byte limit of a scope id against recorded Microsoft Graph ids. It was reasoned, not measured.
title: Comment on issue #5

author: gablooge
text: Carried over from the round 3 review of #31 (B03), for the ingress edge: the database pool is at pgx defaults, `max(4, NumCPU)` connections, so 4 on a small container, shared by every in-flight webhook. Each accept holds a connection for the resolve and the insert. Decide the expected concurrency, size `pool_max_conns` for it (it works in the URL today), and make a saturated pool answer fast with a retryable status, never a hang. Also from #30: put `http.MaxBytesReader` in front of `ids.DeliveryID`, which hashes whatever it is given.
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 3 fix of #32 (B04). The outbox API changed, and this item builds on it:

- Failures are reported with a `Cause`, never with text: `outbox.NewCause(Class).WithStatus(n).WithCode(s)`, passed to `Fail(ctx, c, ladder, cause)` or `MarkDead(ctx, c, cause)`. There is deliberately no way to pass an error string from a remote system, because `err.Error()` of a `*url.Error` quotes the request URL, query-string API key included, and `last_error` is a plain column. A new kind of failure means adding a `Class`. `WithCode` stops accidents, not a caller who passes a bare secret as the code: pass only provider or sink error codes.
- `Claimed` is read-only: `ID()`, `Tenant()`, `Attempt()`.
- `Accept` refuses an ordering key over 512 bytes with `ErrBadOrderingKey`. That is poison, not a server error: park it and answer 2xx, never 5xx (a provider would retry-storm).
- `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` now take the per-key advisory lock and promote the next row, so they wait for an open `Accept` or `Replay` of the same key. Keep accepting transactions short, and never do network I/O inside one.
- The claim is a stored head marker (`docs/adr/0010-outbox-head-marker.md`). Never insert into `outbox` except through `Accept`: a row written without the marker into a key with no head is never delivered.
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text: From the delta review of #32, for the ingress edge: `outbox.Delivery.Provider` must be a constant from the provider registry, never text from the request. `net/http`'s `PathValue` decodes `%00` in `/ingress/{provider}` to a NUL byte (verified), and `Accept` refuses an unstorable provider with an error that is deliberately not a sentinel, because it treats a bad provider as a program bug. So: look the path segment up in the registry first, answer an unknown provider with 404 before anything else happens, and pass the REGISTRY's key to the outbox, not the path segment. Add to acceptance: `/ingress/%00` and `/ingress/<500 random bytes>` answer 404 and store nothing.
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text:
The public webhook tunnel now exists and was tested end to end on 2026-09-19.

- URL: a Cloudflare Tunnel on the maintainer's machine. The hostname is deliberately not written down in this repository, because publishing it invites traffic to a developer machine; it is in `~/.config/lawang/tunnel.env` as `LAWANG_TUNNEL_HOSTNAME`.
- Start it on demand (the token travels in the env file, never on a command line):

```sh
docker run --rm --name sluiceway-tunnel \
  --env-file ~/.config/lawang/cloudflare-tunnel.env \
  cloudflare/cloudflared:2026.9.1 tunnel --no-autoupdate run
```

- Cloudflare forwards ONLY `^/ingress/[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}$` to `http://host.docker.internal:8080` and answers 404 itself for everything else. Checked from the public internet: `/ingress/ping` 200, a POST to `/ingress/clickup` arrives, and `/healthz`, `/v1/...`, `/ingress/../x`, `/ingress/%2e%2e/x`, `/ingress/a/../../x`, `/ingress/a/b`, `/ingress/` and `/INGRESS/x` all get 404. With the container stopped the hostname answers 502.
- A first attempt with a plain `^/ingress/` prefix let `/ingress/../secret.txt` through to a server that normalizes paths. Do not loosen the rule.
- Consequences for the code: the service must listen on port 8080 where the Docker host can reach it (the default `:8080` works); a provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}` (put that in the provider registry, with a test); the ingress handler must still treat every request as hostile, since the tunnel is only a second line.
- Wanted from the item that first uses it: a `make tunnel` target with exactly the command above, and a line in the setup guide saying to stop the container and deregister the webhooks afterwards.

Rules for the credentials: "Credentials for live verification" in `CLAUDE.md` (arrives with #34).
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text:
**Correction to my earlier note on this issue.** I wrote that a provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, taken from the first tunnel routing rule. That contradicts ADR 3 (from #43), which freezes the provider segment of a scope id as `[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}`: lowercase letter first, no hyphen, at most 32 characters. **ADR 3 wins.** A registry that accepted `ms-graph` would produce records that all fail in `Seal`.

The tunnel now enforces the same grammar: Cloudflare forwards only `^/ingress/[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$`. Retested from the public internet on 2026-09-19: `/ingress/clickup` and `/ingress/ms_graph` arrive; `/ingress/ms-graph`, `/ingress/9lives`, `/ingress/Slack`, a 33 character key, `/ingress/../x` and `/healthz` all get 404 at Cloudflare.

For the provider registry: validate a key against ADR 3's grammar at registration, by calling the function in `internal/record` that owns the rule and not by copying the pattern, with a test.
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text:
Done in #47 (commit `04459d8`), CI green.

**What landed.** `internal/provider` with `Provider`, `WebhookSource` and the registry; `internal/ingress` with the edge; `internal/provider/fake`, a strict test double that later items' tests can import.

**The decisions on this issue, and how each is honoured:**

- **ADR 3's grammar, from the function that owns it.** `NewRegistry` calls `record.ValidProviderKey`, which is new here: it is the `validName` the package already had, exported, and the three places in `record` that meant "a provider key" now call it too, so there is one owner. `TestTheRegistryCannotDriftFromTheRecordFormat` asks both about every byte in the first and in a later position of a key and fails if they ever disagree. `ms-graph`, `9lives`, `Slack` and a 33 character key are all refused.
- **`outbox.Delivery.Provider` is a constant of the program.** The edge looks the path segment up first and answers an unknown provider 404 before a byte of the body is read, and everything downstream gets the registry's own key. Two tests hold it: one proves the registry ignores a provider whose `Key()` answers differently on a second call, and one compares the string data pointers of `Entry.Key()` and the string the lookup was made with, since today they hold the same bytes and only their identity tells them apart. `/ingress/%00` and `/ingress/<500 bytes>` answer 404 with the hub never called, along with a NUL inside the segment, a capital, a hyphen, a newline, a slash, a space, the empty segment and a registered provider that is not a `WebhookSource`. A separate test pins that `PathValue` really does decode `%00` to a NUL byte, so the note here does not go stale silently.
- **`http.MaxBytesReader` in front of anything that hashes or reads the body.** It is the first thing the read does after the length check, and its bytes are the only ones anything downstream sees. A body with no end is cut at the cap and answered 413 inside a deadline, which is the test that proves it is not accumulated.
- **Pool sizing.** `store.Open` still leaves pgxpool at `max(4, NumCPU)`, which is right for v0.1 (an accept holds one connection for a few milliseconds, so four to eight are hundreds of deliveries a second). What changed is what happens past that: the accept is bounded at 2 seconds, an order of magnitude over the 200 ms target, and a pool that makes an acquire wait past it answers **503 with a `Retry-After`** rather than holding the provider's connection until its client calls it an outage. `pool_max_conns`, `pool_min_conns` and `pool_max_conn_lifetime` are documented in the `LAWANG_DATABASE_URL` usage text and in architecture 4.
- **`ErrBadOrderingKey` is poison, not a server error.** `ingress.Parked` is 200, and there is no path from a verdict to a 5xx.

**What differs from the design.** Nothing that `docs/architecture.md` does not now say, since the document changed in the same branch: the response-code table and the accept-path detail in 3.1, the pool paragraph in 4, the registry and "what lands when" in 7, `provider/fake/` in the layout in 8, four rows in the failure table in 11.

The one deliberate departure worth naming: **`Registrar`, `Reconciler` and `MemberSource` are not written yet.** All three take types that later items decide (`Subscription` is B07's, `Credential` is B13's and B14's, `Cursor` is B19's, `ScopeMembers` is B23's), and an interface written before its types are settled is a shape every later item rewrites, at a cost that is not free once a provider package implements it. Architecture 7 records which item brings which.

**Left for B07.** The seam is `ingress.Hub`, one method: `Accept(ctx, provider.Entry, body []byte, h http.Header) (Verdict, error)`. It gets the registry entry (so `p.Key()` is the key to store), the exact bytes and the headers. `serve` does not mount the edge yet, because an edge with no hub would answer a provider without storing anything, so `ingress.New` refuses a nil hub and B07 does the wiring with `ingress.Pattern` and `Mount`.

**Worth remembering.** Two mutations survived the first pass and both were test defects, not code defects: the fast path on an honest `Content-Length` masked an off-by-one in the cap until a body of unknown length was tested, and the fake's event fixture happened to re-serialize to itself byte for byte, so a provider that re-serialized its payload would have passed. Both fixtures are now spelled so they cannot flatter the code. 26 of 26 mutations caught in the end.
title: Comment on issue #6

author: gablooge
text:
Carried from the round 1 review of #47 (B06), for the hub:

- **`Verify` is called once per candidate subscription**, so the loop must survive a provider implementation that misbehaves. Architecture 7 says `Verify` never errors and never panics, but nothing enforces that: a panic in one candidate must not take down the accept path, and a slow one must not hold the request open past its bound. Decide whether the hub defends itself here, and test it with a deliberately panicking and a deliberately slow fake.
- **The 503 on a saturated pool** currently rests on `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)`. That is right today. When this item runs real queries, a server-side cancel arrives as SQLSTATE 57014 instead, so also treat `ctx.Err() != nil` as the retryable case.
- **`Handshake` parses unauthenticated bytes on the accept path for every delivery**, before any tenant is known. Keep it cheap and bounded, and make sure a handshake hook cannot be made to do work proportional to the body.
- **This item must add `Registrar`** when it defines `Subscription`. Architecture section 7 now records which item brings which interface, deliberately leaving out the ones whose types are not decided yet.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 1 review of #47 (B06), so the three notes that belong to the hub are not lost when that pull request merges. All three are recorded in `docs/architecture.md` section 7 as well, under "Three things a provider author has to know", so they survive even if this comment is not read.

**N1. The 503 rests on `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)`, and the hub can break it without touching `internal/ingress`.** The reviewer ran a real saturated pool (`pool_max_conns=1`, 8 concurrent deliveries, a hub holding `SELECT pg_sleep(1)`): 7 acquires returned `context.deadlineExceededError` and the one already in a query returned `*pgconn.errTimeout`, and `errors.Is` is true for both, so the edge answers 503 with a `Retry-After` and `store.scrub` does not eat it. The shape that would **not** match is a statement cancelled server side, which comes back as a `*pgconn.PgError` with SQLSTATE 57014 ("canceling statement due to user request") and no context error in its chain. That lands on the `err != nil` branch and answers 500 with an error line, where 503 with a `Retry-After` is the honest answer. Cheap insurance: treat `ctx.Err() != nil` after the call as the deadline case too, not only the error's own chain.

**N4. `Handshake` parses unauthenticated bytes on the accept path, for every delivery and not only for a challenge.** That is inherent to the hook, since a challenge arrives before any subscription exists and nothing can tell the two apart beforehand, and the 200 ms target has room. But it is the one place where a stranger's bytes drive real work before verification, so the guidance a provider author needs is: look at a cheap discriminator first (a header, a query parameter, the first field) and only then parse. Slack and Microsoft Graph both allow this.

**N5. "`Verify` never errors and never panics" is documented and cannot be enforced.** A panic there is recovered per connection by `net/http` and the provider sees a dropped response rather than a status. B07 is where it matters, because `Verify` runs once per candidate subscription: recover around the per-candidate loop, so one provider's panic parks a delivery instead of dropping the connection.

**And one thing #47 changed that B07 inherits.** The seam is now `Accept(ctx, provider.Entry, provider.Request) (Verdict, error)`, where `provider.Request` is `{Method, URL string; Header http.Header; Body []byte}`, and `WebhookSource.Verify(r provider.Request, secret []byte) bool` takes the same value. `Request.URL` is the **public** URL, built from `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` plus the request path and query, never from a header, and it is empty when nothing is configured: a scheme that signs the URL must return false rather than guess. The hub hands the value straight through to `Verify` per candidate.

Also worth a line when metrics land (B25): a counter of unknown-segment 404s belongs next to the warn line #47 adds for a registered provider that is not a `WebhookSource`, so the same mistake spelled in the URL instead of in the wiring is visible too.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
From B06's round 2 review (#47), two things for this item.

**Refuse to start when a registered provider's scheme needs the public URL and none is configured.**
`ingress.New` now warns when `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is unset, naming the variable and saying that a scheme covering the URL will answer 401 for every delivery. That is the cheap half. The real fix belongs here, because the edge does not know which providers a deployment registered or which of their schemes cover the URL, and the hub does: a deployment with a URL-signing provider registered and no base URL configured cannot accept a single delivery, so it should refuse to start rather than answer 401 (the status the contract reserves for a forged signature) on a provider's dashboard where nobody reads it. Architecture 4 says this now.

**How the hub mounts the edge.** `ingress.Handler.Mount(mux)` returns an `http.Handler`, and that returned handler, not the mux, is what belongs in `http.Server.Handler`. It is the mux with a guard in front of it that refuses a path `net/http.ServeMux` would otherwise clean and redirect: over a real socket `//ingress/fake` and `/ingress/fake/../fake` answered 307, and a 307 preserves method and body, so a provider re-POSTs to a path it did not sign and every delivery becomes a 401 that reads as a forgery.

**Also, from the same review, for the per-candidate loop:** `provider.Request.Header` is now a read-only `provider.Header`, so an implementation cannot change what the next candidate reads, and no cloning is needed in the loop. `Verify` still has to be called inside a recover, per architecture 7.

And, carried from round 1: when metrics land (B25), a counter of unknown-segment 404s belongs next to the warn line for a registered provider that is not a `WebhookSource`, so the same mistake spelled in the URL instead of in the wiring is visible too.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
Two more from #47 (B06) that this item must not miss:

- **`Mount` returns the handler you must use.** Its signature is now `func (h *Handler) Mount(mux *http.ServeMux) http.Handler`, and the returned handler wraps the mux to refuse a non-canonical path. Write `srv.Handler = ingressHandler.Mount(mux)`, not `srv.Handler = mux`. Mounting the mux you passed in silently reintroduces the defect it exists to prevent: `net/http.ServeMux` answers `//ingress/x`, `/ingress//x` and `/ingress/x/../x` with a **307 and `Location`**, a 307 preserves method and body, so the provider re-POSTs, the edge signs the cleaned path while the provider signed the original, and every such delivery becomes a 401 that reads as a forgery.
- **Refuse to start when a provider's scheme needs the public URL and none is configured.** `ingress.New` only warns, because it does not know which schemes sign the URL. This item does know, since it wires the registry. Without the check, an unset `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` means every delivery of a URL-signing provider is 401 with nothing else to see.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
Two notes from the round 3 review of #47 (B06), recorded here because the hub is the caller that decides both. Neither is a defect in B06.

**1. `provider.Request.Body` is a rule, not a guarantee.** It is a `[]byte` handed out by value that aliases the edge's own capture buffer. `Verify` runs once per candidate subscription with the same `Request`, so an implementation that normalized the bytes in place (trimming a byte order mark, lower casing, blanking a field before hashing) would change what every later candidate verifies **and** what the hub then stores in the outbox. The symptom would be the one `provider.Header` was built to close, a signature that fails for the second candidate only, except that this one also changes a stored record.

The edge cannot fix it: it builds one `Request` and has no candidate loop. The per-candidate loop is this item's, so this is where a copy would go. It is cheap: copying the slice measures **0.9 us for an 8 KiB delivery and 57 us at the 1 MiB cap** (Apple M5 Pro, 18 GB/s), against an accept path that targets 200 ms with no provider I/O. Ten candidates at the cap is 0.6 ms, 0.3% of the budget, so cost is not the reason to skip it.

Two ways to close it, and the choice is this item's:

- copy `req.Body` per candidate in the loop, which makes it a guarantee and costs the microseconds above;
- or keep the rule and prove it in the hub's tests, by hashing the body before and after each candidate and failing the test if a provider moved a byte.

Architecture 7 and the field's doc comment now say plainly that it is a rule, so nothing reads as a promise the type does not keep.

**2. `provider.Header` is a live view of the request's map, not a snapshot.** `NewHeader` keeps the `http.Header` it is given rather than cloning it, so anything that writes to that map after the wrapper is built is visible through `Get` and `Values`. It is correct today, because the edge passes `r.Header` and `net/http` does not touch it once the handler is called, and `NewHeader`'s doc comment says the caller must not write to it afterwards.

It matters here because the hub is the next thing to build a `provider.Request`. If it ever builds one from a map it keeps and then writes to (adding a resolved value, normalizing a name), the wrapper stops being the guarantee that architecture 7 says it is. Either build the `Request` from a map nothing else holds, or clone at that call site.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
One more from the review of #47, and it is the same failure mode the `Mount` removal existed to close, so it is worth knowing before you wire anything.

**A nested `*http.ServeMux` passed as a `Route.Handler` brings the trailing-slash redirect straight back.** Registering `{GET, "/v1/", sub}` where `sub` holds `GET /v1/x/` answers `GET /v1/x` with **307 `Location: /v1/x/`**, proven over a real socket. `ingress.New` cannot see inside a handler, so its guard does not apply, and the provider (or in this case the operator's client) re-requests against a path the edge then treats differently.

So when the `/v1` operator API arrives: give `ingress.New` one `Route` per endpoint rather than one `Route` holding a sub-mux. If a sub-mux ever becomes worth it, it needs the same non-canonical-path guard in front of it, and a socket test that no route answers with a `Location` header.

This is pre-existing rather than a regression, and it is recorded here because B07 is the first caller.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text:
Done in #48 (CI green).

`internal/hub` resolves a delivery in five steps: delivery keys (bounded and held to storable text
here rather than trusted, and a delivery with none is parked rather than looked up), candidates
under `lawang_resolver` in a transaction that does nothing else and commits before anything is
verified, per-candidate verification over the exact bytes, owner resolution, then the accept under
`TenantTx`. Nothing short-circuits on the first candidate that verifies, because "exactly one"
cannot be told from "the first of two" without asking them all.

Every point on this issue was taken, and here is what was decided where the issue left a choice:

1. **Two transactions.** The resolve is `store.RoleTx(resolver)` and commits; the accept is a
   second transaction under `TenantTx`.
2. **`ingress.New` returns the handler.** `cmd/lawang`'s `newMux()` is gone, `/healthz` is an
   `ingress.Route`, and there is no sub-mux anywhere.
3. **Refusing to start.** `hub.New` refuses when a registered provider implements the new
   `provider.URLSigner` and `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is unset. The usage text for that variable
   says so now.
4. **`Verify` runs once per candidate, and the hub defends itself.** A panic is recovered and a
   `Verify` that does not return is given up on at the accept's deadline. Both **park** the
   delivery rather than route it: a candidate that did not answer cannot be ruled out as the owner.
   Tested with a deliberately panicking and a deliberately blocking fake, the second with a
   deadline of its own so a regression fails rather than hangs.
5. **`Request.Body` is copied per candidate**, so the rule becomes a guarantee. It is also what
   stops a `Verify` that was given up on from writing to the same bytes the accept is storing,
   which under `-race` is a real data race and not only a wrong answer.
6. **`provider.Header`** is passed straight through; the hub builds no header map of its own.
7. **`Registrar` and `Subscription` landed**, with `URLSigner`. `Credential` is declared opaque,
   the way `Hydrated` is, because B13 and B14 decide what a credential holds.
8. **`ctx.Err() != nil` is the retryable case**, so SQLSTATE 57014 reaches the edge as a 503 with a
   `Retry-After` and not a 500.
9. The method-less subtree refusal is untouched and still waits for B08.

**What differs from the design**, all written into `docs/architecture.md` in the same branch and
recorded as [ADR 11](https://github.com/gablooge/lawang/blob/b07-hub/docs/adr/0011-hub-resolution.md):

- **The webhook verification secret is a column of the `subscriptions` table, not a vault entry.**
  `Vault.Fetch` is keyed by `(tenant, provider)` and the accept path derives the tenant *from* the
  secret, so that interface cannot serve this path at all. It is also a different credential: it
  proves a delivery came from the provider and authenticates nothing to it. The API tokens stay the
  vault's (B13), and `lawang_resolver` is granted `SELECT` on six columns of one table and no write
  of any kind.
- **The sentinel tenant is `_parked`**, refused as a tenant by a CHECK on the `tenants` table, and
  `outbox.Park` takes no tenant parameter at all, so there is nothing for a crafted delivery to
  influence. Five fixed `dead_reason` texts, which B25 re-resolves by.
- **An accepted delivery is ordered by the subscription it arrived on.** The hub does not parse a
  delivery and so cannot name an entity. Coarser keeps the guarantee and costs parallelism: one
  subscription's deliveries drain one at a time, which for ClickUp is one queue per workspace per
  tenant. Narrowing it belongs with B08 and B11.

For B25: parked rows carry `dead_reason` in {no owner, ambiguous owner, unreadable delivery, the
provider's verification panicked, the delivery cannot be stored}, and the first two are the ones a
subscription registered later can settle. The metrics note carried on this issue (a counter of
unknown-segment 404s next to the warn line for a registered provider that is not a `WebhookSource`)
is still open and still belongs to B25.
title: Comment on issue #7

author: gablooge
text: From B05 (#43), for the pipeline: the normalizer contract in ADR 4 is that `version` moves on EVERY reported change, a move between containers included, because the record id hashes the scope too. One case is documented and not solved: an entity moved from A to B and back to A with an unchanged provider version yields the first record id again, which the ledger would skip. The supersede and ledger stages are where that case either gets handled or gets a test that pins the documented behaviour. Check the review of #43 for whether the format changes to cover it.
title: Comment on issue #8

author: gablooge
text: From the review of #43, a requirement on the ledger stage that ADR 4 now states: an entity moved from scope A to B and back to A with an unchanged provider version recreates its FIRST record id. The ledger must not skip it silently, because then the sink keeps the record in B: B's members keep what they lost access to, A's members never regain it, and nothing reports it. The case is detectable: the incoming id is already in the ledger, it is not the head of its entity's supersede chain, and the head's scope differs from the incoming record's scope. Dead-letter or count it, and say what an operator does then. Also: supersede chains are linked per (tenant, provider, external_id), never per scope, or a moved record leaves a stale copy behind. And a DEGRADED record (hydration failed) must derive the same scope the hydrated one would, or one version of one entity gets two ids.
title: Comment on issue #8

author: gablooge
text:
From the review of B05 (pull request #43, commit 8bd35e3), a requirement on the ledger stage. It is written down in ADR 4, decision 7 ("What remains: A, B, and back to A"), where it is marked **decided by default, the maintainer may overrule**. If the maintainer overrules it, that ADR changes first.

**The case.** The record id hashes the scope, so a moved entity is a new record. But an entity moved from scope A to B **and back to A**, with a provider version that changed at neither move, produces the first record's id again. A ledger that only asks "have I delivered this id" skips it, the sink keeps the record in B, B's members go on reading what they lost access to, A's members never get it back, and nothing reports an error.

**The requirement.** The ledger must detect this and never skip it silently. Per entity (tenant, provider, `external_id`) it holds the head of the supersede chain and the scope of that head. An incoming record for which all three hold:

1. its id is already in the ledger,
2. it is not the head of its entity's chain,
3. the head's scope differs from the incoming record's scope,

is **dead-lettered with a reason of its own and counted in a metric**. It is not skipped and not delivered. A repeat of the head fails condition 2. A late re-send of an old version fails condition 3, because a record hydrated at drain time carries the scope the entity is in now. What passes all three is an entity that moved back, or a stale degraded record from the old scope, and the ledger cannot tell which, so it does not guess. ADR 4 says what an operator does with such a dead letter.

**Three related things B08 should meet knowingly** (same ADR section):

- The supersede chain is linked per (tenant, provider, `external_id`), not per scope, so that a moved record names what it was in the old scope and the sink replaces it.
- A degraded record (built from the webhook body when hydration fails) must derive the same scope as the hydrated one would, through the same function. Otherwise one version of one entity gets two ids, is delivered twice, and looks like a move. Where the webhook body does not carry what the scope is made of, the record cannot be degraded: retry or dead-letter, never a guessed scope.
- Delete then restore with an unchanged version yields the pre-delete id and is skipped. That fails closed, the scope check above cannot see it, and only the normalizer rule (a restore changes the version) protects it. v0.1 sends no deletes, so this belongs to the item that ships them.

Also from B05: a record whose `ID`, `ExternalID`, `Version` or `Visibility.Scope` is changed after `record.Seal` cannot be marshalled (seal again instead), `ids.RecordID` may not be called outside `internal/record` (a test fails), and `Supersedes` and `Source` may be set after sealing.

author: gablooge
text:
From the review of #7 (PR #48), note 1, with the number filled in.

B07 makes an accepted delivery's ordering key `{provider key}:{subscription id}` (ADR 11, decision 3). The guarantee holds: an entity's versions all land in one key, `outbox_one_head` is per `(tenant_id, ordering_key)`, and a coarser key serializes strictly more than a finer one. The cost is throughput, and it is measurable rather than theoretical.

One subscription is one queue, so for ClickUp, which registers one webhook per workspace, one workspace per tenant drains **one delivery at a time**. At a sink round trip of 150 ms that is about 6.7 deliveries a second for a whole workspace, whatever the worker count, and a workspace busier than that backs up permanently.

The hub cannot make the key finer: naming an entity needs `Parse`, which runs here, on verified bytes, and one delivery can carry several entities. The way out, if this becomes the limit, is for a provider to name its entity cheaply from bytes it has already looked at, the way `DeliveryKeys` does, and for the hub to append it to the key. That is a change to one function and one interface, and it wants a measurement from this item or from #11 before it is worth making.
title: Comment on issue #8

author: gablooge
text:
Built in #49, on `b08-pipeline`, stacked on `b07-hub` (B07 is approved and not merged yet).

`internal/pipeline` is step 5 of the drain path. It is two calls, not one, because hydration talks
to a provider's API and the ledger holds a transaction: `Normalize` parses, hydrates, normalizes and
drops automation noise outside any transaction, `Prepare` does the ledger, the supersede chain and
the masker inside the transaction the worker will commit. The decisions are in ADR 12.

**All six notes carried onto this issue are answered.**

- **A, B and back to A** is dead-lettered with an error of its own (`ErrScopeReturned`) that names
  the tenant, the provider, the entity and both scopes, and counted, exactly as ADR 4 decision 7
  states it. The rule also catches A, B, C, B. Both paths the round 2 review asked for are tested:
  the dead-letter path, and the pruned path, where retention has removed the first record and the
  case becomes an ordinary supersede. That also fixes what retention may never prune, which is a
  head, and it is written into ADR 12 for B25.
- **Equal provider versions are ordered by arrival**, which leans on the outbox's per-entity FIFO.
  That is said in the code and in ADR 12, and tested. The stage does not rely on it alone: it takes
  a transaction-scoped advisory lock on (tenant, provider, external id) before it reads the chain,
  for the paths the ordering key does not cover.
- **The chain is keyed per (tenant, provider, external_id)** and never per scope. A ledger row means
  PREPARED, never merely seen, so a record that was skipped or held back is not written: writing it
  would make a later legitimate arrival of that version look already delivered.
- **The degraded record's scope** is now a stated contract, `provider.Degrader`: the same inputs
  through the same function the hydrated path uses, and `provider.ErrCannotDegrade` where the body
  does not carry what the scope is made of, which retries rather than guesses. The pipeline cannot
  enforce it (it never holds both paths' output for one record), so it is proved for the fake twice,
  directly on the sealed ids and through the ledger.
- **`record.SealedFor`** is asked here and nowhere else, against the tenant of the outbox row, and a
  false is a dead letter.
- **Ordering-key throughput** (the note from #48) is unchanged by this item and is still B11's or
  #11's to measure.

**What differs from the design**, both called out in the pull request:

- the ledger bounds `external_id` at 2,048 **bytes**, where the format bounds it at 1,024
  characters (which can be 4,096 bytes, and a btree tuple cannot hold that). Refused by name as
  `ErrExternalIDTooLong`. If a provider ever mints one that long, the format's own limit should
  become a byte limit in a v2;
- a title or text that **masking** makes longer than the format allows is a dead letter rather than
  something silently cut.

Docs changed in the branch: architecture 3.2, 5 and 7, ADR 12 and the ADR index, the roadmap's
open-decisions table, the README status paragraph, and the backlog.

Left for the items that own them: the outbox row of a dead letter and its `outbox.Cause` classes
(B10), the Prometheus counter for the A, B, A case (B25), and the store that lets a `prepared` row
be re-drained without being prepared again (B10, which owns the crash test).

author: gablooge
text: Carried over from the round 3 review of #32 (B04), for the sinks: never pass a raw error string from a remote system into the outbox's failure columns. `err.Error()` of a `*url.Error` quotes the whole request URL, including a query-string API key, and `last_error` is a plain column. The outbox API is being changed in #32 so that a cause is built from a classification and safe fields (status code, provider error code) and cannot be built from an arbitrary string. The http sink must classify its errors into that shape. Add to acceptance: a sink URL containing a marker secret never appears in any outbox column or log line after a failed delivery.
title: Comment on issue #9

author: gablooge
text:
Carried over from the round 3 fix of #32 (B04). The outbox API changed, and this item builds on it:

- Failures are reported with a `Cause`, never with text: `outbox.NewCause(Class).WithStatus(n).WithCode(s)`, passed to `Fail(ctx, c, ladder, cause)` or `MarkDead(ctx, c, cause)`. There is deliberately no way to pass an error string from a remote system, because `err.Error()` of a `*url.Error` quotes the request URL, query-string API key included, and `last_error` is a plain column. A new kind of failure means adding a `Class`. `WithCode` stops accidents, not a caller who passes a bare secret as the code: pass only provider or sink error codes.
- `Claimed` is read-only: `ID()`, `Tenant()`, `Attempt()`.
- `Accept` refuses an ordering key over 512 bytes with `ErrBadOrderingKey`. That is poison, not a server error: park it and answer 2xx, never 5xx (a provider would retry-storm).
- `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` now take the per-key advisory lock and promote the next row, so they wait for an open `Accept` or `Replay` of the same key. Keep accepting transactions short, and never do network I/O inside one.
- The claim is a stored head marker (`docs/adr/0010-outbox-head-marker.md`). Never insert into `outbox` except through `Accept`: a row written without the marker into a key with no head is never delivered.
title: Comment on issue #9

author: gablooge
text:
From B05 (#43, the record format), for the sinks:

- The strict stub must add the two checks no JSON Schema can make: a record that supersedes itself, and a field name used twice in one object. `internal/record`'s strict decoder already refuses both; the stub should decode with it.
- When the stub compares a repeated id against what it stored, compare content WITHOUT `meta`, which is not part of a record's content.
- `source` is replaced with the sink's configured wire name on the way out. The scope id is NOT rewritten: its first segment stays the internal provider key, because it is the join key with the membership message (ADR 3). A sink treats the scope as opaque, and `source` and the scope's first segment need not match.
title: Comment on issue #9

author: gablooge
text:
From the review of #43 (the record format), for the sinks:

- **Nothing in the format bounds a document.** The largest VALID record is about 12.6 MB from a foreign producer, and about 6.3 MB from Sluiceway itself (`json.Marshal` writes `<`, `>` and `&` as six byte escapes). Unknown fields are allowed and unbounded. The sink's own body limit is the only bound: the `http` sink must set a request size it will send, the stub must set one it will accept, and both must be documented for sink authors. Measured on the strict decoder: a 4.9 MB document with 300,000 unknown fields is accepted in 212 ms and allocates 169 MB (about 35 times its size). Put the body limit BEFORE the decoder.
- **`supersedes` cycles across records** cannot be seen by validating one record. A sink that walks the chain needs a visited set, and the strict stub should show how.
title: Comment on issue #9

author: gablooge
text: From the round 1 fix of #43: the strict stub now has THREE checks beyond the schema, not two: a record that supersedes itself, a field name used twice in one object, and the byte rule (a document is valid UTF-8 with no unpaired surrogate escapes, checked on the raw bytes before parsing). Decoding with `internal/record`'s strict decoder gives all three.

author: gablooge
text: From the delta review of #43: a sealed `record.Record` and the same record decoded from its own document are NOT equal under `==` or `reflect.DeepEqual`, because only the sealed one knows its tenant, although both marshal to identical bytes. The strict stub compares a repeated id against what it stored: compare DOCUMENTS (without `meta`), or field by field, never `Record` values. Mixing a sealed and a decoded record would refuse a legitimate repeat (loud, never a wrong acceptance). It is now stated on `SealedFor`'s doc comment.

title: Comment on PR #47

author: gablooge
text:
Round 2 notes, in b64f6af. Three done, the rest are replies.

### N2 (done). `Request.Header` is no longer a map

`Request.Header` is now `provider.Header`, a struct wrapping the request's own map with `Get` and `Values` and nothing that writes. Not a comment, and not a clone either, because **a clone does not fix this**: the hub hands the *same* `Request` to `Verify` once per candidate, so a per-request clone would be one map shared by every candidate and the second candidate would still read what the first one wrote. The mistake has to be off the table, not made cheaper.

You asked for the number anyway, so: cloning the header of a realistic delivery (ten fields: Host, User-Agent, Content-Type, Content-Length, Accept-Encoding, two Slack signature headers, two X-Forwarded headers, a Cf-Ray) is **365 ns/op, 904 B/op, 4 allocs/op** (Apple M5 Pro, Go 1.26.7, `-benchtime 2s`). Cheap, as you said. It buys nothing here, and the wrapper costs one method call that inlines away and zero allocations, so I did not commit a benchmark of a clone the edge does not do.

`Values` returns `slices.Clone` of the values, since that slice is the one thing a caller could write to. `DeliveryKeys` takes the same type rather than an `http.Header`, for the same reason one step earlier: the hub calls it before the per-candidate loop, so a `Del` there would change what every `Verify` after it sees. The zero `Header` reads as a request with no fields rather than panicking, because a `Request` built by hand in a test must not be a trap.

`TestAHeaderCannotBeUsedToChangeWhatTheNextCandidateReads` writes to what `Values` returned and asserts the next read is unchanged, and that the request's own map is unchanged too. Mutation: `Values` returning the live slice, caught ("a candidate changed what the next one reads: `["tampered" "second"]`").

`Handshake` still gets the live `*http.Request`, deliberately: it runs once, before anything else, and needs the URL and the query. Architecture 7 carries the whole argument as a fourth bullet under "Three things a provider author has to know".

### N1 (decided, recorded on #15). No receive timestamp, and B15 adds it

Decision: **not now, in B15**, and the reasoning is the asymmetry between the two shapes of change. Widening `Verify` from three arguments to a struct had to happen before B07, B11 and B15 implemented it, because it breaks every implementation; adding a field to a struct breaks nothing and costs its author nothing, which was the whole argument for making `Request` a struct. Against that, a `ReceivedAt` here today has no reader and no test that could give it teeth beyond "the edge sets it", and an unused field on a type three items will build on is how a field ends up meaning whatever the first implementation assumed.

So it lands with the first scheme that has a replay window, which is B15 (Slack's five minutes), and #15 now carries the ask with your argument for it: an implementation that calls `time.Now()` inside `Verify` makes the window untestable without smuggling a clock into the provider, so the field, and the decision about whose clock it is, belongs with that item.

### N4 (reply). The normalizer stays in `internal/config`

I thought about the move and left it, for three reasons.

The cycle you are worried about needs `config` to import `ingress`, and the only thing that would make it do so is `config` wanting `ingress.DefaultMaxBody` on the day `LAWANG_MAX_BODY` exists. It will not need it: `Options.MaxBody` already documents 0 as "the default", `ingress.New` applies it, and a `config` that parses an int64 and leaves 0 alone never names the constant. The same is true of `AcceptTimeout`. So the edge that would close the loop is one we have a reason not to draw.

Against that, the move costs either a package for one function or a `config` that imports `internal/provider`, which is a stranger direction than the one we have (configuration depending on the provider layer). And the value really is a configuration variable: someone asking what `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` accepts finds its rules next to every other variable's, which is where they will look first.

If `config` ever does need something from `ingress`, the move is mechanical and the property test moves with it. Happy to be overruled, but I do not want to spend a package on it today.

### N6 (done as well). The 307 with a cleaned path in a `Location`

This turned out to be the same defect as finding 2 rather than a B07 note, so it is fixed here: nothing on this service answers a 3xx any more, and the package comment's "no path segment reaches a log line or a response" is true of the route as mounted, not only of the handler.

### N3, N5, N7, N8

N3 and N5 are answered inline. N7 needs nothing, and thank you for re-running it. N8: the disjunct is gone, and why it was unreachable is written down in the property test instead of in a guard nobody can trip (inline on the blocking finding).

### Round 1's N2 (the chunked body's 2x `MaxBody`)

Still unchanged and still a note. At the 1 MiB default a chunked body costs at most 2 MiB before `MaxBytesReader` stops it, which is the `bytes.Buffer` doubling and not a leak, and `maxPrealloc` keeps an announced length from reserving more than the cap regardless. The day an operator raises `MaxBody` to something where 2x matters is the day to read exactly `MaxBody+1` bytes into a sized buffer, and that day is a one line change with a test that already exists.

text:
Replies to the four notes, for the record. Everything in them is answered; only N3 changed code.

**N1 (`provider.Header` is a live view, not a snapshot).** Agreed, and it is a B07 concern rather than a B06 defect, for the reason you give: the edge passes `r.Header`, which `net/http` does not touch once the handler runs. Recorded on #7 (comment above), together with the forward-looking half of finding 5, since the hub is the next thing to build a `Request` and the two notes have the same shape: a guarantee that holds because of who the caller is today.

**N2 (`Header.Get` has no production caller yet).** Left as it is, on your own argument: it is the read half of a two-method API whose named user is B15's `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp`, and `Values` has a production caller. An API with `Values` and no `Get` would have every provider writing the same index-zero dance.

**N3 (an empty fragment is dropped rather than refused).** Not changed, and now pinned. `https://x#` is accepted because `url.Parse` gives it an empty `Fragment`, while `https://x#f` is refused. It is idempotent, harmless, and the answer is the one the operator meant, so it stays deliberate rather than becoming a refusal. It is not in the table as a row of its own, but the property test covers the shape; if you want a row I will add one in a delta.

**N4 (round 1's, the 2x `MaxBody` on a chunked body).** Unchanged and still a note. `bytes.Buffer` doubles before `MaxBytesReader` stops the read, so a chunked body can cost 2 MiB of transient allocation at the 1 MiB default before it is refused. It is transient, it is bounded, and it is not a leak. The item that raises `MaxBody` for a provider with large payloads (a `LAWANG_MAX_BODY`, if it ever exists) is where this becomes worth an explicit `Grow` with a bounded hint, because the multiplier is what matters and not the constant.

text:
## The three notes, in `581b862`

**N1, the duplicate-pattern pre-check.** I agree with your reading: the behaviour is identical, because `mux.Handle` panics on the second registration and the `recover` produces an error that also names the pattern. So there is no input that tells the branch from its absence, and a test asserting the better message would be asserting my own wording, not a behaviour. ### Should-fix 10: nothing pinned that the helper roles have no grants

Fixed. `internal/store` has `TestHelperRolesHoldOnlyTheGrantsTheDesignNames`, next to `TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity` and guarding every future migration the same way.

It asks Postgres for the **whole** privilege surface of `lawang_resolver` and `lawang_worker`: every table in the schema, crossed with all seven privileges, through `has_table_privilege` OR `has_any_column_privilege` (the two grants in the schema today are column-level, and only the second sees one; DELETE, TRUNCATE and TRIGGER exist only on a whole table, which is why it is both and not one). Anything not on the allowlist fails, and anything on the allowlist that is missing fails too, so a query that returns nothing at all cannot pass. The allowlist is three entries with a reason each: the resolver's SELECT on `subscriptions`, and the worker's SELECT and UPDATE on `outbox`.

Your point was that nothing keeps it true, so the mutation is a migration: adding `GRANT SELECT (token, kind, value) ON redaction_map TO lawang_worker;` to `00004_pipeline.sql` fails the test with `lawang_worker may SELECT redaction_map, and nothing in the design says it should`. (Worth recording: my first attempt at that mutation appended the GRANT after `-- +goose Down`, so it never ran and the mutation survived for a reason that had nothing to do with the test. Moving it above the marker killed it.)

### Note 11: the PR description's claim about RLS as a second lock

You are right, and the description said something the tests do not support. The case the test covers (a record sealed for A, delivered under B, with `tx` and `tenant` both B) has no second lock at all: `SealedFor` is the only thing standing there, which makes it more important than the description implied. The PR body now says that, and says that RLS only catches the different case where the `tenant` argument and the transaction's binding disagree, which no test covers.

### Note 12: lock keys sorted by `external_id`, hashed by `hashtextextended`

Not acted on, agreed on the reasoning. Sorting by the hash would make the argument airtight and I would rather not change the lock's sort key in a review round on a branch three items deep in the stack: the order is total and stable today, and the collision needs a pair of 64-bit collisions across two tenants. Recorded on #10 together with the second half of your note, which is the more useful one: B10 will hold the outbox ordering-key lock and then take entity locks in the same transaction, in the same single advisory-lock namespace, and that cross-module order is written down nowhere. Both are on that issue now.

### Note 13: `apply` panics on overlapping spans

Gone with should-fix 8. The method is unexported now and `findSecrets` is the only producer of a scan inside the package, so the precondition has no reachable caller. I left it as a precondition rather than adding a check, for the reason you gave: adding one would be adding a branch no input can take.

### Note 14: `ErrMaskedTooLong` fires for a whole class, not only a title cut to the limit

Taken, as wording. ADR 12 decision 5 now says a placeholder is 34 characters replacing something between 6 and 21, so any field that is more than roughly 62% short secrets by length outgrows the limit whatever its size, and adds that realistic content is nowhere near that ratio. The framing was misleading about which inputs die here, which is what a reader would act on.

### Note 15: `closingIssuesReferences` empty while the base is `b07-hub`

Nothing to do, agreed. It will resolve when the stack lands on `main`.

### Mutations run this round

Each applied alone to `46148fd`'s parent tree, run, then restored.

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | `compareVersions` is plain byte order again (the round 1 rule) | killed (4 tests, including your reproduction) |
| M2 | the "no order" refusal never fires, two unorderable versions guessed by bytes | killed (2) |
| M3 | decimal counters compared by bytes instead of by their number | killed (3) |
| M4 | the placeholder is `sha256(tenant, kind, value)` (your R17) | killed |
| M5 | the placeholder is `sha256(kind, value)`, unsalted (your R18) | killed (2) |
| M6 | `validPhone` is the round 1 digit count only (IPv4 becomes a phone token again) | killed (2) |

No survivors this round. Your R1 (condition 2 of ADR 4 decision 7) stays where it was: equivalent, marked at the line, and left alone as you confirmed.

text:
## Round 2 addressed: 4a33432, b539cfc

Both blocking findings are closed in code, not in prose, and the description is rewritten where it
was now wrong (decision 1, decision 7, Acceptance, Testing, and a new "Review round 2" section
with the mutation table). CI is green on b539cfc.

**Blocking 1** is closed by taking the inference out. `provider.VersionOrder` is a **required**
method of `provider.Provider`, validated once at registration (`ErrNoVersionOrder`), whose zero
value orders nothing; `compareVersions` does only what was declared. Decimal and base64 are
**proved** (a digit run is checkable, and base64 is decoded under one alphabet to one width);
lexical is the provider's **promise**, with the fixed width checked and every encoding that would
break it named on the contract. Your reproduction is now
`TestABase64CounterIsOrderedByWhatItDecodesTo`, in both directions. All four places in ADR 12 say
this, and decision 3 states the one residual that is **not** closed: a provider author declaring
lexical for an encoding that is not in byte order. That is not closable inside B08, and the record
says so rather than claiming otherwise for a third round.

**Blocking 2** takes your suggestion exactly: one delivery, both rows deleted as the superuser,
**the same delivery** drained again, and an assertion that the two drains really are identical so
the test cannot decay back into varying an input. The property is one sentence at the top of it.

All six should-fix items and both notes are done, each with a reply on its own thread. Note 9 is
carried to #10.

**Thirteen mutations this round, no survivor** (table in the description). The two you named are
both dead: `USING (true)` on `redaction_map` is killed by the new predicate pin and by the new
behavioural test, and a `meta.delivery`-salted digest is killed by the rewritten placeholder test
alone. Mutation 22 from round 1 is still equivalent and still marked at the line.

I have not touched any `review:*` label: the verdict is yours.

I looked for the usual ways such a test goes wrong and found none. The port is ephemeral on loopback, so there is no collision. Every wait is bounded (5s for the log line, 3s client timeout, 5s for the return, 10s context over all of it). The polling loop is a bounded retry and not a timing assumption: nothing depends on how long 10ms is. `t.Cleanup(cancel)` stops the role on every `Fatalf` path, the `exit` channel is buffered so the goroutine never blocks after the test has gone, and the role logs into a locked buffer and never into `t`, so a late log line cannot panic the test. The JSON match on `Msg` and `Addr` relies on `encoding/json` being case-insensitive for field names, which is documented behaviour.

### `migrate bootstrap` after the merge

I did not review the later branch. I only computed the merge in memory (`git merge-tree --write-tree origin/b04-outbox HEAD`, clean, nothing checked out) and read the merged `run`: the later branch's `migrate` case sits in the first switch and returns before the new check is reached, so this commit does not make `migrate bootstrap` unreachable. Two things the merge-forward has to carry, as the implementer already says: the `migrate` row of `TestRunRefusesExtraArguments` expects a message the merged code no longer prints, and the first sentence of the `refuseArguments` comment ("No command takes an argument") stops being true.

### Pull request description

Rewritten and accurate against `7b3a2ee`. I checked each round 3 row of its mutation table against my own runs and they agree, including the two "only" claims (C1 and E1).

### Notes

1. **The usage comment claims more than the tests enforce** (`cmd/sluiceway/main.go:37`, "the text cannot drift from what Load does"). Names and defaults are tied, and the ties have teeth (A1 to A11, A13). Accepted values are not: they are prose in `Variable.Doc` and again in each `Load` error message, and A12 (a third log format accepted) leaves every test green with the help text wrong. Cost: low today, since both lists are short and sit in one file. No action needed here; it matters the first time a variable gains a value.
2. **"Development falls back to the local compose database"** (`internal/config/config.go:64`) points at something that does not exist until **B27**. Hiding the password is right, but host, port and database name are not secret, and without them an operator in development still has to read the source to learn where the process will connect. For B27, or sooner if cheap: say `localhost:5432, database sluiceway` in words.
3. `help` is not in the `Commands:` list of the usage text, although it is a command and is named in the exit code rules. Cosmetic.

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 1

**Verdict: changes requested**

The core of this is sound. The three acceptance lines of #3 each have a real test, run as the plain `sluiceway` role, and the tests that guard the transaction-local binding, `SET LOCAL ROLE`, `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and the pinned `search_path` all have teeth (mutations below). What does not hold up is the membership half of the preflight: it counts good `pg_auth_members` rows instead of asking Postgres whether the application role inherits a helper role, so it can be passed while inheritance is in effect, it can refuse a correct setup, and no test exercises it at all.

**Findings:** 2 blocking, 2 should-fix, 1 note. Details inline.

**Acceptance (#3)**
- No tenant bound returns zero rows: `TestNoTenantBoundReturnsZeroRows`, `TestNoTenantBoundRefusesWrites`. Proven.
- Tenant A cannot read tenant B's row: `TestTenantCannotReadOrWriteAnotherTenant`. Proven.
- Migrations run and re-run as the non-superuser role: `TestMigrationsRunAndRerunAsTheNonSuperuserRole`, which asserts who it is connected as. Proven.

**Mutations run** (each against `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/store/`, then restored)
1. `set_config(..., true)` to `false` in `tenancy.Bind` (session-level binding): killed by `TestNoTenantBoundReturnsZeroRows` and `TestTenantBindingDoesNotOutliveItsTransaction`.
2. `SET LOCAL ROLE sluiceway_worker` to `SET ROLE sluiceway_worker`: killed by `TestHelperRolesAreEnteredExplicitlyAndLeftAtCommit`.
3. Deleted `ALTER TABLE tenants FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`: killed by six tests, as the description says.
4. Removed the `search_path` runtime parameter: killed by `TestHelperRolesAreEnteredExplicitlyAndLeftAtCommit`.
5. Disabled both `case unsafeHelpers > 0` and `case memberOf != 2` in the preflight: **survived, the whole package stays green.** See the blocking comment on `store.go`.

**Probes** (throwaway test against a private Postgres 17 container, deleted afterwards): the three scenarios in the inline comments were each reproduced against `store.Open` as written, not reasoned about.

**`make check`** on the head commit: green (tidy, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race` with the integration tests running, not skipped).

**Note (no action required):** `TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity` looks at `relkind IN ('r','p')`. A materialized view cannot have row-level security at all, so a future `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` over a tenant table would pass this guard while exposing every tenant to whoever can read it. Worth adding `'m'` (and failing on any) when the first one is proposed.
title: Review on PR #31 (commented)

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 2

**Verdict: approved**

Reviewed `baf52f2` on top of `0e7f6a0`. Nothing blocking remains. Both blocking findings of round 1 are fixed and the fix is pinned by tests that fail under the mutations that used to survive. Two new should-fix findings inline, neither of which makes this unsafe to merge, and a few notes below.

**Round 1 findings**

1. **blocking, preflight passes while a helper role is inherited (`store.go`): resolved.** I re-ran both of my reproductions against `store.Open` on this commit, with the B04-style `GRANT SELECT` and `FOR SELECT TO sluiceway_worker USING (true)` policy in place. The indirect `ops` path and the second-grantor `INHERIT TRUE` row are now both refused with `ErrUnsafeRole` and a message that names the helper. `pg_has_role(helper, 'USAGE')` is the right question: it is `has_privs_of_role`, the same function Postgres uses to decide whether a policy's `TO role` applies and whether a privilege is held, so it cannot disagree with what a plain transaction can actually see. I also checked the converse, a path whose near edge is `INHERIT FALSE` and whose far edges inherit: accepted, and a plain `Tx` sees no rows, which is correct.
2. **blocking, helper checks untested: resolved.** Round 1 mutation 5 repeated (all three helper checks disabled): now killed, seven of the eight table cases fail.
3. **should-fix, `memberOf != 2` refuses a correct two-grantor setup: resolved.** Rows are no longer counted. The "two grantors, every membership correct" case and the four-row assertion in `TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin` cover it.
4. **should-fix, bootstrap fails for a `CREATEROLE` admin: resolved**, with one leftover about the revoke, inline. The script is one `DO` statement, so the borrowed grant, the roles and the schema commit or roll back together; an uncommitted membership row is invisible to every other session, so there is no window in which anyone else can use it. The failure path is proven by the 42501 case leaving zero roles behind. Verified by hand on Postgres 16.15 as well as 17.11, since CI only runs 17.
5. **note, relkind `m`: resolved**, `m` and `f` are covered.

**Mutations run** (each restored with `git checkout -- .`)

1. All helper checks disabled in `preflight` (round 1 mutation 5): **killed**, 7 cases of `TestOpenRefusesUnsafeHelperRoles` fail.
2. `pg_has_role(h.oid, 'USAGE')` replaced by a direct `pg_auth_members` lookup with `inherit_option` (the natural wrong simplification): **killed**, by exactly the intermediate-role case.
3. `REVOKE sluiceway FROM CURRENT_USER` removed from the bootstrap: **killed** by `TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin`.
4. `borrow := true` (always grant and revoke, ignoring whether the admin already had `SET`): **survived**, `./internal/store/` and `./cmd/...` stay green. See the inline comment on `roles.sql`.

**Probes** (throwaway test on a private cluster plus SQL against scratch Postgres 16 and 17 containers, all deleted afterwards)

- `ALTER ROLE sluiceway SET role = 'sluiceway_worker'`, and the same through `options=-c role=...` in the URL: `Open` refuses. The preflight reads `current_user`, which is the effective role a plain `Tx` would run under, so this is the right identity to test. (`SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION` needs a superuser, which is refused first.)
- `ALTER ROLE sluiceway SET row_security = off`: `Open` succeeds, and every query on a tenant table then fails with `query would be affected by row-level security policy` (42501), in a plain `Tx` and in a worker `RoleTx`. Postgres errors, it does not bypass. Fails closed.
- `pg_read_all_data` and `pg_write_all_data` granted to the login, `pg_read_all_data` to the resolver: accepted, and both still see zero rows with no tenant bound. Those roles give privileges, not `BYPASSRLS`, and role attributes are never inherited, so the safety of the application role does not depend on what the helper roles are members of. A reverse grant (`sluiceway` to a helper) is refused by Postgres as circular.
- An extra `ADMIN`-only membership from a second grantor: accepted, no rows visible. But see the inline comment on `store.go`.
- Schema `sluiceway` already present and owned by another role: see the note below.

**Notes (no action required)**

- **The preflight runs once, at `Open`.** A grant changed by an administrator while the process runs is not seen until the next start. I consider this an accepted limit and not a finding: the preflight is a guard against misconfiguration, anyone who can change memberships can also set `BYPASSRLS` or read the tables directly, and re-checking per transaction would cost a round trip for no defence against that actor. The one case where the actor is not an administrator is the `ADMIN OPTION` comment inline.
- **A schema that exists with a different owner is silently accepted** by `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS` (unchanged from round 1), the preflight only checks that the schema exists, and the first failure is `Migrate` saying `failed to create version table "goose_db_version": ERROR: no schema has been selected to create in (SQLSTATE 3F000)`. Reproduced. It fails closed and I found no isolation consequence (tables are still created and owned by the application role if the owner grants `CREATE`), so this is only about the operator being pointed at the wrong thing. Comparing `nspowner` with `current_user` in the preflight would turn it into a clear refusal.
- The private-cluster helper removes its container in `t.Cleanup`, also when the container started but never became ready, and the testcontainers reaper covers a killed process. I saw no leftover containers from my runs.

**`make check`** on `baf52f2`: green (tidy, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race` with the integration tests running against Docker, not skipped).
title: Review on PR #31 (commented)

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 3 (supplementary sweep)

**Verdict: needs maintainer.** 2 blocking, 8 should-fix, 5 notes.

Rounds 1 and 2 covered the preflight, memberships, ADMIN OPTION, the bootstrap and RLS, and I did not redo them. This round applied the wider checklist (test comprehensiveness, wider security, performance, dead code, improvement, documentation) to `f9d9ee3`. The core is still sound: every Go-level probe I could think of for the transaction helpers came back clean. What I found is one leak of URL parts into the log, one test case with no teeth, and a doc comment that states something about isolation that Postgres does not do.

**On the label.** Both blocking findings have small, mechanical fixes and nobody has disagreed about them. The label is `review:needs-maintainer` only because this is the third round and the cycle is capped at three; whether to run one more implementer pass is the maintainer call, not mine. Finding 1 also has a real decision inside it (should a connect error name the host), which CLAUDE.md currently answers with no.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | the three Done-when lines of #3 against their tests (unchanged since round 2), plus the whole store suite on Postgres 16.15, the documented minimum that CI never runs: green | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | mutations M1 to M3 below | 1 blocking (M1); M2 and M3 feed other findings |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of `store`, `tenancy`, `testdb`, `cmd`; error paths and early returns; panic and cancellation on a one-connection pool; Open against refused, unresolvable, blackholed and wrong-password targets; Postgres 15; the Down section | 2 should-fix (the list below, and the version check inline) |
| Correctness | `pgx.BeginFunc` rollback on panic, pool release of a non-idle connection, `Migrate` on `pool_max_conns=1`, preflight precedence on a never-bootstrapped database | 0 |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | isolation spot-checked only (rounds 1 and 2); ordering not applicable, there is no queue in this diff; secrets: every error path of `Open` through the real binary | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix (touches isolation) |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | every SQL string built by concatenation (bootstrap `format` with `%I` and booleans, `testdb` database name from a ULID, constant password); `current_tenant()` is not SECURITY DEFINER and the policy references it by OID, so search_path gives it nothing to escalate; `tenant_id` regex anchoring including a trailing newline; test passwords; the new dependencies are the ones in architecture section 12 and testcontainers is not linked into the binary. `govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so it was not run | 0 |
| Performance | EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of the policy on 200,000 tenants; pgbench of role entry plus bind; pool defaults read from pgx v5.11.0; connect timeout measured; per-test timing | 2 should-fix, 3 notes |
| Dead code | searched callers of every new exported identifier, on this branch and on `origin/b04-outbox` | 1 should-fix |
| Codebase improvement | Go rule versus SQL domain, sentinels, the shape of `RoleTx`, comments against behaviour | 1 should-fix, 1 note |
| Documentation | architecture sections 4 and 12, ADR 1 and 2, `roles.sql` header (followed by hand on a fresh 16.15 database: works as written), README status, backlog tick and log, roadmap table, godoc, PR description | 1 should-fix, 1 note |

Standing rules: no `Co-Authored-By` or other attribution trailer on any of the five commits, and no em dash in the diff.

**`make check`** on `f9d9ee3`: green (tidy, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race` with the integration tests running, not skipped).

### Mutations (each restored with `git checkout -- .`)

- **M1** `tenant_id` domain `{1,64}` to `{0,64}` (accepts the empty string): **survived**, all three changed packages green. Blocking, inline on `store_test.go`.
- **M2** the URL parse error wrapped with `%w` instead of replaced: **survived** `TestOpenNeverEchoesTheURL`. pgx redacts the password, which is the only thing the test looks for. Part of blocking finding 1.
- **M3** the Postgres version check disabled: **survived**, `./internal/store/` and `./cmd/...` green. Should-fix, inline.

### Probes (a throwaway test file and scratch containers, all deleted)

- Panic inside `RoleTx` after `Bind`, pool of one: the next transaction on the same connection is `sluiceway`, no tenant, zero rows. Clean.
- Context cancelled before commit, and cancelled while a statement is in flight (`pg_sleep`), pool of one: `RoleTx` and `TenantTx` return the context error (in 301 ms for the in-flight case), and the next transaction runs on a new connection, because pgxpool destroys a connection that is released outside the idle state. Clean, no role or tenant survives.
- `sluiceway migrate` on Postgres 15: refused with `Postgres 16 or newer is required, server reports 150019`; the bootstrap fails there with a syntax error at `INHERIT`. Correct, and untested (M3).
- The documented flow on a fresh Postgres 16.15: `migrate bootstrap` piped to `psql`, the ALTER ROLE password step, `migrate` (1 applied), `migrate` (0), and again with `pool_max_conns=1` (goose holds the lock and migrates on one connection, no deadlock).
- The Down section run by hand as the application role inside a transaction: all four statements succeed and leave nothing behind.
- EXPLAIN as the application role, 200,000 rows: `Index Scan using tenants_pkey` with the inlined `NULLIF(current_setting(...))` expression as the Index Cond, 4 shared buffers, 0.04 ms, for SELECT and UPDATE, bound and unbound. The SQL function is inlined and the domain does not get in the way of the index. No finding.
- Go rule versus SQL domain on 15 boundary strings (trailing and leading newline, CR, tab, accented and fullwidth letters, 64 and 65 characters, empty): they agree on all of them today.

### Findings that are not on a line

**should-fix, tests that are missing for code that is correct today.** Named cases, not a percentage:
1. `migrate` in `cmd/sluiceway` has 0% coverage: nothing runs the command end to end (exit 0 and the count, exit 1 as a superuser); it was smoke-tested by hand only.
2. The connect-failure path of `Open` has no test at all, and it is where blocking finding 1 lives.
3. Panic and cancellation on a pooled connection. I probed both and they are clean, but the property rests entirely on pgx internals (the deferred rollback in `BeginFunc`, and the pool destroying a non-idle connection), so a pgx upgrade or a move away from `BeginFunc` could leave a role or a tenant on a reused connection with a green suite. Two short tests on `pool_max_conns=1` would pin it. This one touches isolation.
4. The Down section is never executed by any test, and no command exposes it. It works today; it will rot as B04 onwards add migrations. Either an up, down, up test, or a line in ADR 2 saying Down is not supported.
5. CI runs Postgres 17 only, while 16 is the documented minimum and the reason for it (`WITH INHERIT FALSE`) is version-specific. I ran the suite on 16 by hand: green. Making the image overridable and adding 16 to the CI matrix would keep it that way.

**should-fix, documentation.**
- README still says "There is no runnable code yet". That stopped being true with B01 on the base branch, so this diff did not break it, but after this PR an operator can bootstrap and migrate a real database, and the status paragraph is the first thing a reader sees.
- The PR description is still the text of the first submission. It does not mention what rounds 1 and 2 added: the `pg_has_role` preflight, the ADMIN OPTION refusal, `ErrSchemaNotOwned`, the CREATEROLE path with the borrowed and restored membership, or `NewRawCluster`.

### Notes (no action here)

- **For B10 (worker drain):** `RoleTx` plus `Bind` costs two extra round trips per transaction. pgbench on 16.15 puts the server side at 0.030 ms for `SET LOCAL ROLE` and 0.034 ms for `set_config`, so the cost is the network: about 1 ms at a 0.5 ms round trip, under 1% of the 200 ms accept budget. `BEGIN`, the role and the binding can go out as one pgx batch if a per-row re-bind ever shows up in a profile. Not worth doing now.
- **For B10 as well:** see the inline comment on `RoleTx`. The safe shape for per-tenant work after a claim is a second transaction under `TenantTx` (the backlog line for B10 already says two transactions), not a `Bind` inside the helper role.
- **For B06 and B10:** `Open` leaves the pool at the pgx defaults: `max(4, NumCPU)` connections, no minimum, 1 h lifetime, 30 min idle, 1 min health check. On a 1 or 2 CPU container that is 4 connections shared by the webhook edge, or by every drain goroutine. It is tunable today through `pool_max_conns` and friends in the URL, which works (I used it) but is written down nowhere; B28 should document it and B10 should size the drain pool against it.
- **For B04 onwards:** the policy is index-friendly only when the table has an index that leads with the tenant column. `tenants` has its primary key; every later table needs one.
- **For B27 and B28:** `psql` exits 0 when the piped bootstrap fails unless `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` is given, so a scripted bootstrap followed by `migrate` does not stop at the failure (it fails closed at `migrate` with `ErrNotBootstrapped`, so this is only about where the operator is pointed). And the ALTER ROLE password line in the header, run through `psql -c`, puts the password in shell history and in the server log under `log_statement = ddl`; the quickstart should suggest the psql `password` meta-command instead.
