author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 1

**Verdict: changes requested**

Two blocking findings, both small to fix: the tests of the scope id's canonical form survive three mutations of the property they exist for (inline, `scope_test.go`), and the strict decoder accepts a document that is not valid UTF-8 and silently rewrites an identity in it (inline, `decode.go`). Everything else is should-fix or a note. One point is a product decision for the maintainer (the A, B, A move), and I say below why I think the format can ship with it as long as the pipeline does not stay silent about it.

Head reviewed: 89a22ba. `make check` green locally (tidy, sqlc diff, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`, Docker up, no SKIP in the changed packages). CI `check` passes. Coverage of `internal/record` and `internal/ids` is 100 percent of statements. `govulncheck` is not installed here, so it was not run. The one new dependency (`santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`) is test-only and `go list -deps ./cmd/sluiceway` does not contain it.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | each part of the one "Done when" line against its test, against the SCHEMA compiled with and without format assertion, and again with an independent validator (Python `jsonschema` 4.26) | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 19 schema mutants, 13 scope pattern mutants, 24 Go mutants, listed below | 1 blocking |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage, boundaries, astral characters, invalid UTF-8, lone surrogates, hostile documents | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix |
| Correctness | decoder state machine, timestamp parser, scope parser bounds, Seal order, Go against schema by 51 million fuzz executions | 0 beyond the above |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | tenant never in the envelope, tenant and scope in the id, move cases worked through, errors never quote values | 1 should-fix (needs the maintainer) |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | control and bidirectional characters, hostile documents measured, scope id in URLs, `origin.untrusted`, `external_id` uniqueness, supersede cycles | 4 should-fix, 2 notes |
| Performance | benchmarks re-run, all four numbers reproduce; hostile documents measured | 1 note |
| Dead code | callers of every exported identifier | 0 (no production caller yet, as with `ids` after B02, stated in the description) |
| Codebase improvement | the `ids` and `record` boundary | 1 should-fix |
| Documentation | ADR 3 and ADR 4 statement by statement, architecture 1, 5, 6, 8, 12, roadmap table, ADR index, backlog tick and log line, README, PR description, every other place that might still say a record carries members | 2 should-fix |

### Independent validator

Python `jsonschema` 4.26.0, `Draft202012Validator`, with and without `FormatChecker`. The schema passes `check_schema`. The section 6 example and all six golden files validate. 64 bad records, 62 refused both ways, among them every case that leans on the dollar anchor in Python's dialect (a trailing newline on `id`, `supersedes`, `source`, `kind`, `container.kind`, `visibility.scope`, `occurred_at` and on a field name), a Kelvin sign and a capital in a field name, Arabic-Indic digits and U+2028 in `occurred_at`, lowercase hex, a redundant escape, an escaped NUL and DEL, a raw colon, 513 bytes. The two accepted are February 30 and February 29 of a common year, which is what the ADR says the pattern cannot catch. Worth knowing: on this machine Python's `FormatChecker` has no `date-time` checker at all (`rfc3339-validator` is not installed), so "format assertion on" silently checks nothing there. The pattern is what holds, and it does. Length counting agrees for astral characters (1,024 emoji in `title` accepted, 1,025 refused, 1,048,576 emoji in `text` accepted) and for combining sequences (counted as code points) in Go, in the Go validator and in Python. I ran the same 75 documents (the 1 MiB astral text aside) through the Go decoder and the Go validator: no disagreement with Python on any of them.

Where the two pipelines do disagree is below the schema: a document with a raw invalid UTF-8 byte. See the inline finding on `decode.go`.

### Golden vectors

Recomputed with Python `blake3` 1.0.9 from the recipe in the file's comment: 12 of 12 `delivery_id` and 10 of 10 `record_id` vectors match. The id in the architecture example is vector 1 (`tenant_a`).

### The design decisions

**1. The scope in the record id: I sign it, and the residue needs the maintainer.** The argument is right: with the old recipe a move with an unchanged provider version is the ledger's "already delivered", silently. What I worked through:

- *A to B.* New id, and no stale copy in A as long as the ledger links the supersede chain per (tenant, provider, external_id) and not per scope, so the moved record names the old one. ADR 4 and the schema description of `supersedes` both say so. That is a requirement on B08 and should be on its issue.
- *A to B and back to A, provider version unchanged.* `id(A, v)` is the first id again, the ledger skips it, the sink keeps the record in B. B's members keep a record they lost, A's members do not get it back, and nothing reports an error. That is the original bug again, and undoing a move is the most likely reason for a second move. It also cannot be fixed at the sink: even if the ledger let it through, a sink is idempotent on `id` and would drop it, and the first record would have to supersede the second, which supersedes the first. Only a version that moves can express it.
- *Should the format carry something now (a move counter, the previous scope)?* I do not think so. `version` is opaque to a sink, so the fix can arrive after v0.1 inside v1: the normalizer derives the version from the move event, or the pipeline folds a counter it keeps in the ledger into `version`. Neither re-keys a record already delivered. So the format does not paint itself into a corner here.
- *What I ask for:* ADR 4 says "the ledger skips it" and stops. The ledger can tell this case from a late re-send with state it needs anyway: the computed id is known, it is not the head of its entity's chain, and the head's scope differs from the incoming record's scope. A late re-send of an old version, hydrated at drain time, carries the scope the entity is in now, which is the head's scope (a degraded record built from an old webhook body is the exception, and it deserves the same attention). That case must not be a silent skip (dead-letter it, or at least count it). See the inline comment on ADR 4. Whether a documented leak of this kind is acceptable in a public contract is the maintainer's call.
- *An edit and a move in one event:* the version moves, fine. *Two tenants:* the tenant is hashed, vectors 1 and 2 differ, fine. *Same class, other direction:* a delete followed by a restore with an unchanged version yields the old id and is skipped, so the entity stays deleted at the sink. That fails closed, but the scope check above does not see it, so the normalizer rule is all there is for it.
- *A cost the ADR does not list:* a degraded record (hydration failed) must derive the same scope as the hydrated one would, or one version of one entity gets two ids and is delivered twice. Note for B08 and B11.

**2. The `format` field: I sign the field, not yet the promise.** The list of what forces v2 has a hole that two people would argue about. See the inline comment on ADR 4 ("a limit tightened"). The closed `kind` is livable: the issue's own acceptance line demands that an unknown kind is refused, and v0.1.0 (M6) comes after all five providers (M3), so the set freezes with all five built. After that, a sixth provider that needs a new kind costs every sink a v2, including the sinks that never look at `kind`. That is a price knowingly paid.

**3. The scope id grammar: I sign it.** I could not find two strings with the same parts, a string that parses two ways, or parts that cannot be encoded apart from the documented refusals. `FuzzParseScopeID` ran 60 seconds here, 26 million executions, no failure. Python agrees with the Go parser on every bad scope I tried. The 512 bytes hold for Graph: with `outlook:mailfolder:` in front, 164 bytes of id fit even if every byte needs escaping, a 160 character base64 id with padding comes to 199 bytes, and to 475 bytes in the impossible case that all 152 characters were plus, slash or equals. A 400 character realistic id still fits (469), a 480 character one is refused, loudly. "The first segment need not equal `source`" is defused well enough: the schema says it on `source`, the architecture table says it, and "opaque, compare for equality" is repeated everywhere. Two things are wrong around it: the tests of the canonical form (blocking, inline) and the claim about URLs (inline on ADR 3).

**4. The rest.**

- *`delete` as a tombstone now:* signed, the reasoning (a closed `op` cannot grow) is right. It exposes a gap: the uniqueness domain of `external_id` (inline on the schema).
- *`visibility` closed, everything else open:* signed.
- *Lowercase `propertyNames`:* signed. I verified the Kelvin argument against `encoding/json`: `{"kind":"task","<U+212A>ind":"evil","id":"a","ID":"b"}` decodes to `kind="evil"`, `id="b"`, and a long s in `source` lands in the `source` field too.
- *`meta.raw_ref` dropped:* signed.
- *Strict `UnmarshalJSON`, duplicates refused:* signed. Refusing a duplicate name is right for a decoder a sink may reuse, for the reason given (validator keeps the first, consumer keeps the last). 23 microseconds and 485 allocations per record is about 43,000 records per second per core, which is far above what a sink behind an HTTP call will see. The decoder has one hole: invalid UTF-8 (blocking, inline).
- *Caps in characters:* Go and the schema count the same thing, code points, also for astral characters and combining sequences, in three validators. The test table only has two-byte characters (inline, should-fix).
- *`occurred_at`, no leap second:* signed. `time.Time` cannot hold second 60 and `time.Parse` refuses it, so a normalizer meets the problem before the format does. Such an event is not lost: it is a normalizer failure, which architecture section 11 dead-letters with a reason, and it can be replayed after a fix. Note for B11 and every provider after it: clamp second 60 to 59 when parsing provider times.

**5. "A record carries only its scope, never its members."** I searched the README, the architecture, the roadmap, the backlog and the code for every other place that implies members travel in a record. None is left. Principle 3 ("salt the record id with the tenant") is still true as written.

### Mutations and probes

All applied in my detached worktree, tests run, file restored with `git checkout`.

Schema mutants, all caught unless marked: `scope` not required in `visibility`; `kind` any string; `occurred_at` without its pattern (caught without format assertion too); without pattern and companion; `visibility` opened; `propertyNames` removed at the top, and in `author`; `title` 1,025; NUL allowed in `text`; `origin.untrusted` not required; the scope's companion pattern removed; `supersedes` any string; the tombstone rule removed; `meta.delivery` 129; `reply_parent` 1,025; `format` any string; `audience` open; `source` 65; year 0999 allowed; leap second allowed.

Scope pattern mutants, one per branch of the escape alternation: escaped digit, escaped uppercase letter, `%7E`, `%7F`, `%2D`, `%5F`, control bytes, a 33 character provider and kind, all caught. **Survived:** lowercase hex in the high-byte branch (`%c3%a9`), an escaped lowercase letter (`%61`), a provider that starts with a digit.

Go mutants, all caught unless marked: `RecordID` without the scope (6 tests fail); decode without presence checks; without the null check; `visibility` not closed; field names unchecked; duplicates let through; only nested duplicates refused; timestamp spelling unchecked; bytes instead of characters; off by one on the character count; non-UTC accepted; invalid UTF-8 in a Go value accepted; self-supersede accepted; NUL allowed in content; lowercase second hex digit; escaped DEL; Seal without the namespace check, without the tenant check, without the source check; Marshal without Validate; empty `Ref` accepted. **Survived:** the scope parser accepting an escaped lowercase letter (`%61`). **Equivalent, proves nothing:** `second > 60` in `validTimestamp`, because the `time` package refuses second 60 right after it.

Fuzz: `FuzzDecodeAgreesWithSchema` 200 seconds, 51 million executions, no disagreement. `FuzzParseScopeID` 60 seconds, 26 million, none.

Benchmarks re-run, all reproduce: Validate 175 ns and 0 allocations (example), 6.5 microseconds (20 KB), 0.26 ms (1 MiB); Marshal 2.35 microseconds, 7 allocations; Unmarshal 23.2 microseconds, 485 allocations.

Hostile documents through the strict decoder (one `json.Unmarshal` each): 300,000 unknown top-level fields in 4.9 MB: accepted, 212 ms, 169 MB allocated in 5.1 million allocations. One unknown object with 300,000 keys, 4.9 MB: accepted, 150 ms, 114 MB. An 8 MB unknown string: 75 ms, 59 MB. Nesting 9,000 deep: accepted, under 3 ms. Nesting 10,001 and 2,000,000 deep: refused in 0.1 ms by `encoding/json`'s depth limit. The largest valid `text` written as escaped astral characters is a 12.6 MB document: accepted, 129 ms, 92 MB allocated. Everything is linear in the input, nothing is quadratic, and the amplification is about 35 times the document size in allocations for the many-fields case.

### Notes (no action here)

- **B09:** nothing in the format bounds a document. The largest valid record is about 12.6 MB on the wire from a foreign producer, and about 6.3 MB from Sluiceway itself (`json.Marshal` writes `<`, `>` and `&` as six byte escapes, so 1,048,576 of them is six times the text). Unknown fields are unbounded. The `http` sink and the stub need a body limit chosen with those numbers in mind, and the decoder's cost above is per document, so the limit is the only bound.
- **B09:** `supersedes` cycles across records (A names B, B names A) cannot be refused by a format that sees one record at a time. A sink that follows the chain needs a visited set. The strict stub is the place to show it.
- **B11 and every provider:** second 60 in a provider timestamp, see above.
- **Sink documentation (B28):** Python's `jsonschema` checks `date-time` only when `rfc3339-validator` is installed and otherwise accepts everything without a warning. The `$comment` in the schema says "assert formats if your validator can"; a sentence that the pattern is the real guard would stop a sink author from feeling safer than they are.
- **Standing rules:** no trailer on the commit (asked git's trailer parser), no tool attribution and no em dash in the diff, the commit message or the description. No control, invisible or look-alike characters in any changed file: the only non-ASCII characters are deliberate test data and the middle dot in two headings. I can confirm the tool problem the description mentions: my own probe files had their Unicode escapes turned into literal characters by the write tool, a NUL among them.

text:
## Review, round 2

**Verdict: approved.** No blocking finding. 2 should-fix, 5 notes. Both should-fix items are cheap today and contested after v0.1.0, and one of them (the character test survives four drift mutants) is of the kind `CLAUDE.md` step 5 sends back to the implementer once, with a delta review, before the item is left behind.

Head reviewed: 8bd35e3 on top of 89a22ba. `make check` green locally (tidy, sqlc diff, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`, Docker up), no SKIP in `internal/record` or `internal/ids` under `-v`. CI `check` passes. Coverage of both changed packages is 100 percent of statements. The pull request touches neither `.claude/` nor `CLAUDE.md`, so an ordinary verdict applies. `govulncheck` is still not installed here. No new dependency in the delta.

### Status of the round 1 findings

| # | Round 1 finding | Status | How I checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | blocking: scope canonical form survives mutants | **resolved** | all four survivors re-applied one at a time: lowercase hex in the high-byte branch (killed by `TestEveryEscapeHasOneVerdictInGoAndInTheSchema`), `60` widened to `6[0-9A-F]`, Go accepting an escaped lowercase letter, a digit-first provider in the schema (killed by `TestEveryCharacterOfTheProviderAndKindSegments`). All killed by more than the fuzz seeds |
| 2 | blocking: invalid UTF-8 and lone surrogates rewritten | **resolved** | my own 29 raw documents, below. `0xFF` and `0xFE` in `external_id` are both refused, so they can no longer become one identity. Lone high and lone low escapes refused. Valid pairs (uppercase, lowercase and mixed hex, a million pairs back to back, the raw astral character) accepted |
| 3 | should-fix: A, B, A skipped silently | **resolved** as a documented requirement on B08, present on issue #8, marked as the maintainer's to overrule. My position is below |
| 4 | should-fix: the compatibility promise named the wrong direction | **resolved** | ADR 4 decision 1, schema `format` description, `FormatV1` comment and architecture 6 all state the reader's rule |
| 5 | should-fix: `origin.untrusted: false` undefined | **resolved** | schema, Go comment, ADR 4 decision 10, architecture 6, roadmap |
| 6 | should-fix: "safe in a URL" was false | **resolved** | ADR 3 section and the `scopeId` description read correctly, the round trip test runs in `make check` |
| 7 | should-fix: uniqueness domain of `external_id` | **resolved** | schema pattern, `checkExternalID`, `Seal`. Mutants E1 to E5 and S5 to S7 below, all killed |
| 8 | should-fix: line breaks and bidirectional controls in identifiers and names | **resolved**, with two new should-fix items on the fix (inline) |
| 9 | should-fix: "`Seal` is the only way to an id" not enforced | **resolved**. The seal in `Marshal` is the real guard and holds under every probe that is an accident. The caller scan has three holes (inline note) |
| 10 | should-fix: no astral maximum-length case | **resolved** | the UTF-16-counting mutant is now killed by `TestSchemaAndGoAgreeOnDocuments` |

The four round 1 notes: the leap second note and the cleaning requirement are on issue #11, the ledger requirement is on issue #8.

### The exhaustive comparison (mine, not the implementer's)

Every code point from U+0000 to U+FFFF (surrogates aside) plus 12 astral ones (an emoji, four code points of the tag block, two variation selectors from the supplement, a musical format character, a shorthand format control, U+10000, U+FFFFF, U+10FFFF), one character per document, in **each of the nine fields** that has a character rule, so all four classes: **571,500 documents**.

- Go strict decoder against the Go schema validator (compiled with and without format assertion): **0 disagreements**.
- Python `jsonschema` 4.26.0 (`Draft202012Validator`, documents passed through `json.dumps` and `json.loads` as a sink would see them) against the Go verdicts: **0 disagreements**. Against the rule as ADR 4 states it, written out again in my script: **0 disagreements**.
- ECMAScript (Node 26), the three `not` patterns compiled **with and without the `u` flag**, the whole BMP plus astral: 380,958 checks, **0 disagreements** with the stated rule. All 16 patterns of the schema compile in both modes.
- Go RE2 directly: the three `not` patterns against `charRule.refuses` for **all of Unicode** (3,336,192 comparisons, 0.2 seconds): 0 disagreements.
- The schema file is pure ASCII (checked byte by byte), and the patterns use only `^`, `$`, classes, ranges, `(?:)`, `{m,n}`, `?`, `+`, `.` and two-digit hex escapes. No look-around, no named class, no Go-only or Python-only syntax.
- **Where it is not portable:** Ruby. See the inline finding on the schema.

### My position on what freezes

**The character rules: signed, once the two inline items are fixed.** I tried to find a real identifier that is refused and did not find one. Slack ids and timestamps, ClickUp ids and custom task ids, HubSpot numeric ids, Graph ids (base64url with `=`, `!`, `-`, `_`), Graph `changeKey` and etag versions, a Teams `19:<email>2`, GUIDs: all printable ASCII, all accepted. The one family that can break it is an identifier **a sender controls**: if B16 ever builds `edges.reply_parent` or an `external_id` from a mail header (`In-Reply-To`, `internetMessageId`), RFC 5322's obsolete syntax and real spam put tabs, control bytes and raw 8-bit bytes there, and a stranger's mail then dead-letters. That is a note for B16, inline on ADR 4: such an identifier is escaped or hashed injectively, never cleaned, and preferably never used (Graph's own message id is ASCII).

Display names and titles are the opposite: real data **is** refused, routinely. A zero-width space pasted into a Slack display name, a right-to-left mark a Hebrew or Arabic keyboard leaves after a name, the soft hyphens and zero-width spaces that marketing mail puts into its sender name to dodge filters, a tab in a ClickUp task name pasted from a spreadsheet, a tab or an encoded line break in a mail subject. So "normalizers clean before `Seal`" is not an edge case, it is on the hot path of every provider, and for Outlook on a large share of inbound mail.

Is "the format refuses, the normalizer cleans" the right split? Yes, for three reasons. A sink gets a guarantee (one line, no reordering) it could not have if the format merely recommended cleaning. A schema cannot repair anyway, so repair could only ever live on the Go side, and then `Validate` and the schema would stop agreeing. And for identifiers repair would be wrong: removing a character from an id merges two entities. Would I accept a dead letter for a real mail over a tab in its subject? Only as the visible symptom of a normalizer bug, never as normal operation, and that is what this is, provided forgetting is hard. Today forgetting is easy: nothing in the repository cleans, and a fixture with a clean name passes. What I would do, and what issue #11 already asks for in part: (1) B11 adds the cleaning functions in `internal/record` next to the rules, for `author.display` and `title` **only**, with a test over every code point that a cleaned value always passes `Validate` and that cleaning is idempotent. (2) The provider conformance harness feeds every normalizer one hostile fixture (a display name with U+200B, U+200F and U+202E, a title with a tab and a line feed) and requires `Seal` to succeed. With (2) a provider cannot forget. Cleaning does not need to be part of the format's contract with a sink. One sentence of wording is worth adding when B11 lands, and wording may change within v1: `title` and `author.display` are cleaned copies and not byte-exact, so a sink must not match them against the source. Is the cost stated loudly enough? In ADR 4 (decision 9 and the cost section), in the Go comments and on issue #11, yes.

**The tag characters: signed as left out, and the stated reason is true.** I checked it: a literal range from U+E0000 to U+E007F compiles and works in Go, in Python and in ECMAScript with the `u` flag, and is a syntax error ("Range out of order in character class") in ECMAScript without it, because the class is read in UTF-16 units. The spelling in units (a high surrogate, then a class of low ones) compiles in both modes and matches only without the flag. So no single spelling serves both ECMAScript modes (and .NET's engine works in UTF-16 units as well, which I did not test). There is a second, better reason the ADR does not give: tag characters are legitimate in a display name. The flags of England, Scotland and Wales are U+1F3F4 followed by tag characters, so refusing them in `author.display` would refuse real names. For identifiers nothing legitimate uses them, and the consequence (an id that differs invisibly, or carries smuggled text) is a sink-side duty that the `identifier` description already states ("not every invisible character", "treats it as foreign text"). A Go-only refusal inside `Validate` or the decoder would break "Go and the schema agree" and I would not do it. If the project ever wants it, the place is `Seal` alone: "Sluiceway produces less than the schema allows and the schema stays" is exactly what decision 1 permits.

**`external_id` begins with the provider key: signed.** The architecture example complies (`slack:C0GENERAL:1752064245.000200`), and so do all six golden files. `edges.reply_parent` sharing the grammar is right: edges come from fields of the source, never from text, so a parent in another provider cannot occur, and `Seal` holds both to the sealing provider's key. One contradiction is written down nowhere in this repository: issue #6 (the tunnel) says "a provider key must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}` (put that in the provider registry, with a test)", and ADR 3 freezes `[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}`. ADR 3 wins, because it is the public one and the stricter one (every ADR 3 key passes the tunnel's rule). But a registry built from issue #6 as written would accept `ms-graph`, or a 40 character key, and every record of that provider would then fail in `Seal` with "provider is not a provider key". Note for B06: the registry validates keys with the ADR 3 grammar (the tunnel's pattern is the rule for the path segment, not for the key), and its test seals a record with every registered key.

**The compatibility rule: signed, both halves.** It is livable. The change the project is most likely to want before v1.0 that it forbids is a sixth `kind` (HubSpot's CRM objects or a calendar event will not sit well in the five), which the ADR already prices. The second is refusing one more invisible character after an incident. The first half of the rule would allow that, the second half forbids it, and the rule should win, because the wish has another road: `Seal` refuses it and the schema stays. A raised limit (the 512 bytes of a scope id against real Graph ids) is the one that would hurt, and the ADR already orders B16 and B17 before v0.1.0 for it. One sentence is missing and the inline finding on the schema shows why it matters: a pattern respelled without changing the set of strings it matches is wording, not a change, and needs an exhaustive proof.

**`origin` two-valued: signed.** The argument is sound: the only thing a sink could do with "known inside" that it cannot do with "no signal" is relax a guard, and membership of the author says nothing about quoted or forwarded words. A sink author who reads only the schema gets it right, the descriptions say NO SIGNAL in so many words. What no description fixes is that `untrusted: false` reads as "trusted" in code, where descriptions are not visible. That is the field's name, it was the architecture's before this pull request, and whether to rename it before it freezes is the maintainer's call, not a finding against this change.

**The A, B, A rule: signed as written.** It is implementable with state the ledger needs anyway (per entity the head and the head's scope, per id its presence), and I could not make it miss the case: A, B, C, B is caught too, and an edit after the dead letter heals it (a new id that supersedes the record in B). It misfires only on a stale record that was not hydrated: after a real move from A to B, a degraded record built from an old webhook body, or a replayed dead letter whose hydration fails again, is dead-lettered where it used to be skipped correctly. That is noise an operator can discard, the ADR says so, and the alternative is guessing. Reconciliation cannot trigger it, because it lists current state, which is the head. Two things B08 should know: with equal versions the chain order is arrival order, so the rule leans on per-entity FIFO (B04's ordering key must be the entity), and pruning ledger rows by retention turns the case into an ordinary new record that supersedes the head, which is the correct outcome.

**The sealed representation: signed.** Probes below. It catches every accident I could construct. What it does not cover is by design or out of its reach, see the inline note: the tenant, `Op` and `Kind`, and a deliberate type conversion.

**The byte rule: signed.** `hasUnpairedSurrogate` is correct on every case I tried, including an odd and an even number of backslashes in front of `uD800`, a high surrogate followed by a non-surrogate escape, by an escaped backslash and then the text `uDC00`, by a one-character escape, surrogates in unknown values and in unknown field **names**, and mixed-case hex. It is one forward pass with no backtracking. Measured linear: 1, 2, 4 and 8 MB of backslash pairs in an unknown field decode in 18, 25, 40 and 77 ms.

### Coverage

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | unchanged from round 1 and still proven. The example, the goldens and the id recipe are byte for byte what they were | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 42 mutants of the delta (5 round 1 survivors, 11 Go character rules, 8 schema, 5 external id, 5 seal, 8 byte rule), all killed. Then 6 drift mutants outside the sampled code points: 4 survive | 1 should-fix |
| Tests are comprehensive | 100 percent statement coverage, my own 29 raw documents, 23 seal probes, boundaries in three kinds of character | 0 |
| Correctness | `hasUnpairedSurrogate` by cases and by reading, the order of the byte checks, `null` and `[null]` into a `Record`, Seal and decode pinning | 0 |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | can a sealed record change scope, tenant, op; the A, B, A rule worked through five sequences; errors still never quote a value | 2 notes |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | real provider identifiers and names against the character rules, tag characters, header-derived identifiers, hostile documents re-measured, no new dependency | 1 note |
| Performance | benchmarks re-run (all reproduce), hostile documents re-measured, linearity of the new byte passes | 0 |
| Dead code | every new identifier of the delta has a production caller inside the package. No cleaning helper was added without a caller, which is right | 0 |
| Codebase improvement | the caller scan, pattern portability | 1 should-fix, 1 note |
| Documentation | ADR 3 and ADR 4 statement by statement against the code, architecture 5 and 6, roadmap, backlog log line, description, issues #6, #8, #11 | 1 note (issue #6) |

### Mutations and probes

Each mutant applied alone by a script that restores the file, `go test ./internal/record ./internal/ids`, probe tests removed first so that they could not kill anything themselves.

**Killed (42):** R1 to R4, the four round 1 survivors. R5 UTF-16 counting. Go character rules: U+061C passes; U+206A to U+206F pass; a display name lets U+200B through; lets U+200E through; U+2029 passes; C1 stops at U+009E; DEL passes; the embeddings start at U+202B; `meta.delivery` checked as content; `container.id` checked as one line; `title` checked as a display name. Schema: `oneLine` without U+2029; `displayName` refuses U+200C; `identifier` stops at U+2069; without the soft hyphen; `reply_parent` any identifier; a 33 character key in `externalId`; a hyphen in it; `meta.delivery` with no character rule. External id in Go: `Seal` without the colon; without the reply parent check; nothing after the colon; a hyphen in the key; `reply_parent` any identifier. Seal: `Marshal` ignores it; decoding leaves none; the seal forgets the version; forgets the scope; `Seal` pins before it mints. Byte rule: no `utf8.Valid`; no surrogate check; high followed by high accepted; the low half read again; the escaped character not skipped; DB not a high surrogate; DF not a low one; only the first half of the document checked.

**Survived (4), inline:** the schema's `identifier` also refuses U+3164; Go's identifiers also refuse U+3164; Go's identifiers also refuse U+3000; the schema's `oneLine` also refuses U+3000. (Go refusing the tag characters, and U+FFF9, are killed: both are in the sample.) **Equivalent, proves nothing:** `Seal` leaving a `Source` that is already set, because `Seal` has refused every other value by then.

**The caller scan, three throwaway files that really mint ids while the test stays green:** a `go:linkname` to `ids.RecordID` from `internal/outbox`; a function value in a package directory named `bin` (`internal/outbox/bin`); a one-line wrapper added to `internal/ids` and called from `internal/outbox`.

**Seal probes (from outside the package):** sealed value, pointer, copy, inside a slice, a map and an embedding struct: marshalled. Zero `Record`, a record rebuilt field by field, scope changed, id changed, a decoded record with its scope changed, a changed record inside a slice, a map and an embedding struct: refused. Scope changed and changed back: marshalled, correctly. `Op` changed to `delete`, `Kind`, `Audience` and `Source` changed after `Seal`: marshalled, by design. `type w record.Record` and `json.Marshal(w(r))` with a changed scope: marshalled, no `Validate` and no seal (deliberate evasion, not an accident). `[null]` into `[]Record`: refused. `null` into `*Record`: nil pointer and no error, which is `encoding/json`, not this package.

**Hostile documents, one `json.Unmarshal` each, round 1 numbers in parentheses:** 300,000 unknown top-level fields, 4.4 MB: 220 ms (212). The largest valid `text` as escaped astral pairs, 12.6 MB: 132 ms (129). An 8 MB unknown string: 84 ms (75). Nesting 9,000 deep: 0.5 ms. The two new passes cost between 2 and 12 percent and everything is still linear.

**Benchmarks, three runs:** `Validate` 185 ns and 0 allocations (example), 0.56 microseconds (20 KB), 20.2 microseconds (1 MiB), which is faster than round 1 because the text is no longer walked rune by rune. `Marshal` 2.44 microseconds, 7 allocations. `Unmarshal` 23.4 microseconds, 485 allocations. All four reported numbers reproduce.

**Fuzz:** `FuzzDecodeAgreesWithSchema` 180 seconds, 44.8 million executions, no failure. `FuzzParseScopeID` 120 seconds, 26.0 million, none.

### Hygiene

`git log origin/main..HEAD --format='%h %(trailers:only,unfold)'` shows no trailer on either commit. No authorship trailer, no tool attribution line and no em dash in the diff, in the commit messages, in the description or in the replies. Byte-level scan of all 33 files of the diff as they are at HEAD (every C0 and C1 control except tab and line feed, U+00A0, U+00AD, U+061C, U+017F, U+212A, U+200B to U+200F, U+2028 to U+202E, U+2060 to U+206F, U+FEFF, the Hangul fillers, variation selectors, tag characters, every character of category Cf, Cc, Zl, Zp, Co or Cn, invalid UTF-8 and surrogates encoded as CESU-8): **nothing found.** The only non-ASCII characters in the diff are visible: the middle dot in `docs/backlog.md` and `docs/roadmap.md`, `e` with acute, `u` with diaeresis, sharp s, two CJK ideographs and the hot beverage sign, all in test data and golden files. The literal NUL, line separators and surrogate pair the implementer reported are gone. I can confirm the tool problem again: my own probe had a byte order mark where I had typed an escape.

### Notes (no action in this pull request)

- **B06:** issue #6 states a provider key grammar that contradicts ADR 3, see the position on `external_id` above.
- **B08 and B09:** the tenant is not in the seal, and cannot be checked by `Marshal`. A record sealed for tenant A and handed to `Sink.Deliver` under tenant B marshals fine, and no sink can notice, because the tenant is in no field. The ids differ per tenant, so it is detectable only by the ledger. B08 should carry the tenant next to the record from `Seal` to `Deliver` in one value that nothing reassigns, and the inline note says how the seal could help.
- **B08:** the two remarks on the A, B, A rule above (arrival order with equal versions, retention).
- **B11 and B16:** identifiers are never cleaned, and header-derived identifiers, inline.
- **B11:** the conformance fixture with a hostile name and title, above.

## Delta review of d5e1023 (after round 2)

**Verdict: approved.** Nothing blocking. One commit on top of `8bd35e3`, reviewed as `git diff 8bd35e3 d5e1023` (13 files, no change under `.claude/` or to `CLAUDE.md`). The replies were read as claims, and every claim below was re-run here. Two small should-fix findings and two notes are inline. One of the should-fix findings is a mutant of `SealedFor` that survives, so it touches isolation: the code is right today, and the missing case is one line.

### Status of the round 2 findings

| Round 2 | Status | How I checked |
|---|---|---|
| should-fix: the three `not` patterns do not compile in Ruby | **resolved** | The old file fails `Regexp.new` in Ruby 4.0.6 with "invalid multibyte escape" for all three, the new file compiles all 16. Old and new spelling give the same verdict for every code point (table below). The file is pure ASCII (`LC_ALL=C grep -nP '[^\x00-\x7F]'` prints nothing). |
| should-fix: the character test is a sample, four drift mutants survive | **resolved** | All four are killed now, each by the exhaustive test and by a named accepted case. The old sample test still lets all four through, as expected, which is why the new test is needed. |
| note: three holes in the caller scan | **resolved** | The three throwaway files, dropped in again one at a time, are each named by the test. |
| note: the seal does not cover the tenant, `Op`, `Kind`, a type conversion | **acted on** | `SealedFor` fails closed in every probe I tried. `Op` and `Kind` are held. The conversion is documented as out of reach on `Record` and in ADR 4, which is the right call. |
| note: identifiers are never cleaned, sender-controlled identifiers | **acted on** | In ADR 4 decision 9, accurate, with one imprecise pointer that was mine (inline). |
| notes 4 and 5 of round 2 | no action was asked for, none taken | |

### The respelling, across dialects

The three patterns of `8bd35e3` against the three of `d5e1023`, one string per code point, all 1,112,064 code points (U+0000 to U+10FFFF less the surrogates). "Rule" is the range table of ADR 4 written out again in each script.

| Engine | Old against new | New against the rule | Refused (identifier, displayName, oneLine) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Go RE2 (go1.26.7) | 0 disagreements | 0 (this is the new Go test) | 96, 94, 67 |
| Python `re` (3.14.7) | 0 | 0 | 96, 94, 67 |
| ECMAScript, no flag (node 26.8.1) | 0 | 0 | 96, 94, 67 |
| ECMAScript, `u` flag | 0 | 0 | 96, 94, 67 |
| Ruby 4.0.6 (Onigmo) | the old spelling does not compile | 0 | 96, 94, 67 |

All 16 patterns of the new file compile in Python, in Ruby, and in ECMAScript both with and without `u` (32 compilations). Only the three patterns differ between the two files. Document level, Python `jsonschema` 4.26, old schema against new schema, one character per document over the whole BMP: `author.id` (the identifier class) 0 disagreements, 96 refused, and `title` 0 disagreements, 67 refused. **Zero disagreements anywhere, which is the claim.**

Putting the file of `8bd35e3` back: `TestNoPatternUsesAnEscapeThatOnlySomeEnginesRead` fails, naming all three patterns, and `TestEveryCodePointInGoAndInThePatterns` stays green. That is correct: same strings, unportable spelling.

### Coverage, scaled to the delta

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | no "Done when" line changed; the two should-fix findings of round 2 against their new tests | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 11 character mutants, 7 seal mutants, the old schema file, 9 scan probes, listed below | 1 should-fix |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of `internal/record` and `internal/ids` is 100.0% of statements, `SealedFor`, `currentSeal`, `Seal`, both `UnmarshalJSON` included; the 19 named accepted cases run as 19 subtests, each through `Seal`, `Marshal`, the schema and the decoder; `-v` shows no SKIP anywhere under `internal/` | 0 |
| Correctness | `UnmarshalJSON` builds the record from a zero value, so a decode over a sealed record cannot keep a tenant; a failed decode and a `null` leave the record untouched (still its own tenant's, which is right); a failed `Seal` returns the zero `Record` | 0 |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | tried to get a record sealed for tenant A accepted as tenant B, every way listed below; tenant ids are case sensitive in `tenancy.Parse` and in the `tenant_id` domain, and so is `SealedFor` | 0 (the test gap is counted above) |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | no new input path, no new dependency, `go mod tidy -diff` clean | 0 |
| Performance | the exhaustive test: 0.06 s per rule without the race detector, 5.6 to 6.8 s per rule under `-race` with the four rules in parallel, 8 s for the test alone; `internal/record` takes 25.5 s of a 31 s `make check`. Acceptable, and what ADR 4 says ("a tenth of a second, or about six under the race detector") is true. The seal is six compares of short strings | 0 |
| Dead code | `SealedFor` has no production caller, like everything in this package until B08. Its caller is named on the method (the stage that writes the ledger and calls `Sink.Deliver`), in ADR 4 (B08), in architecture section 5 and on issue #8. Acceptable. `onTheWire` is in a `_test.go` file | 0 |
| Codebase improvement | the stricter rule inside `internal/ids`: no false positive on a doc comment or a doc link that says `RecordID`, none on an example test. A struct field named `RecordID` inside `internal/ids` would be reported, with a message that explains itself: no cost today | 0 |
| Documentation | ADR 4 decisions 1, 7 and 9, architecture section 5, the backlog line, the godoc of `Record`, `SealedFor`, `MarshalJSON`, `Seal` and `ids.RecordID`, the pull request description | 1 should-fix, 2 notes |
| Hygiene | no trailer on any of the three commits (git's own trailer parser); no tool attribution line in the diff, the commit messages, the description or the replies; no em dash; byte scan below | 0 |

### Mutations and probes

Character rules. Each applied alone by script and restored. "Exhaustive" is `TestEveryCodePointInGoAndInThePatterns`, "sample" is the old `TestEveryCharacterRuleInGoAndInTheSchema`, "named" is the accepted cases in `TestWhatTheCharacterRulesLeaveAlone`.

| Mutant | Exhaustive | Sample | Named |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 the schema's `identifier` also refuses U+3164 (round 2) | killed | survives | killed |
| M2 Go also refuses U+3164 (round 2) | killed | survives | killed |
| M3 Go also refuses U+3000 (round 2) | killed | survives | killed |
| M4 the schema's `oneLine` also refuses U+3000 (round 2) | killed | survives | killed |
| M5 Go also refuses the tag characters U+E0000 to U+E007F (astral) | killed | killed | killed |
| M10 Go also refuses U+1D173 to U+1D17A (astral, invisible, outside the sample) | killed | survives | survives |
| M6 Go's C1 range one too wide (U+00A0, just outside) | killed | killed | survives |
| M7 the schema's `displayName` range one too wide (U+2070, just outside) | killed | killed | survives |
| M8 the schema's `identifier` loosened, U+202E no longer refused | killed | killed | survives |
| M9 Go refuses U+10FFFF, the last code point | killed | killed | survives |
| M11 Go also refuses U+180E | killed | killed | survives |

The exhaustive test kills all eleven. M10 is the one that shows what it adds: an astral range that neither the sample nor any named case reaches. The old sample did already reach the edges of the refused ranges (M6, M7), so that part was sound before.

The seal, against the package's own tests:

| Mutant | Result |
|---|---|
| S1 `SealedFor` ignores the tenant | killed |
| S2 `SealedFor` accepts the empty tenant | killed |
| S3 `SealedFor` ignores the seal | killed |
| S4 the decoder keeps the tenant of the record it decodes over | killed |
| S5 the seal drops `Op` | killed |
| S6 the seal drops `Kind` | killed |
| S7 `SealedFor` compares tenants without regard to case | **survives** (inline) |

Tenant A as tenant B, from outside the package (a throwaway `record_test` file): a copy, through a pointer, through an interface, out of a map, through a channel: sealed for A and for nothing else. Decoded from its own document, A's document decoded over a record sealed for B (`json.Unmarshal`, a `json.Decoder`, `UnmarshalJSON` called directly, a slice decoded over sealed elements), the zero `Record`, A's record with B's id assigned: sealed for nobody. Tenants `""`, `Tenant_A`, `TENANT_A`, `tenant_A`, with a leading or trailing space, with a trailing NUL: all false. `Seal` with an empty or an invalid tenant returns the zero `Record`. Sealing A's sealed record again for B moves the tenant and the id together. **`SealedFor` fails closed in every case.**

The caller scan, throwaway files in the real tree, one at a time:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| C1 `internal/outbox/bin/x.go` with `var Mint = ids.RecordID` | caught |
| C2 a wrapper in `internal/ids/zzmint.go` | caught |
| C3 a `go:linkname` pull in a new package | caught |
| C5 `cmd/bin/x.go` | caught |
| C9 a wrapper in a subpackage `internal/ids/sub` | caught |
| C6 a doc comment and a doc link in `internal/ids` that say `RecordID` | clean, correctly |
| C7 an example test `ExampleRecordID` in `internal/ids` | clean, correctly |
| C8 a struct field named `RecordID` in `internal/ids` | reported (a false positive nobody has a reason to hit) |

Hygiene: `git log origin/main..HEAD --format='%h %(trailers:only,unfold)'` shows no trailer on `89a22ba`, `8bd35e3` or `d5e1023`. A byte scan of all 13 touched files, the three commit messages, the description and the replies for em dashes, literal C0, DEL and C1 characters, U+00A0, U+00AD, U+061C, U+180E, U+2028, U+2029, U+FEFF, zero-width, bidirectional, tag and variation selector characters: 0 flagged, no CRLF. The delta adds no non-ASCII byte at all. What non-ASCII the touched files hold was there before and is visible (a middle dot in the backlog headings, accented letters and a coffee cup in test data).

`make check` on `d5e1023`: green (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race -count=1 ./...`), 31 s. Both fuzz targets for a minute each: `FuzzDecodeAgreesWithSchema` 16.4 million executions, `FuzzParseScopeID` 14.7 million, no failure. CI on `d5e1023`: `check` passes.

### For the orchestrator

- **Issue #9 (B09):** copy the inline note on `SealedFor` about `==`. It is written down only in the pull request description and in a test helper, and B09's author reads neither.
- **Issues #11 and #16:** copy the inline note on ADR 4: the scope id's escaper is not the tool for a mail header.
- Issue #8 already has the `SealedFor` requirement.

text:
## Delta review of the rename (a5a38ad, aef813c)

**Verdict: approved**

Scope: only the two commits added since the approval at 6693f04. The format design, the schema
rules, the character rules and the seal were not re-reviewed.

Every claim in the description was checked by experiment. All of them hold. One should-fix remains,
about the durability of the fix rather than the fix itself.

### The rename is provably 1:1

I rebuilt each of the 21 changed files from its parent blob by applying nothing but the three token
substitutions (`sluiceway` to `lawang`, `Sluiceway` to `Lawang`, `SLUICEWAY` to `LAWANG`) and
compared the result with the committed blob byte for byte. 70 occurrences, 21 files, matching the
description exactly. 20 of the 21 files are byte-identical to the substitution. The single
exception is `internal/ids/callers_test.go`, and the only difference there is gofmt realigning one
map key (`"cmd/lawang/main.go":` gained four spaces); collapsing whitespace makes it identical too.

So no length constraint, pattern, enum value, field name or `required` entry could have moved. In
`record.v1.schema.json` all 16 occurrences sit in `$id`, `title`, a `description` or the `format`
`const`. No golden file drifted beyond its `format` line.

### The frozen strings agree with each other

`lawang.record/v1` appears in `record.go:42` (`FormatV1`), the schema `const`, `testdata/example.json`,
all six golden files, ADR 4 and architecture section 6, and nowhere disagrees.
`https://gablooge.github.io/lawang/schema/record/v1.json` is the same string in the schema `$id`
and in `SchemaID`. ADR 4's media type is `application/vnd.lawang.record.v1+json`.
`git grep -in sluice` and `git grep -n "gablooge/sluiceway"` both return nothing.

Architecture section 6 and `internal/record/testdata/example.json` are byte-identical outside the
test as well: the one fenced JSON block in `docs/architecture.md` is 690 bytes with
sha256 `ad608f56...`, and so is the fixture.

### The merge kept both sides

Rather than read the resolution, I recomputed it: `git merge-tree --write-tree 6693f04 905a23d`
produces exactly one conflict, `README.md`, and the resulting tree differs from the committed merge
tree in `README.md` alone. The resolution is precisely the branch's bullet (a scope's members are
synced separately under the same scope id rather than carried in the record) with `Sluiceway`
changed to `Lawang`, and nothing else. Nothing from `main` was dropped and nothing from B05 was
reverted.

I also checked line by line, after normalising the name, which lines of each parent are absent from
the merged tree in `README.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/backlog.md` and `docs/roadmap.md`.
Every absence maps to an intended change: B05 replacing the "proposed" section 6, the old record id
recipe without the scope, and roadmap open decisions 3 and 4; and `main` removing the "private until
M6" sentences and realigning the `cmd/` row of the package layout. `main`'s alignment fix survived
byte for byte (both files have the same spacing at that row). The README status paragraph is the
merge of both: `main`'s wording plus B05's "and the record format is settled". No conflict marker
survives anywhere in the tree.

### `internal/ids/testdata/golden.json` is untouched, and its vectors are right

The blob id is `d94b9a07...` at both `8bd35e3` and `aef813c`, so the file is bit-identical. I also
recomputed every vector independently with the Python `blake3` package (1.0.9) from the recipe the
file states: 12 of 12 `delivery_id` and 10 of 10 `record_id` vectors match. The project name is in
none of the hashed parts, which is why it had to stay unchanged.

### The caller guard really was blind, and really is not now

This is the one genuine correctness fix and it is a real one. Verified both ways:

- With the repaired constant and a real second caller planted in `internal/outbox`,
  `TestRecordIDHasNoCallerOutsideRecord` fails and names the file.
- With the constant put back to `github.com/gablooge/sluiceway/internal/ids` and the same caller
  still planted, the whole `internal/ids` package is **green**. The guard resolves nothing, and its
  meta-test, which builds synthetic sources from the same constant, stays self-consistent and
  cannot notice. That is exactly the failure mode the description claims, reproduced.

`cmd/lawang/main.go` in the path table names a directory that exists (`cmd/` holds only `lawang`).

### Which evasions the repaired guard catches

16 probes, each planted as a real file in the tree, the guard run, the file deleted.

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| plain call from another package | caught |
| aliased import | caught |
| dot import | caught |
| function value, never called | caught |
| wrapper in a third package, used from a fourth | caught at the wrapper |
| `go:linkname` pulling `RecordID` out | caught |
| caller under a directory named `bin` at depth (`internal/outbox/bin/`) | caught |
| import path spelled with a Go string escape (`internal/\x69ds`) | caught (it unquotes, a grep would not) |
| caller in a file excluded by a build tag (`//go:build zzneverset`) | caught (stricter than the doc comment promises) |
| wrapper inside `internal/ids` | caught |
| caller in a subpackage of `internal/record` (`internal/record/zzsub/`) | caught |
| `go:linkname` with a tab instead of a space | missed, but see below |
| caller in the top-level `bin/` | missed, intentional and pinned by `skippedDir("bin")` |
| caller in a `_test.go` file | missed, intentional |
| caller under a `testdata/` directory | missed, intentional (the Go tool does not build it) |
| caller in `internal/record` itself | missed, that is the one allowed package |

The tab case is not an evasion. I checked whether the Go compiler honours it: with a space or two
spaces the bodyless function compiles (the directive is honoured), with a tab it fails with
`missing function body` (the directive is not honoured). The scan's `//go:linkname ` prefix test
therefore matches the compiler exactly. Go 1.26.7.

So the four remaining misses are the four the test's own tables and doc comment already declare,
and they were settled in round 2.

### Build, tests, CI

- `make check`: green (tidy, sqlc diff against Docker, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`).
  Timings are not suspicious: outbox 17.2s, store 18.5s, record 25.8s.
- `go test -count=1 -v ./...`: 771 `--- PASS`, **0 `--- SKIP`**, 0 `--- FAIL`. No integration test is
  silently skipped.
- Fuzz, 60s each: `FuzzParseScopeID` 15,531,946 execs, `FuzzDecodeAgreesWithSchema` 14,718,236 execs,
  no failures.
- `make build` then `./bin/lawang version` prints `aef813c`. I confirmed that check discriminates:
  built with no `-X`, or with the old module path in `-X`, the same binary prints `dev-00f82b9b2d26`.
  So the symbol genuinely resolves under the new path.
- Coverage of the two packages is still 100.0% of statements.
- `gh pr checks 43`: `check pass 2m5s`.

### Hygiene

- Trailers: `git log 8bd35e3..HEAD --format='%h %(trailers:only,unfold)'` shows no trailer on any
  commit, the two new ones included.
- The rename diff, the merge resolution and both new commit messages contain no em dash, no en dash,
  no tool attribution line, no authorship trailer and no tool name. The rename diff is pure ASCII.
  (Searching those phrases over the whole `6693f04..aef813c` range does return hits, but only
  because the merge brings in `main`'s own rule text, which is prose stating the rules.)
- Byte scan of all 67 files touched by the delta for C0 controls, DEL, C1, U+00A0, U+00AD, U+061C,
  U+200B to U+200F, U+2028 to U+202E, U+2060 to U+206F, U+3000 and U+FEFF: **0 files affected**.
  `record.v1.schema.json` is still pure ASCII (16,146 bytes).
- Token shapes (`xoxb-`, `pat-`, `pk_`, `eyJ`, `postgres://`, long hex, long base64) in the delta: none.
- The PR body carries no em dash and no tool attribution. Its two remaining mentions of the old name
  are historical prose about the rename itself, which is correct.
- The branch changes no file under `.claude/` and not `CLAUDE.md` (`git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD`
  confirms), so the rules are not being changed by the change under review.

### Coverage

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| The rename is 1:1 | all 21 files rebuilt from the parent by pure token substitution, compared byte for byte | 0 |
| The caller guard fix | planted a real caller, reverted the constant to prove the fix load-bearing, 16 evasion probes, compiler behaviour for the tab case | 1 should-fix |
| Frozen strings | format const, schema const, example, six goldens, ADR 4, architecture 6, `$id`, `SchemaID`, media type | 0 |
| The merge | committed merge tree compared against git's own mechanical merge tree; per-line loss check against both parents on four documents | 0 |
| Golden vectors | blob id against 8bd35e3, plus all 22 vectors recomputed with Python `blake3` | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | M1 and M2 below | 0 |
| Correctness | the delta changes one test constant and 70 name occurrences; no logic, no query, no endpoint, no new identifier | 0 |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | no tenant, scope, role, grant, RLS or id recipe touched; golden ids bit-identical; no credential or token shape in the delta | 0 |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | no pattern, `maxLength` or closed set changed (proved by the byte-level 1:1 result); `go.mod` and `go.sum` untouched by these two commits | 0 |

| Dead code | the delta adds no identifier; `cmd/lawang/main.go` in the path table names a directory that exists; no reference to `cmd/sluiceway` survives | 0 |

| Documentation | README status paragraph and the resolved bullet, backlog B05 row, roadmap, architecture 6 and 12, ADR 3 and 4, schema descriptions | 2 notes |

### Mutations and probes

| Id | What | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | `idsImportPath` reverted to the old module path, with a real `ids.RecordID` caller planted in `internal/outbox` | **`internal/ids` stays green.** This is the bug the commit fixes, reproduced. |
| M2 | the same planted caller with the repaired constant | killed: `callers_test.go:39: internal/outbox/zzplanted_caller.go refers to ids.RecordID` |

All probe files were deleted and the worktree restored to `aef813c` clean.

**note (documentation).** The B05 log row in `docs/backlog.md` changed by one word and records
nothing about what this delta found. The row's stated purpose is "anything worth remembering", and
