text:
## Review, round 1

**Code verdict: approved.** No blocking findings. I could not break the rename: the setting, the roles, the schema and the module path agree everywhere, and I proved it against a Postgres I bootstrapped myself rather than trusting the suite.

**Label: `review:needs-maintainer`**, because this pull request changes `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/agents/*.md`, and an agent bound by those rules cannot approve a change to them. That is the project rule, not a judgement on the code. The code verdict above is the one to decide from.

### Coverage

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | no linked issue (`closingIssuesReferences` empty), so I judged against the description: every claim in it except one is true, see F6 | 1 note |
| Tests have teeth | mutations M1 to M6 below, on the setting name in SQL, the setting name in Go, the worker role literal, the linker module path, the usage-text credential guard, and the ids tripwire after #43 | 0, all six mutations were caught except M6, which is a future risk, see F4 |
| Tests are comprehensive | no new behaviour, so no new cases are owed. Coverage of the changed packages is unchanged from `main`: config 100.0%, cmd/lawang 90.7%, appversion 94.7%, store 89.9%, tenancy 81.2%. 0 `--- SKIP` across 160 tests in `internal/store`, `internal/tenancy` and `cmd/lawang` with Docker up, so the testcontainers integration tests really ran | 0 |
| Correctness | consistency of the four coupled names across SQL, Go literals, the `search_path` constant, `internal/testdb` and the bootstrap script, by grep and then by running them; end-to-end isolation proof P0 to P6 below | 0 |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | row-level security proved live after the rename (own bootstrap, own container); no credential value anywhere in the diff; the real tunnel hostname is gone from the tree; the two load-bearing credential literals still match what they guard (M5) | 1 note (F5) |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | no input path, no crypto and no dependency changed. `go.mod` changed only its `module` line, `go mod tidy -diff` clean. `govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so I did not run it | 0 |
| Performance | not applicable: no query, index, loop or transaction boundary changed. The only SQL edits are identifier renames, and the plans are the same plans | 0 |
| Dead code | searched for callers of every renamed identifier (`Schema`, `RoleResolver`, `RoleWorker`, `setting`, `devDatabaseURL`); no renamed identifier lost its callers and none became unreferenced | 0 |
| Codebase improvement | `git grep -in sluiceway` returns exactly one line, the backlog log entry, as intended. Checked the forms a case-preserving script misses: inside identifiers, inside URLs, base64 (`c2x1aWNld2F5`) and hex (`736c756963657761`), file and directory names, `.github/`, generated code (`internal/outbox/outboxdb/queries.sql.go`), `testdata`, git-ignored-but-committed files, and the commit message. Nothing left. Checked the reverse too, see below | 2 should-fix (F2, F3) |
| Documentation | README status paragraph, the new name sentence, the backlog log line, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/roadmap.md`, ADRs 1, 2 and 10, `growth/README.md`, `SECURITY.md`, the `CLAUDE.md` tunnel paragraph | 1 should-fix (F1), 2 should-fix (F2, F3), 2 notes |
| Standing style rules | `git log origin/main..HEAD --format='%h %(trailers:only,unfold)'` shows no trailer at all. No "generated with" or tool attribution in the commit message, the description or any file. Zero U+2014 and zero U+2013 in the diff; zero non-ASCII bytes on any added line | 0 |

`make check` on `bd28237`: **green**, exit 0. `go mod tidy -diff`, `sqlc diff`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint run` (0 issues), `go test -race -count=1 ./...` all eight packages ok. CI on the pull request is also green.

### The isolation proof, from my own bootstrap

I did not use testcontainers. I started a `postgres:17-alpine` of my own, piped `./bin/lawang migrate bootstrap` into it as the superuser, set a password on the `lawang` role, and ran `lawang migrate` as that non-superuser role. Three roles created (`lawang`, `lawang_resolver`, `lawang_worker`, all `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS`), schema `lawang` owned by `lawang`, 2 migrations applied, 4 policies present with `{lawang_worker}` on the two claim policies, and `lawang.current_tenant()` reading `current_setting('lawang.tenant', true)`.

Then, connected as the application role:

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| P1 tenant `acme` bound: own outbox rows / rows of `other` / own tenants rows | 1 / 0 / 1 |
| P2 same connection rebound to `other`: own rows / rows of `acme` | 1 / 0 |
| P3 unbound transaction: outbox rows / tenants rows | 0 / 0 |
| P3b unbound INSERT | refused, `new row violates row-level security policy for table "outbox"` |
| P3c bound to `acme`, INSERT with `tenant_id = 'other'` | refused, same error |
| P4 `SET LOCAL ROLE lawang_worker` | sees 2 rows across tenants, `current_user = lawang_worker` |
| P4b worker reading `raw_body` | refused, `permission denied for table outbox` |
| P5 after COMMIT, `current_setting('lawang.tenant', true)` | empty, and a fresh transaction on the same connection sees 0 rows |
| P6 binding the OLD name `sluiceway.tenant` | 0 rows, so nothing in the database still answers to the old setting |

The container was removed afterwards.

### Mutations

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | setting name in the **SQL only**: `migrations/00001_tenancy.sql`, `lawang.tenant` back to `sluiceway.tenant` | **caught, loudly.** 9 failures in `internal/store` (`TestNoTenantBoundReturnsZeroRows`, `TestTenantCannotReadOrWriteAnotherTenant`, `TestRebindingMovesTheTransactionToAnotherTenant` and six more) and the whole `internal/outbox` suite, every one an explicit `SQLSTATE 42501` refusal. Nothing went quietly invisible, which is the failure mode that matters here: the policy fails closed on the write, not only on the read |
| M2 | setting name in the **Go only**: `internal/tenancy/tenancy.go` | **caught.** The same 9 `internal/store` failures plus the whole `internal/outbox` suite. Worth knowing: `internal/tenancy`'s own package tests stayed green, so the guard on this constant lives in `internal/store`, not next to the constant |
| M3 | module path in the `-X` linker flag: `github.com/gablooge/sluiceway/internal/appversion.Version` | **the check has teeth.** The mutant binary printed `dev-c7d13b02e197-dirty`; the real `make build` output prints `bd28237`. The trap on issue #29 is closed and the flag in the `Makefile` really lands |
| M4 | `SET LOCAL ROLE lawang_worker` to `sluiceway_worker` in `internal/store/store.go` | **caught.** 8 `internal/store` failures including `TestHelperRolesAreEnteredExplicitlyAndLeftAtCommit` and `TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin`, plus the outbox claim suite |
| M5 | made the usage text print `devDatabaseURL` | **caught.** `TestUsageDocumentsTheConfigurationAndTheExitCodes` failed with "the usage text prints a URL with credentials", so the renamed `lawang:lawang` literal in the guard still matches the renamed dev URL. The other deliberate literal, `strings.Replace(tdb.URL, "lawang:lawang_test@", ...)` in `internal/store/store_test.go`, matches `internal/testdb`'s user `lawang` and password `lawang_test` |
| M6 | the #43 question: merged `origin/b05-record-format` into this head locally, renamed **only the import lines** in `internal/record`, and planted a second caller of `ids.RecordID` in `internal/outbox` | **not caught. See F4.** With `idsImportPath` left at the old path both tripwire tests passed with a real second caller present. After correcting the constant, `TestRecordIDHasNoCallerOutsideRecord` failed and named the planted file |

### What happens when #43 lands

I did not raise the record format, the JSON Schema, ADR 3 or ADR 4: they are not on `main` and not in this diff, as agreed. I checked the opposite direction instead, by merging `origin/b05-record-format` into this head in a throwaway worktree merge.

- **Merge cost is trivial.** Only two conflicts, both prose: `README.md` and `docs/backlog.md`. `go.mod` merged cleanly (this branch changed line 1, #43 adds `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`), and so did `internal/ids/ids.go`, which both branches touch.
- **The `goimports` `local-prefixes` rename in `.golangci.yml` is the thing that keeps #43's files lintable.** With the merged tree I ran `golangci-lint run ./internal/record/... ./internal/ids/...`: 0 issues. Had that line kept the old prefix, every `internal/record` file would have had its import grouping rewritten.
- **One real hazard, F4 below.**

### Findings

**F1 should-fix. `SECURITY.md` promises a button that does not exist yet.** Inline.

**F2 should-fix. `docs/architecture.md:435`.** Inline.

**F3 should-fix. `migrations/bootstrap/roles.sql:24`.** Inline.

**F4 should-fix, for the follow-up commit, not for this one. `internal/ids/callers_test.go` on `b05-record-format` hard-codes the module path, and the tripwire it guards goes silently dark if only the imports are renamed.**

```go
const (
	idsImportPath = "github.com/gablooge/sluiceway/internal/ids"
```

`TestRecordIDHasNoCallerOutsideRecord` walks the repository and resolves references to `ids.RecordID` through that constant. If the follow-up commit renames the import statements (which it must, or nothing compiles) but leaves this string, the scan resolves nothing, finds nothing, and passes. Its own meta-test, `TestTheRecordIDScanSeesEveryKindOfReference`, builds its synthetic sources from the same constant, so it stays self-consistent and passes too; and the `files < 10` guard only counts Go files, so it passes as well. Nothing in the suite notices.

**Fails when:** after the follow-up rename, someone adds a second caller of `ids.RecordID` outside `internal/record`. That is precisely the caller ADR 4's promise rests on, one id never appearing with two scopes, and the tripwire that exists to name them at once says nothing.

**Proven:** merged #43 locally, renamed only the import lines in `internal/record`, planted `zzProbeSecondMinter` in `internal/outbox` calling `ids.RecordID`. With the stale constant: `ok github.com/gablooge/lawang/internal/ids`. After changing the constant to `github.com/gablooge/lawang/internal/ids`: `callers_test.go:39: internal/outbox/zz_probe_caller.go refers to ids.RecordID`.

**Suggested direction:** in the follow-up commit, rename the whole repository by string, not by import fixer, so this constant travels with the imports. A plain `git grep -n gablooge/sluiceway` after the follow-up would also catch it. The stale `"cmd/sluiceway/main.go": true` entry in the same file's path table is harmless (the new path classifies the same way) but should go with it. Nothing to do on this pull request.

**F5 note. `CLAUDE.md:96` still names the zone.** The hostname is gone, but the row for `cloudflare.env` still names the variable `CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN_<owner>`, which tells a reader of the public repository which zone the tunnel lives in. Only the subdomain label is missing, and a label is cheap to guess from the project name. The cost is small and this is your call, not a defect: rename the variable to something zone-neutral if you want the removal to be complete, or leave it, since the zone is your public personal domain anyway.

**F6 note. The description says something the code does not do.** It claims the rename touched "the `depguard` allowlist in `.golangci.yml`". There is no `depguard` linter configured, on `main` or on this head. The one changed line in that file is `formatters.goimports.local-prefixes`, which is the more important of the two anyway (see the #43 note above). Worth correcting so the description describes the code as it is.

**F7 note, expected, not blocking.** `ghcr.io/gablooge/lawang:v0.1.0` in `docs/backlog.md`, and the `github.com/gablooge/lawang/issues` and `/milestones` links, are dead until you rename the repository on GitHub. After the rename GitHub redirects the old paths, so renaming these now is the right order. Noted here only so it is a known state and not a surprise.

**F8 note. `CLAUDE.md:100` says the repository "is public".** It is not yet, and line 3 of the same file says "private until v0.1.0". The sentence is a justification that becomes true soon, so the content is right, but the tense is not. "it will be public" costs nothing and removes a contradiction inside one file.

### The tunnel paragraph, checked line by line

No real hostname survives anywhere in the diff or the tree: `git grep -inE '<owner>|lawang-dev|sluiceway-dev'` returns exactly one line, the `CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN_<owner>` variable name of F5. The operational content is intact: the `docker run --rm --name lawang-tunnel` with `--env-file ~/.config/lawang/cloudflare-tunnel.env` and the pinned `cloudflare/cloudflared:2026.9.1`; the `^/ingress/[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$` rule with the `/ingress/../x` history and "do not loosen the rule"; the ADR 3 grammar sentence and the requirement that the provider registry enforce it from the same function; stopping the container and deregistering the webhooks; and "everything that arrives through it is hostile input". The credential directory is documented as `~/.config/lawang/` in `CLAUDE.md`, `implementer.md`, `pr-reviewer.md` and `bizdev.md`, and the variable is `LAWANG_CREDENTIALS_DIR`.

### Smaller things I checked and found correct

- The README's new sentence is two lines, plain, and true, and it sits above the pitch where a stranger meets the name first. The status paragraph below it is still accurate.
- The backlog log line (`docs/backlog.md:239`) records the date, what changed, why it had to happen before v0.1, that there is no migration path, and the two things in the same commit that are not a rename.
- `cmd/sluiceway` to `cmd/lawang` was a real `git mv`: the diff shows `cmd/{sluiceway => lawang}/`, so history follows.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `sqlc.yaml` genuinely never named the project, as claimed.
- `internal/ids/testdata/golden.json` is untouched, which is what the recipes promise.
- The generated `internal/outbox/outboxdb/queries.sql.go` is consistent with the migrations: `sqlc diff` is clean.
- No renamed string had to match an external system. The only external names in the tree are image tags (`postgres:17-alpine`, `sqlc/sqlc:1.31.1`, `cloudflare/cloudflared:2026.9.1`) and they are untouched.
title: Review on PR #44 (commented)

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 1

**Verdict: changes requested**

One blocking finding, five should-fix, six notes. `make check` is green on `04459d8` (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`), with no `--- SKIP` anywhere and the container-backed packages taking their usual time (`outbox` 17.7 s, `store` 19.3 s), so nothing silently skipped. CI green. No trailer on the commit (git's own parser reports none), no tool attribution in the diff or in the pull request body, no em dash in either, no control or invisible character in any touched file. Nothing under `.claude/` or `CLAUDE.md` is touched, so an ordinary verdict applies.

**The two acceptance lines hold under my own experiments, not only under the suite's.**

*Byte identity.* Over a real `httptest` server, with both a known `Content-Length` and chunked transfer, the hub received the exact bytes for: a duplicate JSON key, `1.0` and `1e2` and a 30 digit integer, escaped unicode including an escaped NUL and a surrogate pair, a lone unpaired surrogate escape, a leading UTF-8 BOM, and a body with raw `\xff\xfe` inside a string. A `Content-Length` that understates the body (5 promised, 20 sent) hands the hub exactly the 5 declared bytes and answers 202, which is `net/http`'s framing and not something this edge loosens.

*Memory.* Measured, not assumed. Against the 1 MiB default cap, a body of unknown length costs the handler a constant **4.00 MiB of allocation whether the body is 2 MiB, 10 MiB, 64 MiB or 256 MiB** (`runtime.MemStats` delta around one `ServeHTTP`, status 413 each time). So the cost is bounded by the cap and not by what the sender sends, which is what the acceptance line asks. Two numbers worth keeping: a body at exactly the cap with an honest length costs 1.02 MiB and lands in a buffer of 1,056,768 bytes (the pre-sizing works), while the same body with an unknown length costs 4.01 MiB and lands in a buffer of 2,097,152 bytes, because `bytes.Buffer` doubles. See note N2.

*Decision 2, by identity rather than by value.* At the edge, not only in the registry test: the string the hub is handed has the same `unsafe.StringData` as the compile-time constant `fake.DefaultKey`, so it is the program's own constant and not the decoded path segment. Over a real server, `/ingress/%00`, `/ingress/fa%00ke`, a 500 byte segment of `%01%ff%00qZ`, `/ingress/fake%2f..%2f..%2fetc`, `/ingress/FAKE` and `/ingress/fake%20` all answer 404 with the body `no such provider` and the hub never called.

*Decision 4, against a real Postgres.* `testdb` container, `store.Open(... &pool_max_conns=1)`, a hub that runs one `db.Tx` with `SELECT pg_sleep(1)`, 8 concurrent deliveries, `AcceptTimeout` 300 ms. All 8 answered **503 with `Retry-After: 5` in 303 ms**, none queued, none 500. The error mapping survives the real pool: 7 acquires returned `context.deadlineExceededError` and the one already in a query returned `*pgconn.errTimeout`, and `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)` is true for both, so `store.scrub` does not eat it. See note N1 for the one case that would still land on 500.

**Judgement on the 404 and on the verdict mapping.** The 404 is safe and I would keep it. Nothing has happened when it is answered, no body read and nothing stored, so there is nothing for a retry to fix; a real provider only ever posts to the URL Lawang gave it; and the unknown case and the registered-but-not-a-`WebhookSource` case are byte-identical from outside, including the absence of any header that would separate them. It leaks nothing useful either: provider keys are guessable words, and a scanner learns the same thing from the fact that `/ingress/slack` answers at all. Walking every return in `ServeHTTP`, the statuses a real provider can receive that are not a signature failure are 404 (its provider is not a webhook source, a wiring bug, see finding 2), 413, 400, 503 and 500, plus whatever 2xx or 4xx its own handshake asks for. Every one of those is now in the architecture 3.1 table, so there is no drift. The verdict mapping itself is right for what a provider does on receipt: 202 and 200 stop the retry, 401 is the only authentication signal, 503 carries a `Retry-After` that every provider honours, and a zero verdict is a 500 rather than a silent 200.

**Will the interfaces carry B07, B11 and B15?** B07 and B11 yes: the hub seam gets the entry, the exact bytes and the headers, which is everything the resolve, the per-candidate verify and the outbox insert need, and ClickUp signs the body alone. B15 yes: Slack's v0 base string is built from the body and the `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp` header, both present. **B18 no**, and that is finding 1 below.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | both "Done when" lines and the five decisions in the issue comments, each re-run as my own experiment (byte identity over real HTTP, allocation measured, real saturated pool, key identity at the edge) | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 15 mutations of my own, listed below, a meaningful sample of the implementer's 26 plus new ones | 1 blocking |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of the four changed packages (ingress 100%, provider 100%, fake 99.0%, record 100%; the only uncovered line is the unreachable `json.Marshal` error), error paths, boundaries, `-race -count=3` three times clean | 1 blocking (the hole coverage did not show), 1 note |
| Correctness | every return in `ServeHTTP` mapped to the contract, the cancelled-sender branch, `readBody`'s three exits, the shallow request copy, the zero verdict | 1 note |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | no tenant anywhere in this package, no database, no credential read, no live test, no fixture holding anything token-shaped (searched for `xoxb-`, `pat-`, `pk_`, `eyJ`, long hex and base64 runs), test secrets are obvious literals, `ErrBadOrderingKey` has no path to a 5xx | 0 |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | body cap in front of everything that touches the body, pre-allocation bounded separately, handshake reply bounded, accept bounded, path segment used only as a map key, constant-time compare with a fail-closed missing secret, no new dependency, `govulncheck` is not installed on this machine so it was not run | 3 should-fix |
| Performance | allocation measured at four body sizes and at the cap, the real pool saturation run above, no query in this change | 1 note |
| Dead code | searched for callers of every new exported identifier | 1 note |
| Codebase improvement | the interface set against B18's stated needs, the duplicated `printableASCII`, the unwired edge | 1 should-fix, 1 note |
| Documentation | architecture 3.1, 4, 7, 8 and 11 against the code, backlog tick and log line, README status paragraph, the roadmap's open-decision table (no entry matches this change, so no ADR is owed), doc comments on every exported identifier, the pull request description against the code as it now is | 1 should-fix |

### Mutations I ran

Each was applied to the detached checkout, the relevant tests run, then `git checkout -- .`.

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | the registry carries its own hand-written key pattern (hyphen allowed) instead of calling `record.ValidProviderKey` | caught, `TestTheRegistryCannotDriftFromTheRecordFormat` fails on `"a-"` |
| R2 | `record.ValidProviderKey` itself loosened to allow a hyphen, so the registry and the record agree and drift together | caught, the record schema cross-check and `TestNormalizeRefusesAnObjectItCannotTurnIntoARecord` fail. The grammar is pinned in both directions, not only relative to itself |
| R3 | `Lookup` hands back the caller's own string | caught, `TestLookupReturnsTheRegistrysStringAndNotTheCallers` |
| R4 | `http.MaxBytesReader` removed | caught, three subtests, including the endless body that now hangs until the 10 s deadline |
| R5 | the cap off by one (`maxBody+1`) | caught, only by the unknown-length case, which is exactly the fixture the implementer added after its own first pass |
| R6 | the handshake runs after the hub | caught, all three handshake cases |
| R7 | `Parked` answers 500 | caught, `TestTheVerdictDecidesTheStatus/parked` |
| R8 | the handshake gets a readable body | caught, `TestTheHandshakeCannotReadTheBodyTwice` |
| R9 | the content type check removed from `writeReply` | caught, the newline case is 200 instead of 500 (no header was actually injected, because `net/http` sanitizes, so this test earns its keep by the status alone) |
| R10 | the accept is not bounded (`WithCancel` instead of `WithTimeout`) | caught, `TestASaturatedAcceptPathAnswersFastWithARetryableStatus` |
| R11 | the 404 echoes the path segment and logs it | caught, several subtests including the 500 byte segment |
| R12 | the fake verifies with an empty secret | caught |
| R13 | the fake takes the first of two signature headers | caught |
| R14 | the fake stops refusing unknown fields | caught |
| R15 | **the fake stops checking `utf8.Valid`** | **survived**, `go test ./...` fully green. Finding 1 |

### Findings that are not inline

**N1 (note). The 503 rests on `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)`, and B07 can break it without touching this file.** My real-pool run shows the two error shapes pgx produces today both match, so this is right as it stands. The shape that would not match is a statement cancelled server side, which comes back as `*pgconn.PgError` SQLSTATE 57014 ("canceling statement due to user request") with no context error inside it; that lands on the `err != nil` branch and answers 500 with an error line, where the honest answer is 503 with a `Retry-After`. Cheap insurance when the hub lands: treat `ctx.Err() != nil` after the call as the deadline case too, rather than only the error's own chain.

**N2 (note). A chunked body at the cap holds twice the cap, and an oversize one churns four times it.** Measured above: 1.02 MiB allocated and a 1,056,768 byte buffer when the length is announced, against 4.01 MiB allocated and a 2,097,152 byte buffer when it is not. With the 1 MiB default and webhook-sized bodies this is nothing, but the live cost per in-flight chunked request is 2x `MaxBody`, which is what an operator who raises `MaxBody` for Microsoft Graph would be sizing the container against. A single `make([]byte, 0, maxBody+1)` read with `io.ReadFull`-style accounting would make it 1x for both paths. Not worth changing now, worth knowing before `MaxBody` is ever raised.

**N3 (note). Two exported methods have no caller outside tests: `provider.Registry.Keys` and `provider.Entry.Provider`.** `Handler`, `Pattern` and `Mount` are a different case and I agree with the reasoning in the description: they are this item's deliverable, B07 wires them, and a 503 stub in `serve` would be a worse thing to own than an unmounted route. `Keys` and `Provider` are speculative API with no named future caller in the description. Both are one line and harmless; the cost is only that a later item inherits them as contract. Say which item needs them, or drop them until it arrives.

**N4 (note). `Handshake` parses unauthenticated bytes on the accept path, for every delivery and not only for a challenge.** The fake runs a full strict JSON decode of up to `MaxBody` before anything is verified. That is inherent to the hook (a challenge arrives before any subscription exists), and the 200 ms target has room, but it is the one place where a stranger's bytes drive real work before verification. Worth a line in the `WebhookSource.Handshake` doc comment telling a provider author to look at a cheap header or query discriminator first and only then parse, which is what Slack and Graph both allow.

**N5 (note). "`Verify` never errors and never panics" is documented and cannot be enforced.** Nothing here can make it true, and a panic would be recovered per connection by `net/http` and seen by the provider as a dropped response rather than a status. B07 is where it matters, because `Verify` runs once per candidate subscription: consider recovering around the per-candidate loop there so one provider's panic parks a delivery rather than dropping the connection.

**N6 (note). `printableASCII` is now written twice, in `internal/ingress/ingress.go` and in `internal/provider/fake/fake.go`, with identical bodies and no test tying them together.** The two serve different purposes (one guards a response header, one guards a provider id), so this is not the `ValidProviderKey` situation and I am not asking for a shared helper. It is only worth knowing that the next provider package will write it a third time, and that is the point at which it should move somewhere shared with a test.

### On the two mutations the description says survived its first pass

Both fixes are real: R5 confirms the unknown-length fixture is what catches the off-by-one, and the `event` fixture in `fake_test.go` is now genuinely out of field order with whitespace in it, so a provider that re-serialized its payload would fail. The lesson did not reach the third fixture of the same kind, which is finding 1.

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 2

**Verdict: changes requested**

1 blocking, 2 should-fix, 7 notes. The round 1 blocking finding is fixed and I confirmed it by
re-running my own mutation. The blocking finding this round is in the new work, in
`config.NormalizePublicBaseURL`, which is the function the whole signed-URL argument rests on.

`make check` is green on `820b08d` (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`),
with no `--- SKIP` anywhere and the container-backed packages taking their usual time (`record`
26.8 s, `store` 19.1 s, `outbox` 17.8 s), so nothing was silently skipped. CI green.
`go test -race -count=2` on the four changed packages is clean. Coverage: `internal/ingress` 100%,
`internal/provider` 100%, `internal/provider/fake` 99.0% (`Handshake` 92.9%, the rest the
unreachable `json.Marshal` error), `internal/config` 100%. Git's own trailer parser reports no
trailer on either commit; no tool attribution in the diff, in the description or in a comment; no
em dash and in fact no non-ASCII byte at all in the diff; no token shape (`xoxb-`, `pat-`, `pk_`,
`eyJ`, long hex or base64). No new dependency (`mime`, `slices` and `path` are standard library).
`govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so it was not run. Nothing under `.claude/` or
`CLAUDE.md` is touched, so an ordinary verdict applies.

### Round 1, finding by finding

| Round 1 | Status | How I checked, not how it was answered |
|---|---|---|
| **blocking** `utf8.Valid` survives its mutation | **fixed** | I deleted the line (and its import) again: six of the seven cases of `TestBytesThatAreNotUTF8AreRefusedBeforeTheDecoder` fail. The `json.Valid` guard is honest, not decorative: I broke one fixture into something that is not valid JSON and the test failed with "this fixture no longer isolates the UTF-8 check" rather than passing. |
| should-fix `Verify` cannot carry HubSpot v3 | **fixed** | `provider.Request{Method, URL, Header, Body}`, and `Hub.Accept` takes the same value. Dropping `Method` or `Header` from what the edge fills in is caught. See "does it carry B07 to B18" below. |
| should-fix the silent not-a-`WebhookSource` 404 | **fixed** | Removing the `Warn` line fails `TestARegisteredProviderThatIsNotAWebhookSourceIsLoggedAndStill404`; the response stays byte-identical to the unregistered 404 and that test asserts it. |
| should-fix the handshake content type | **fixed** | Dropping the 64 byte cap, the media type allowlist or the parameter check each fails `TestAHandshakeReplyAProviderMayNotAskForIsRefused`. |
| should-fix 401 from a handshake | **fixed** | Allowing 401 again fails the same test. |
| should-fix the README status paragraph | **fixed** | It now names B07 and says a POST is a 404 from the mux. |
| N3 `Registry.Keys` and `Entry.Provider` | **resolved** | `Keys` is gone; `Provider` keeps a doc comment naming B08. |
| N6 duplicated `printableASCII` | **resolved** | One copy left, in `internal/provider/fake`. |
| N1, N4, N5 | **carried into the design** | Architecture 7 now carries all three under "Three things a provider author has to know". |
| N2 (2x `MaxBody` for a chunked body) | **open, still a note** | Unchanged and still fine at the 1 MiB default. |

**On the two further untested checks the implementer found, and the one it kept.** Both are real
and both are now caught: deleting `len(ev.ExternalID) > maxProviderID` fails
`TestParseRefusesAnEventThisProviderWouldNotHaveSent/external_id_too_long`, and deleting
`ev.OccurredAt = ev.OccurredAt.UTC()` fails `TestAnOffsetTimeIsNormalizedToUTC` (I checked that the
UTC assertion is the one with teeth: the `Equal` assertion alone would pass either way, because it
compares instants). **The judgement on `len(want) != sha256.Size` is right.** I deleted the disjunct
and ran `TestVerifyRefusesEverythingARealProviderRefuses`: green, including `signature is short` and
`signature is long`, so the behaviour is pinned by tests that do not depend on which line implements
it and the line genuinely changes no answer. Keeping it with a comment that says so is honest;
deleting it would lose no coverage either. That is note N7 below and needs no action.

**My own sweep for the same shape.** I mutated twenty more checks across the three touched
packages, chosen for looking like they might be satisfied by a neighbouring layer: every one was
caught (table below). I did not find a fourth instance of the pattern.

### The new work: what I attacked and what I found

**The URL the edge computes.** Over a real TCP connection with hand-written request lines, against
a base of `https://lawang.example.test`, with `Host`, `X-Forwarded-Host` and friends all set to
`attacker.example`:

| Request line | Answer | What the edge signs |
|---|---|---|
| `/ingress/fake` | 202 | `https://lawang.example.test/ingress/fake` |
| `/ingress/fake/` | 404 (mux, pattern has no trailing slash) | not called |
| `//ingress/fake` | **307**, `Location: /ingress/fake` | not called |
| `/ingress//fake` | **307**, `Location: /ingress/fake` | not called |
| `/ingress/fake/../fake` | **307**, `Location: /ingress/fake` | not called |
| `/ingress/fake/..%2ffake` | 404 (`%2f` is not a separator for the mux) | not called |
| `/ingress/%66ake`, `/ingress/fak%65` | 202 | the escaped spelling verbatim, `.../ingress/%66ake` |
| `/ingress/FAKE`, `/ingress/fake;x=1` | 404 | not called |
| `/ingress/fake?a=1&a=2` | 202 | `...?a=1&a=2`, repeats kept in order |
| `/ingress/fake?` (bare) | 202 | `...?`, the bare question mark survives (`ForceQuery`) |
| `/ingress/fake?a=%2Fb`, `?a=/b`, `?a=%c3%a9`, `?a=%C3%A9` | 202 | raw query verbatim, hex case included |
| `/ingress/fake?a=1#frag` | 202 | `...?a=1#frag`. A fragment cannot reach the server as a fragment: `url.ParseRequestURI` does not split one in a request line, so it lands in `RawQuery` and is signed as sent. |
| a 4000 byte query | 202 | signed in full (bounded only by `MaxHeaderBytes`) |
| `POST http://attacker.example/ingress/fake?a=1` (absolute URI) | 202 | `https://lawang.example.test/ingress/fake?a=1`, the attacker's host discarded |

So: **no request can put a byte of its own choosing into the base part**, and I could not make two
different requests produce the same signed string. The split at the first `?` is unambiguous (a raw
`?` cannot appear in the path, and `EscapedPath` keeps `%3F`), so `EscapedPath + "?" + RawQuery` is
injective. The three 307s are the interesting result and are finding 2.

**`NormalizePublicBaseURL`.** It refuses what the implementer claims: credentials, a query, a bare
`?`, a fragment, a non-http scheme, no host, `..`, `.`, `//` inside the path, a control character,
a scheme-relative URL, a path-only value. It is idempotent on everything in its own accepted table.
It is **not** idempotent on two shapes that are not in that table, and both produce a wrong signed
string or a startup failure. That is finding 1.

On the questions you asked that are not defects: a default port is kept (`https://x:443` stays
`https://x:443`) and an uppercase host is kept (`https://EXAMPLE.com` stays). I think keeping both
is the right call and I am not asking for a change, because the string has to match the spelling in
the provider's own dashboard, and lowercasing a host the operator copied from there would create the
mismatch rather than remove it. It is worth one clause in the doc comment saying so, because "owns
the one spelling" reads as if it canonicalizes and it deliberately does not (note N3). An IPv6
literal (`https://[::1]:8443`), a unicode host and a punycode host all pass through unchanged, and a
path prefix works (`https://x/lawang` plus `/ingress/fake` gives `https://x/lawang/ingress/fake`),
which is the reverse-proxy case.

**Fail closed when unset.** Verified: with no base configured the edge still serves, `Request.URL`
is `""`, and a HubSpot-shaped verifier returns false, so the delivery is 401. Making the empty case
guess from `r.Host` instead is caught by
`TestWithNoPublicBaseURLTheEdgeServesAndAURLSigningProviderRefuses`. The behaviour is right. What is
missing is any signal to the operator, which is finding 3.

**`provider.Request` against B07, B11, B15 and B18.** B07 gets the entry, the exact bytes and the
headers, which is what a resolve, a per-candidate verify and an outbox insert need. B11 (ClickUp,
body only) and B15 (Slack v0, `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp` and the body) are covered. B18 (HubSpot
v3: method, full public URI, body, `X-HubSpot-Request-Timestamp`) is covered, which was the point of
the change. Nothing is missing that would break an implementation later, because `Request` is a
struct: a field added in B15 or B18 costs its authors nothing, which is the reason not to invent one
now. Two things a later item will want and does not have: a receive timestamp, for Slack's and
HubSpot's replay windows (an implementation will otherwise call `time.Now()` inside `Verify`, which
makes the window untestable without a clock), and nothing for TLS state, which nothing needs behind
a tunnel. Both are notes, N1 and N2, not asks.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | both "Done when" lines re-proved by mutation after the refactor (A1 to A3 below), plus the five decisions in the issue comments, which round 1 checked and the delta does not touch | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 26 mutations of my own this round: the three round 1 ones re-run, 20 new ones over the delta, 3 acceptance ones. All 26 caught. The honesty of the new `json.Valid` guard probed directly | 0 |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of the four changed packages, the accepted and refused tables of the normalizer against inputs they do not contain, the Load-then-New composition | 1 blocking (the two input shapes neither table has) |
| Correctness | the mux's behaviour in front of the handler over a real socket, `publicURL` on 21 request lines, `Load` then `New` on the same value | 1 should-fix |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | no tenant, no database, no credential read, no live test in this change; no fixture holding anything token-shaped; the normalizer's refusals never echo their input (a database URL pasted into the wrong variable stays unprinted), and `Config.String` still redacts | 0 |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | whether a sender can steer any byte of the signed URL (it cannot), whether two requests can collide on one signed string (they cannot), the handshake reply allowlist, the body cap, no new dependency, `govulncheck` not installed | 0 |
| Performance | no query in this change; `publicURL` is one concatenation per request, `mime.ParseMediaType` runs only on a handshake reply and only on at most 64 bytes, `slices.Contains` over two entries. Nothing here grows with anything | 0 |
| Dead code | searched for callers of every new exported identifier: `config.NormalizePublicBaseURL` has two, `Config.PublicBaseURL` has none outside `config` itself and `provider.Request.Method` has no reader, both justified by B07 and B18 | 2 notes |
| Codebase improvement | the `internal/ingress` to `internal/config` edge, `Request.Header` being the live map, the normalizer's contract | 3 notes |
| Documentation | architecture 3.1, 4 and 7 against the code, the backlog log line, the README paragraph, the usage text, doc comments on every new exported identifier, the description against the code as it now is | folded into finding 1 (three documents state the postcondition the function does not keep) |

### Mutations and probes

Round 1 findings, re-run:

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | `utf8.Valid` deleted from `decodeStrict` (and the import) | **caught**, six subtests of `TestBytesThatAreNotUTF8AreRefusedBeforeTheDecoder` |
| R2 | the `external_id` length bound dropped | **caught**, `.../external_id_too_long` |
| R3 | `occurred_at` not normalized to UTC | **caught**, `TestAnOffsetTimeIsNormalizedToUTC` |
| R4 | `len(want) != sha256.Size` dropped | survives, correctly: the behaviour is pinned by `signature is short` and `signature is long`, which stay green because `hmac.Equal` refuses a short digest |
| P1 | one UTF-8 fixture broken into invalid JSON | the test **fails loudly** with its own "this fixture no longer isolates the UTF-8 check" message |

The delta, twenty mutations, all caught:

| # | Mutation | Test that failed |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | the percent-encoded prefix check dropped | `TestThePublicBaseURLIsNormalizedAndNeverGuessed` |
| M2 | the credentials check dropped | same, and `TestNewRefusesAPublicBaseURLItCannotUse` |
| M3 | `ForceQuery` dropped from the query check | `TestThePublicBaseURLIsNormalizedAndNeverGuessed` |
| M4 | the fragment check dropped | same |
| M5 | the trailing slash kept | same, and `TestLoadCarriesThePublicBaseURLThrough` |
| M6 | the `path.Clean` check dropped | same |
| M7 | any scheme allowed | same |
| M8 | the host check dropped | same, and `TestNewRefusesAPublicBaseURLItCannotUse` |
| M9 | `Load` ignores `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | `TestVariablesAreExactlyWhatLoadReads` and two more |
| M10 | `ingress.New` keeps the raw spelling instead of the normalized one | `TestTheSignedURLComesFromConfigurationAndNeverFromTheRequest` |
| M11 | `publicURL` drops the query | same |
| M12 | `publicURL` falls back to `r.Host` when the base is empty | `TestWithNoPublicBaseURLTheEdgeServesAndAURLSigningProviderRefuses` |
| M13 | `Method` not carried into `Request` | `TestTheSignedURLComesFromConfiguration...` |
| M14 | `Header` not carried | three tests, including `TestConcurrentDeliveriesKeepTheirOwnBodies` |
| M15 | `handshakeStatus` allows 401 again | `TestAHandshakeReplyAProviderMayNotAskForIsRefused` |
| M16 | the content type length cap dropped | same |
| M17 | the media type allowlist dropped | same |
| M18 | the content type parameters unchecked | same |
| M19 | the not-a-`WebhookSource` warn line removed | `TestARegisteredProviderThatIsNotAWebhookSourceIsLoggedAndStill404` |
| M20 | the warn line demoted (covered by M19's handler level) | same |

Acceptance, re-proved after the refactor:

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | `http.MaxBytesReader` removed | caught, `TestAnOversizeBodyIsRefusedWithoutBeingReadIntoMemory` |
| A2 | the edge trims the body before handing it on | caught, `TestTheVerifierGetsByteIdenticalInput` |
| A3 | the honest `Content-Length` refusal never fires | caught, `TestAnOversizeBodyIsRefused...` |

### Findings that are not inline

**Finding 3 (should-fix) is inline on `Options.PublicBaseURL`. The notes:**

**N1 (note, for B15 and B18). `Request` has no receive timestamp.** Slack and HubSpot both want a
replay window (Slack's guidance is to refuse a timestamp more than five minutes old), and with no
field for it an implementation will call `time.Now()` inside `Verify`, which makes the window
impossible to test without smuggling a clock into the provider. Adding a field later is free,
because `Request` is a struct, so this is not an ask now: it is a line for B15's issue.

**N2 (note). `Request.Header` is the request's live map, and "read-only" is only a comment.** In B07
`Verify` runs once per candidate over the same `Request`. A provider that calls `Header.Set` or
`Header.Del` (normalizing a signature header, say) changes what every later candidate sees, and the
symptom is an intermittent signature failure on the second candidate only. One clone in B07's
per-candidate loop, or one more clause on `Hub.Accept`, closes it.

**N3 (note). "owns the spelling" reads stronger than what the function does.** It normalizes the
scheme case, a trailing slash and a path prefix, and deliberately leaves the host case and a default
port alone. I agree with leaving them alone (the string has to match the provider dashboard, which
the operator copied from), but the doc comment would be better for saying which spellings it does
not touch, since the next person to debug a 401 will go looking there first.

**N4 (note). `internal/ingress` now imports `internal/config`, and I would move the function
instead.** It is acyclic today and the one-owner property is worth having. The cost is the direction:
`Options.MaxBody` and `Options.AcceptTimeout` are exactly the shape of a future `LAWANG_MAX_BODY`,
and on the day `config` wants `ingress.DefaultMaxBody` for its documented default the cycle is
there and the fix is this move under time pressure. What I would do: put `NormalizePublicBaseURL`
in a leaf of its own (or in `internal/provider`, next to `Request.URL`, whose contract it serves)
and have `config` and `ingress` both call it. That keeps the single owner and leaves the HTTP edge
independent of environment parsing. Not blocking anything today.

**N5 (note). `Request.Method` can only ever be `"POST"`.** `Pattern` is `POST /ingress/{provider}`,
so the mux answers 405 or 404 for anything else and the handler never sees another method. Inline
on the doc comment.

**N6 (note, for B07). The mux's 307 puts a cleaned path into a `Location` header before the handler
runs.** The package comment's "no path segment reaches a log line or a response" is true of the
handler and not of the route it is mounted on. The tunnel refuses those paths and `serve` does not
mount the route yet, so there is nothing to do here; it belongs next to B07's wiring.

**N7 (note). `len(want) != sha256.Size`:** covered above, the call is right, no action.

**N8 (note). `!strings.HasPrefix(p, "/")` in `NormalizePublicBaseURL` looks unreachable.** A URL that
got past the host check always has an absolute or an empty path, and I could not construct an input
that reaches that disjunct. Statement coverage reads 100% because it is a disjunct and not a
statement. Harmless, and cheaper to notice now than in a year.

text:
## Review, round 3

**Verdict: approved**

0 blocking, 5 should-fix, 4 notes. Round 2's blocking finding and both should-fix findings are
fixed, and I confirmed each by reproducing the defect first and then the fix, not by reading the
reply. The five should-fix findings are all in the new work; none of them makes the change unsafe
to merge and none of them is a mutation that survives, so the cycle does not need the maintainer.

`make check` is green on `b64f6af` (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test
-race`), with **no `--- SKIP` anywhere** and the container-backed packages at their usual cost
(`record` 26.9 s, `store` 19.7 s, `outbox` 17.3 s), so nothing was silently skipped. CI is green on
this exact head sha. `go test -race -count=2` over the four changed packages is clean and
deterministic. Coverage: `internal/config` 100%, `internal/provider` 100%, `internal/provider/fake`
99.0%, `internal/ingress` 99.2% (the gap is one branch, finding 4). Git's own trailer parser
reports no trailer on any of the three commits; no tool attribution in the diff, the description or
a comment; no em dash anywhere in the diff or in the description; the only non-ASCII bytes in the
delta are two `cafe` fixtures that exist to test a non-ASCII path prefix; no token shape (`xoxb-`,
`pat-`, `pk_`, `eyJ`, long hex or base64). No new dependency (`path` and `slices` are standard
library). `govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so it was not run. Nothing under
`.claude/` or `CLAUDE.md` is touched, so an ordinary verdict applies.

### Round 2, finding by finding

| Round 2 | Status | How I checked, not how it was answered |
|---|---|---|
| **blocking** `NormalizePublicBaseURL` is not idempotent on `https://x//` and `https://x/a%20b` | **fixed** | Both shapes are refused or fixed-point now. More to the point I wrote **my own corpus**, without reading theirs: 79 targeted shapes (IDN and punycode hosts, an IPv6 zone id, `http://@host`, `http://:8080`, a non-numeric and an empty port, a 5000 byte host, upper and lower case escapes, a path of exactly `/`, `\`, `%`, `%zz`, a tab, a newline) plus 400,000 randomized strings, held to a **stronger** postcondition than theirs: idempotent, no trailing slash, parses, and the answer concatenated with `/ingress/fake?a=1` parses back with the same host, a path ending in the request path and the query intact. 25,958 random inputs were accepted and every one held. I then ran `FuzzNormalizePublicBaseURL` myself: **183,552,075 executions, 4 minutes, no counterexample** (52 new interesting inputs, all of which held). I could not find a third shape. |
| should-fix the mux answers 307, it does not refuse | **fixed** | Reproduced on this very commit over a real socket: serving the bare mux, `//ingress/fake`, `/ingress//fake` and `/ingress/fake/../fake` each answer `307` with `Location: /ingress/fake`. Serving what `Mount` returns, all three answer 404 with no `Location` and a body byte-identical to the unknown-provider answer. The comment is corrected too. Two caveats about how exact the guard is, findings 2 and 4. |
| should-fix an unset `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is silent | **fixed** | The `Warn` names the variable and says 401. I re-ran all three mutations: removing it, demoting it to `Debug` and making it unconditional each fail `TestAnUnsetPublicBaseURLIsSaidOutLoudAtStart`. The quiet assertion on the configured case has teeth. |
| N2 `Request.Header` is the live map | **fixed, and better than asked** | I attacked the wrapper from another package by every reflection-free means: there is no exported field, it is a struct so there is nothing to type-assert to, embedding promotes the methods only, a struct copy aliases nothing writable, `Values` returns `slices.Clone` and `[]string` of immutable strings is deep enough, and the zero value reads as empty rather than panicking. **Their argument that a clone would not have fixed it is correct**, and I proved it: with one `Request` per delivery and `Verify` once per candidate, a per-request clone still lets candidate 1 change what candidate 2 reads (`"first"` becomes `"normalized"` for the second reader). See note N1 for the one property the wrapper does not have. |
| N1 no receive timestamp | **deferred to B15, accepted** | Recorded on #15 with the argument for it. Adding a field to a struct breaks no implementation, which is the reason `Request` is a struct. |
| N3 "owns the spelling" oversold | **fixed** | The doc comment has a "What it deliberately does not touch" section. I mutated the function to lowercase the host: caught by the `https://EXAMPLE.com:443` row. |
| N4 move the normalizer out of `internal/config` | **disputed, and I accept the dispute** | See the last section. |
| N5 `Request.Method` "as the sender spelled it" | **fixed** | The comment now says it is always POST and why the field exists. |
| N6 the 307 puts a cleaned path in a `Location` | **fixed here rather than deferred** | Same fix as finding 2. |
| N7, N8 | **resolved** | N8's disjunct is gone and its premise is asserted in `checkNormalizedFixedPoint` instead, which is the right place: a guard nobody can trip proves nothing, an assertion that would fire proves the premise. |
| round 1 N2 (2x `MaxBody` on a chunked body) | **open, still a note** | Unchanged and still fine at the 1 MiB default. |

I withdraw nothing: every round 2 finding reproduced on `820b08d` before I checked the fix.

### Coverage

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | the two "Done when" lines of #6 are untouched by this delta, and I re-proved the two the delta could have broken (the body cap, byte-identical input) by mutation after the refactor | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 10 mutations of my own this round (table below), all caught, including the four the implementer claims and three they do not | 0 |
| Tests are comprehensive | my own corpus and fuzz run against the normalizer (above), coverage of the four changed packages line by line, the guard's branches over a real socket | 1 should-fix (finding 4) |
| Correctness | `canonicalPath` against `net/http`'s own `cleanPath` and `findHandler` in the Go 1.26.7 source, 18 hand-written request lines over a real socket against both the guarded and the unguarded wiring, the `Header` wrapper from outside its package | 2 should-fix (findings 2, 3) |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | no tenant, no database, no credential and no live test in this delta; the guard's 404 carries no sender-controlled byte (fixed string, `nosniff`, fixed content type) and logs nothing, so no log forging; the normalizer's refusals still never echo their input, which matters because a database URL pasted into the wrong variable lands here | 0 |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | whether the host `%` refusal refuses a legitimate host (it does not: `[::1]`, `[::1]:8443`, `xn--80ak6aa92e.com` and an IDN host are all accepted, only a zone id and an escape are refused), whether a sender can still steer a byte of the signed URL through the guard (it cannot), whether an absolute-form or asterisk-form request line gets past it (it does not), no new dependency | 1 should-fix (finding 1) |
| Performance | the guard runs per request on the accept path: `canonicalPath("/ingress/fake")` is **11.6 ns/op, 0 B/op, 0 allocs/op** (`path.Clean` returns its input without allocating when the path is already clean), against a 200 ms accept target. Nothing else in the delta runs per request | 0 |
| Dead code | searched for callers of every identifier the delta adds: `provider.Header`, `NewHeader` and `Values` have production callers, `Get` has only test callers today (note N2), `canonicalPath` and `canonicalPathOnly` are called by `Mount`, and the `!strings.HasPrefix(p, "/")` disjunct N8 asked about is gone | 0 |
| Codebase improvement | the `Mount` signature's failure mode, the `Header` wrapper's boundary, `Request.Body` as the one field the fix did not cover | 2 should-fix (findings 3, 5) |
| Documentation | architecture 3.1, 4 and 7 against the code line by line, the backlog log line, the README paragraph, the usage text, the doc comments on everything new, the description against the code as it now is | 1 should-fix (finding 5) |

### Mutations and probes

| # | Mutation or probe | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | `TrimRight` back to `TrimSuffix` | **caught**: the property plus five rows ("`https://lawang.example.test:8443//` = `...:8443/`, want `...:8443`") |
| M2 | `EscapedPath() != Path` back to `RawPath != ""` | **caught**: the property, on the escaped space, hash and question mark, with the message naming the second-pass refusal |
| M3 | the host `%` check deleted | **caught**: `http://%25` and the IPv6 zone id rows |
| M4 | the answer rebuilt with `(&url.URL{...}).String()` | **caught**: `/a!b` comes back `%21` |
| M5 | the host lowercased (my own, not theirs) | **caught**: the `EXAMPLE.com:443` row, so "deliberately does not touch" is pinned and not just documented |
| M6 | `Header.Values` returns the live slice | **caught**: `TestAHeaderCannotBeUsedToChangeWhatTheNextCandidateReads`, and my own probe |
| M7 | `Mount` returns the bare mux | **caught**: four 307s with the `Location` assertion, plus four rows of `TestPathTraversalNeverReachesTheHandler` |
| M8 | `canonicalPath` uses bare `path.Clean` | **caught**: `POST /sub/` answers 404 instead of 418 |
| M9 | the unset-base-URL warn demoted to `Debug` | **caught** |
| M10 | the same warn made unconditional | **caught**, by the assertion that a configured base URL logs nothing |
| P1 | my own corpus: 79 targeted shapes plus 400,000 random strings, held to a stronger postcondition than theirs | no counterexample, 25,958 accepted |
| P2 | `go test -fuzz FuzzNormalizePublicBaseURL`, 4 minutes | **183,552,075 executions, no counterexample** |
| P3 | 18 request lines over a real socket, against the bare mux and against `Mount`'s return | the three 307s reproduce on the bare mux and are 404 through the guard; `POST /sub` is still a 307 through the guard (finding 2) |
| P4 | the `Header` wrapper attacked from another package | read-only holds; a per-request clone would not have (their claim confirmed) |
| P5 | `h.Mount(mux); srv.Handler = mux` compiled, vetted and linted | **nothing complains** (finding 3) |

**On the committed fuzz seeds:** they are seeds, not a corpus that will grow. Two files, 83 bytes
total, and my 183 million execution run added nothing to `testdata` (new interesting inputs go to
`GOCACHE`). `testdata/fuzz` only grows when the fuzzer finds a failure, which is what you want.

### Findings that are not inline

All five findings are inline. The notes:

**N1 (note, for B07 / #7). `provider.Header` is a live view of the request's map, not a snapshot.**
`NewHeader` keeps the map, so anything that writes to it after the wrapper is built is seen through
`Get` and `Values` (I checked: a `Set` after `NewHeader` is visible). That is correct today, because
the edge passes `r.Header`, which `net/http` does not touch once the handler is called, and
`NewHeader`'s doc comment says the caller must not write to it afterwards. It is worth knowing in
B07 only because the hub is the next thing to build a `Request`, and if it ever builds one from a
map it keeps, the wrapper stops being a guarantee.

**N2 (note). `Header.Get` has no production caller yet.** `Values` is called by the fake's `Verify`;
`Get` is called only from tests. It is the minimal read half of a two-method API whose named user is
B15 (`X-Slack-Request-Timestamp`), so this is not the `Registry.Keys` case from round 1 and I am not
asking for it to go.

**N3 (note). An empty fragment is dropped rather than refused.** `https://x#` is accepted and comes
back as `https://x`, because `u.Fragment` is `""` and the check is on the value rather than on
`u.RawFragment` or the raw string, while `https://x#f` is refused. Idempotent and harmless, and the
answer is the one the operator meant. One table row would pin that it stays deliberate.

**N4 (note). Round 1's N2 stands:** a chunked body can cost 2x `MaxBody` before `MaxBytesReader`
stops it, which is `bytes.Buffer` doubling and not a leak, and fine at the 1 MiB default.

### The N4 dispute: I accept it, with one counter-example on the record

The ask was to move `NormalizePublicBaseURL` out of `internal/config` so that `internal/ingress`
does not import `internal/config`. The reply keeps it, on the argument that the cycle needs `config`
to import `ingress`, that the only edge that would do so is `config` wanting `ingress.DefaultMaxBody`
for a future `LAWANG_MAX_BODY`, and that a parser which leaves 0 alone never names the constant.

**I accept the dispute.** Two of the three reasons are stronger than my note was: spending a package
on one function, or having `config` import `internal/provider`, are both worse shapes than the
import that exists, and an operator looking up what `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` accepts really does
look in `internal/config` first. The single-owner property is what matters and it is kept.

One counter-example for the record, in case the day comes. The edge that would close the loop is not
the parser, it is the **usage text**: `Variables()` spells `LAWANG_LISTEN_ADDR` as
`Default: defaultListenAddr`, that is, it prints the real default value rather than a literal. The
natural spelling of a `LAWANG_MAX_BODY` entry is therefore `Default: ingress.DefaultMaxBody`, and
that is an import of `ingress` by `config`. The escape is a literal in the usage string, which is
cheap, so the reply's conclusion still holds; it just holds for a slightly different reason than the
one given. Not an ask, and not a second round of the same disagreement.

### What I could not break

I tried to find a third normalizer shape and failed, over my own corpus, 400,000 random strings and
183 million fuzz executions. I tried to reach the underlying header map from outside the package
without reflection and failed. I tried to get a request past the guard that the mux would then clean
and redirect, and failed for every `cleanPath` shape: the guard reads the decoded path and the mux
cleans the escaped one, and since decoding only adds characters, an escaped path that is not
canonical always has a decoded path that is not canonical either. The one redirect the guard does
not cover is a different mechanism, and it is finding 2.

text:
## Delta review of cc03b72

**Verdict: changes requested**

1 blocking, 3 should-fix, 3 notes, over the one commit since round 3 (604 insertions, 81 deletions, 8 files). All five round 3 findings are fixed and I confirmed each by reproducing the defect and then the fix, not by reading the reply. The blocking finding is in the new routing block, in `coveredBy`, which is the function that decides when the auto-registered slash-less route is safe to add.

`make check` is green on `cc03b72` (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race`), with **no `--- SKIP` anywhere** (zero matches for "skip" in the whole run) and the container-backed packages at their usual cost (`record` 27.3 s, `store` 16.9 s, `outbox` 16.9 s), so nothing was silently skipped. CI is green on this exact head sha. Coverage after the delta: `internal/ingress` **100.0%**, `internal/config` 100%, `internal/provider` 100%, `internal/provider/fake` 99.0%. Git's own trailer parser reports no trailer on any of the four commits. No tool attribution in the diff, the description or a comment; no em dash anywhere in the delta; the only non-ASCII bytes added are the four IDN fixtures that exist to test the new host rule; no token shape (`xoxb-`, `pat-`, `pk_`, `eyJ`, long hex or base64). No new dependency. `govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so it was not run. Nothing under `.claude/` or `CLAUDE.md` is touched, so an ordinary verdict applies.

### The five round 3 findings

| Round 3 | Status | How I checked, not how it was answered |
|---|---|---|
| 1. `u.Host` accepts a URL with no machine, and an IDN host | **fixed** | `u.Hostname()`, a trailing-colon check and an ASCII-host check, each with table rows. I mutated all three back: `u.Hostname()` to `u.Host` fails `refuses_a_port_and_no_host`, deleting the colon check fails `refuses_an_empty_port`, weakening the ASCII check to `b >= 0xff` fails all three IDN rows. `xn--80ak6aa92e.com` and `xn--caf-dma.example` are still accepted. No refusal quotes the value, and `ingress.New` wraps it with `%w` and no value either. |
| 2. the guard reads the decoded path, and misses the second redirect | **fixed** | Both halves. Reverting the guard to `r.URL.Path` fails the socket test; through the guard `POST /echo/a%2f%2fb` now reaches the handler with `seg == "a//b"`, exactly as the bare mux does. For the second redirect I served the same table through a bare mux and through `New`: `POST /sub` is `307 Location: /sub/` on the bare mux and 404 with no `Location` through `New`, and the same for `//sub/`. Four mutations of the new code (no shadow route, `coveredBy` always false, `subtreeRoot` without `{$}`, `subtreeRoot` without `{name...}`) are each caught by a different case of `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`. But see finding 1: the rule that decides **when** to add the shadow route is wrong. |
| 3. `Mount`'s return value could be dropped | **fixed, and I could not get around it** | `New` returns `http.HandlerFunc`, not `*http.ServeMux`. From another package I tried a type assertion to `*http.ServeMux`, to an `interface{ Handle(string, http.Handler) }` and to an `interface{ Unwrap() http.Handler }`: all three fail. The whole exported surface of the package is now `Hub`, `Verdict` (and its constants), `Route`, `Options`, `New`, `DefaultMaxBody` and `DefaultAcceptTimeout`, and none of them yields a mux; `edge` and its `serveHTTP` are unexported, so there is nothing to put on a mux of one's own. The claim that dropping is impossible holds. |
| 4. the `escaped == ""` branch is unpinned | **fixed** | `internal/ingress` is at 100.0% of statements, and deleting the disjunct (`if escaped[0] != '/'`) fails `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected`, because the two request lines are in the refused list now. |
| 5. architecture 7 promises what `Request.Body` does not give | **fixed** | The bullet now separates the header guarantee from the `Body` rule, the field's doc comment says the same at length, and #7 carries both options with the measurement. See "On leaving `Request.Body` a rule" below. |

I withdraw nothing: every round 3 finding reproduced on `b64f6af` before I looked at the fix.

### Coverage

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | the delta touches no "Done when" line of #6 directly, so I re-proved the two it could have broken after the `Mount` removal: byte-identical input and the body cap both still hold over a real socket through what `New` returns, and the webhook route answers 202 under every route table in my probes | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 13 mutations of my own on the new code (table below), 12 caught, 1 survived (note N1) | 0 |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of the four changed packages line by line (`internal/ingress` is 100.0% now), plus the route shapes the new table does **not** test: a wildcard route at the depth of a subtree root, two caller routes whose shadows conflict, a route under `/ingress/`, a pattern whose last segment percent-decodes to a slash | 1 blocking, 2 should-fix |
| Correctness | `subtreeRoot` and `coveredBy` against `net/http`'s own `parsePattern`, `matchPath`, `exactMatch` and `matchOrRedirect` in the Go 1.26.7 source, then 30 request lines over a real socket against both the guarded wiring and a bare mux with the same table | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | no tenant, no database, no credential and no live test in this delta. The new 404 body is a package constant and carries no sender byte; the shadow handler logs nothing; the three new config refusals never echo the value, which matters because a database URL pasted into the wrong variable lands there. A route is this program's own wiring, never sender input, which is why finding 3 is should-fix and not blocking | 0 |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | whether a request line can still reach a redirect through `New` (yes, in one exotic route shape: finding 2), whether an absolute-form or asterisk-form line can smuggle a host or a path past the guard (it cannot: both are 404, and `http://attacker.example/echo/a` arrives with the host discarded), `%zz` and a bare `%` (400 from `net/http`'s own parser, before any handler), a `%00` inside a wildcard segment (delivered escaped, as the mux does), CONNECT (refused when non-canonical, which is the documented over-refusal). No new dependency | 1 should-fix |
| Performance | the delta adds work at construction only. `newMux` is O(routes^2) through `coveredBy`, on a slice whose length is the number of routes the binary wires, run once at start. Per request the guard is unchanged (11.6 ns, 0 allocs, measured in round 3) and the shadow routes add nodes to a tree that is already O(segments) per lookup | 0 |
| Dead code | searched callers of everything the delta adds: `Route`, `Route.pattern`, `Route.check`, `newMux`, `subtreeRoot`, `coveredBy`, `notFoundBody`, `routeMethod`, `routePath` all have callers; `Mount`, `Pattern` and the exported `Handler` are gone from the tree with no stale reference outside two comments that name the old shape on purpose. `New` and `Route` still have only test callers, which is the item's known gap and B07's job | 0 (1 note) |
| Codebase improvement | the shape of the new routing API: whether `Route` lets a caller do the unsafe thing easily (it does, finding 3) and whether the safe thing has a rule that is actually safe (it does not, finding 1) | covered by findings 1 and 3 |
| Documentation | architecture 109 to 129 and 317 to 330 and the section 7 bullet against the code, the backlog log line, the README status paragraph (still true: `serve` does not mount the edge), the usage text for `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, every new doc comment, the description against the code as it now is, and the notes carried onto #7 | 1 should-fix (finding 4), 1 note |

### Findings

Findings 1 to 3 are inline. Finding 4 is not in the diff:

**4 (should-fix). Issue #7 still tells B07 to call `Mount`, in two comments that this delta made false.** The comments of 2026-09-20T12:34:32Z and 12:37:37Z say, in bold, "**`Mount` returns the handler you must use.** Its signature is now `func (h *Handler) Mount(mux *http.ServeMux) http.Handler` ... Write `srv.Handler = ingressHandler.Mount(mux)`, not `srv.Handler = mux`." There is no `Mount`, no exported `Handler` and no mux to pass. The round 3 close-out comment on #7 adds the `Request.Body` and `Header` notes but does not correct either of those. #7 is the very next item and the one that wires this package, and the carried notes are how a finding survives the merge, so a note that is now wrong costs B07 a dead end before it reads the doc comment on `New`. The fix is one more comment on #7 saying that `New` owns the mux and takes `Options.Routes`, and that `/healthz` moves into a `Route`, which `cmd/lawang/serve.go` already says in a comment.

### Mutations and probes

Each mutation was applied to a file copy, run against the package, and restored; the tree is byte-identical afterwards.

| # | Mutation or probe | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | the guard back to `r.URL.Path` | **caught**: `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected` |
| M2 | the slash-less route never registered | **caught**: `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`, three cases with the `Location` assertion |
| M3 | `coveredBy` always false | **caught**: `the_caller_covers_the_root_for_every_method` |
| M4 | `subtreeRoot` drops the `/{$}` spelling | **caught**: `an_exact_trailing_slash`, that case only |
| M5 | `subtreeRoot` drops the `{name...}` spelling | **caught**: `an_explicit_multi_wildcard`, that case only |
| M6 | `Route.check` drops the upper case method rule | **caught**: `a_lower_case_method` |
| M7 | `Route.check` drops the leading slash rule | **caught**: `a_host` |
| M8 | `u.Hostname()` back to `u.Host` | **caught**: `refuses_a_port_and_no_host` |
| M9 | the ASCII host check weakened to `b >= 0xff` | **caught**: all three IDN rows |
| M10 | the trailing-colon check deleted | **caught**: `refuses_an_empty_port` |
| M11 | the duplicate-pattern pre-check deleted | **SURVIVED** (note N1) |
| M12 | the shadow dedupe (`registered[shadow]`) deleted | **caught**: `two_spellings_of_the_same_subtree` |
| M13 | the `escaped == ""` disjunct deleted | **caught**: the socket test |
| M14 | the ASCII host check weakened to `b >= 0xc0` | **SURVIVED** (note N2, and no input can tell it apart) |
| P1 | `POST /v1/{resource}` and `POST /v1/tenants/`, through a bare mux and through `New` | bare mux: 418 from the wildcard handler, **no `Location`, no redirect**. Through `New`: **404 `no such provider`**. Finding 1 |
| P2 | `GET /v1/{id}/` and `GET /v1/{name}` | `net/http` accepts both. `New` refuses at start with `pattern "GET /v1/{id}" ... conflicts with pattern "GET /v1/{name}"`, a pattern the caller never wrote. Finding 1 |
| P3 | reach the mux from outside the package | failed, three ways (see round 3 finding 3 above) |
| P4 | 14 request lines over a socket against the guarded wiring and a bare mux with the same table | the guard is aligned: `a%2Fb` and `a%2e%2e` reach the handler through both, `POST /sub`, `//sub/` and `POST http://attacker.example` are 307 on the bare mux and 404 through `New`, `%zz` and `%` are 400 from `net/http` before any handler, CONNECT with a dotted path is the documented over-refusal |
| P5 | a route whose path is `/a/%2F` | `New` accepts it and `POST /a` answers **307 `Location: /a/`** through the handler `New` returns. Finding 2 |
| P6 | eight route shapes aimed at the webhook endpoint | `/ingress/{p}` is refused (conflict), `/ingress/{p...}`, `/ingress/`, `/`, `/ingress/{provider}` with no method and `/ingress/{provider}/` all leave the edge answering 202. **`POST /ingress/fake` takes it over**, 418 instead of 202. Finding 3 |
| P7 | `POST * HTTP/1.1` against a plain handler and against a bare mux | the handler **is** reached, with `EscapedPath() == "*"`, `RequestURI == "*"`. Through a bare mux it is 400. See below |

### The `POST *` correction: right on the substance, wrong on the mechanism

The substantive half of the correction holds and round 3 was wrong: `net/http` does not reject `POST * HTTP/1.1`, it parses to `url.URL{Path: "*"}` (`net/url`'s `parse` has an explicit `if rawURL == "*"` branch), it reaches a plain handler, and `EscapedPath()` is `"*"`, not `""`. So the guard's `escaped[0] != '/'` disjunct is genuinely load-bearing and M13 confirms a test sees it.

The mechanism half is wrong, and it is worth putting on the record because it means the 400 was never a redirect at all. It does not come from "the mux's own redirect handler after cleaning": `ServeMux.ServeHTTP` (`net/http/server.go:2815`, Go 1.26.7) opens with `if r.RequestURI == "*" { ... w.WriteHeader(StatusBadRequest); return }`, before any matching, cleaning or redirect. I checked the other way round too: `http.RedirectHandler("/*", 307)` answers 307 with `Location: /*`, so had the request got as far as the redirect it would not have been a 400. Nothing committed says otherwise (the code comment and the test comment both only claim that `"*"` reaches a handler, which is true), so this changes no line; it changes the reason.

### On the three-spellings claim

I read the Go 1.26.7 source rather than inferring. The claim is right about the mechanism and wrong as an enumeration. `matchOrRedirect` (server.go:2731) redirects from `/x` when `exactMatch(n2, "/x/")` holds, and `exactMatch` (server.go:2772) is true either when the matched pattern's last segment is not a multi, or when it is a multi and the segment count equals the slash count. A single `{name}` can never be the match, confirmed at routing_tree.go:181 ("We skip this step if the segment is a trailing slash, because single wildcards don't match trailing slashes"), which is why `POST /ingress/{provider}` has no root. So a trailing slash and `{name...}` cover the multi case and `{$}` covers the non-multi case, three spellings, as claimed.

The gap is in the non-multi case. `parsePattern` (pattern.go:158) stores `{$}` as `segment{s: "/"}`, and a **literal** segment is stored as `pathUnescape(seg)`, so a last segment written `%2F` produces the identical `segment{s: "/"}`. That is a fourth spelling, and P5 shows it redirects. Finding 2.

### On the IDN refusal

I think it is right, and I tried to argue the other way. Go does no IDNA conversion anywhere on this path, so `https://café.example` would go into an HMAC base string as those UTF-8 bytes while DNS, the provider's dashboard and therefore the URL the provider signed all carry `xn--caf-dma.example`: a 401 per delivery, the status this contract reserves for a forgery, with nothing in the process to see. An operator with an IDN domain already owns the punycode spelling, because that is what their certificate and their DNS zone hold, so the conversion is not new work. The refusal happens at start, names the variable and gives the fix in the message itself ("an internationalized name in its punycode (`xn--`) form"), the usage text says the same, and neither string echoes the value. `xn--80ak6aa92e.com` and `xn--caf-dma.example/a/b/` are accepted, so the punycode path is pinned and not just asserted. One read is enough to fix it.

### On leaving `Request.Body` a rule

Accepted, and the reasoning is stronger than the measurement. A copy at the edge would protect nothing: the edge builds **one** `Request`, and it is the hub that hands that same value to `Verify` once per candidate, so the second candidate reads the first candidate's damage whether or not the edge copied once. Only the per-candidate loop can close it, and it does not exist yet. The measurement (0.9 us at 8 KiB, 57 us at the cap, against 200 ms) settles the cost question the other way, which is the right thing to record.

What is recorded on #7 is enough on its own: the comment of 2026-09-20T13:32:04Z states the aliasing, the symptom, both remedies and the numbers, and architecture 7 and the field's doc comment carry the rule for anyone who never opens the issue. My one reservation is finding 4: the same issue also carries two comments telling B07 to call a function that no longer exists, and an item whose carried notes are half stale is an item whose notes get skimmed.

### Notes

**N1 (note). The duplicate-pattern pre-check in `newMux` changes no answer, only a message.** Deleting the `if registered[rt.pattern()]` refusal leaves the whole package green, because `mux.Handle` panics on the second registration and the `recover` turns that into an error that also contains the pattern, which is all `TestARouteNewCannotServeIsRefusedAtStart` asserts. The loop that fills `registered` is still needed for the shadow dedupe, so this is not dead code, but the refusal is a nicer message with no test that can tell it from its absence. This is the same shape the round 1 lesson names: a check whose test is satisfied by a neighbouring layer. Either assert the better message (`two routes for "GET /healthz"`) or drop the branch.

**N2 (note). The ASCII host boundary is not pinned, and cannot be.** Weakening `b >= 0x80` to `b >= 0xc0` leaves `internal/config` green, because every non-ASCII byte in a valid UTF-8 host is preceded by a lead byte of 0xC2 or more. No input distinguishes the two, so there is nothing to ask for; recorded so that nobody "tightens" it later thinking a test covers it.

**N3 (note, for B07 and B08). The shadow route answers `no such provider` for a path that has nothing to do with providers.** When the operator API mounts `/v1/`, `POST /v1` will answer 404 with that body. Indistinguishability is the reason the constant is shared and it is right for `/ingress/...`, but an operator reading `no such provider` from `/v1` will look in the wrong place. Worth a thought when the operator API lands, not a change here.
