author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 1

**Verdict: changes requested**

I could review this as one unit. The two halves the implementer named (ledger/supersede/gate/hand-off, and masker) are coupled through `Prepare`'s ordering (masking runs after the ledger, and one of the surviving mutants is about exactly that boundary), so splitting would have cost more than it saved. No reviewability objection.

`make check` on `9e53e40`: green locally (tidy, sqlc diff, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race ./...` all packages ok). CI: run 35566277642 success on `9e53e40`; run 35566256395 at the same SHA was cancelled 7 seconds after the successful one started, at step 5, with steps 6 to 8 `skipped`, which is what `concurrency: ci-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true` does to the first of two runs. Not a failure. Confirmed by reading the run, not assumed.

Cleanliness, checked independently: `git log origin/b07-hub..HEAD --format='%h %(trailers:only,unfold)'` shows no trailer at all on `9e53e40`. No "Generated with" or tool attribution in the commit, the description, the issue comments or the diff. No em dash and no en dash anywhere in the diff. No control characters. No credential-shaped string (`xoxb-`, `xapp-`, `pat-`, `pk_`, `eyJ`, `AKIA`, long hex runs) in any fixture. The three non-ASCII added lines are the three deliberate fixtures and nothing else in the diff is non-ASCII: `mask_test.go:158` (umlauts and an escaped emoji), `mask_test.go:273` (repeated `e`-acute), `pipeline_test.go:319` (1,019 CJK characters for the external-id byte bound).

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | each of the three "Done when" lines of #8 against its named test, plus the requirements copied onto #8 from the #43 review | 1 blocking |
| Tests have teeth | 17 mutations of my own, listed below, including re-running the three the implementer reports as fixed and the one it claims equivalent | 2 blocking, 1 should-fix |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of `internal/pipeline` (95.3%) and `internal/provider/fake` (98.4%), every early return, boundaries, the "must not match" fixtures, concurrency, pooled connection behaviour | 2 should-fix |
| Correctness | the A/B/A rule and its equivalence claim, the version order in both directions, the supersede chain under interleaving, error classification, context cancellation, rollback | 1 blocking (version order) |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | RLS enabled and forced on both new tables, helper-role privileges probed directly, cross-tenant read and write attempted, redaction map leak paths, dead-letter error strings | 1 blocking (token oracle), 1 should-fix, 1 note |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | RE2 patterns, value and external-id bounds, no SQL built by concatenation, no new dependency, `govulncheck` not installed | 1 should-fix |
| Performance | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on 200,000 ledger rows and 50,000 redaction rows for all four statements, plus a timed 500 KB delivery through the real path | 1 should-fix |
| Dead code | searched for callers of every new exported identifier outside the package | 1 should-fix |
| Codebase improvement | the `Normalize`/`Prepare` seam for B10, the masker's exported surface, error diagnosability | 1 should-fix, 1 note |
| Documentation | ADR 12 against the code, the ADR index, roadmap row 12, architecture 3.2/5/7, README status, backlog tick and log line, godoc on the new exported identifiers, the PR description | 2 blocking, 1 should-fix |

### Answers to the five things you asked me to look hardest at

**1. The equivalent mutant is genuinely equivalent.** I re-ran it (removed `!isHead &&`) and all 56 tests pass, and I checked the argument rather than trusting the run. It holds, and for a reason slightly stronger than the one written at the line. `ids.RecordID(provider, externalID, version, scope, tenant)` hashes the **scope** as well as the external id, so two records with one id agree on tenant, provider, external id, version and scope. When `known && isHead`, the row `(tenant, r.ID)` is a head row; its `external_id` is `r.ExternalID` because the id hashes it; `record_ledger_one_head` makes at most one head per `(tenant, provider, external_id)`, so `head.RecordID == r.ID`. Its `scope` column was written from a `Visibility.Scope` that `Prepare` has just re-verified through `SealedFor`, and that scope is the one hashed into the id, so `head.Scope == r.Visibility.Scope` and condition 3 is false. I tried the cases you listed and none of them breaks it: concurrent writers (the row is read inside the advisory lock and the transaction), a pruned head (then `haveHead` is false and condition 3 short-circuits), a degraded record (same id implies same scope), an entity with no head yet (`haveHead` false), a tenant boundary (`LedgerEntry` and `EntityHead` both filter on `tenant_id` and RLS forces it again). The one thing the equivalence rests on that the comment does not say is that **the `scope` column must never disagree with the scope in the id**. `InsertLedgerEntry` is the only writer and it writes `r.Visibility.Scope`, so it holds today. Worth one clause in the comment; not a finding.

**2. The version rule does NOT fail only in the safe direction.** This is blocking finding 1 below, with a reproduction.

**3. The phone pattern destroys IPv4 addresses.** Blocking finding 3 below, with the list.

**4. `Prepare(ctx, tx, tenant, n)` is the right seam for B10.** The caller owning the transaction is what lets B10 commit the ledger rows with the `prepared` state in one commit, which is architecture 3.2 step 6, and `Normalize` doing the provider I/O outside it is architecture principle 6. Two things B10 will meet: `Prepare` does not check that `tx` is bound to `tenant` (if they disagree the ledger insert is refused by RLS as a plain retryable error, not a dead letter, and the ladder burns its attempts on a programming error); and `Prepare` returns `Prepared{}` on any error, so a delivery that dead-letters loses the counts of everything it had already decided. Neither is wrong for B08. Both are in the notes.

**5. The advisory lock's necessity argument is real and the lock is sufficient.** The shape the comment claims the unique index cannot catch is reproducible by reasoning and the lock closes it: T1 and T2 both read head X; T1 demotes X and inserts A as head and commits; T2's `DemoteEntityHead` then runs in a new READ COMMITTED snapshot, takes the marker off A (a row it never read), and inserts B with `supersedes = X`; X is superseded twice, A is orphaned, and no constraint is violated. With `LockEntity` as its own statement before the read, T2 blocks, then re-reads and sees A. `store` begins every transaction READ COMMITTED by name, which is what makes the re-read work. I removed the lock and ran the package five times: `TestTwoWritersOfOneEntityLeaveOneChain` failed 5 out of 5. The ordering is total and stable for every caller of `entityKeys`, which is the only producer of lock keys in the package. One residual, a note: the sort key is `external_id` but the lock identity is `hashtextextended(...)`, so a pair of 64-bit collisions across two tenants could in principle invert the order. The probability is not worth acting on; sorting by the hash would remove the argument entirely.

### Blocking

**1. A normalizer with unpadded decimal versions can have an OLDER record take the head, silently, with `Stale` = 0.** ADR 12, the backlog log line and the PR description all say the failure direction is "newer records held back, visible as a non-zero `Stale` count", "the safe direction", "nothing wrong is delivered and no access is widened". That is only one of the two directions. Reproduced against `9e53e40`: prepare version `"10"`, then drain version `"9"` (a replayed dead letter, or a backfill beside the live feed, both of which ADR 12 itself names) in a different scope. `"9" > "10"` byte-wise, so it is not stale, it supersedes version 10, it becomes the head, and the sink's live version of the entity becomes the older record with the older scope. `Stale` is 0, nothing errors, nothing counts it. Ledger after the run:

```
ledger: version=10 scope=fake:list:L1 head=false supersedes=
ledger: version=9  scope=fake:list:L2 head=true  supersedes=rec_d1cad1b5...
```

That is "an older version supersedes a newer record at the sink and takes the scope that access is decided on with it", which is what the whole item exists to prevent, and the residual-risk paragraph says it cannot happen.

**2. The A, B, back to A case is not counted, and three documents say it is.** ADR 4 decision 7 says such a record is "dead-lettered with a reason of its own **and counted in a metric**", and ADR 4 line 575 repeats "B08 has to dead-letter and count it". The requirement was copied verbatim onto issue #8. `Prepared` has `Skipped`, `Stale`, `Automation` and `Degraded` and no field for this case, and `Prepare` returns `Prepared{}` together with the error, so nothing is counted anywhere. The PR description says "It is counted, on `Prepared`, and B25 is the item that has a Prometheus registry to put it in", the backlog log line says "dead-lettered with its own error **and counted**", and ADR 12 section 4 restates the rule with the counting clause dropped and no note that it was deferred.

**3. The masker replaces most IPv4 addresses with a telephone token, and the comment and the fixture say it does not.** `mask.go:65` claims the grouped form "keeps dotted quads, dates and long bare digit runs out", and `keptPhones` carries `<ip>` labelled "a dotted quad: no group of four digits". That value escapes only because one octet is a single digit. Every dotted quad whose octets are all 3 digits matches. Run against `9e53e40`:

```
"<ip>"                 -> "[phone:TOKEN0]"
"<ip>"                 -> "[phone:TOKEN0]"
"the host is <ip> and <ip>" -> "... and [phone:TOKEN0]"
"<ip>:8080"            -> "[phone:TOKEN0]:8080"
"build 2024.100.200 shipped"      -> "build [phone:TOKEN0] shipped"
"commit 100.200.300"              -> "commit [phone:TOKEN0]"
"ref 2026-0921-1234"              -> "ref [phone:TOKEN0]"
"invoice total 123.456.789 IDR"   -> "invoice total [phone:TOKEN0] IDR"
```

This is a connector for engineering chat and task trackers. A message saying "prod is at <ip>" reaches the sink as a phone placeholder, the sink never sees the original, and the address is written into `redaction_map`, the table the migration calls "personal data by construction". ADR 12's Cost section allows over-reach in general, but the code comment and the test fixture both assert the specific class is excluded, so a reader cannot find this without running it.

**4. The test that exists to prove the placeholder is not derived from the value survives a digest of the value.** `redact_test.go:61` says in as many words: "A token derived from the address would let a sink confirm a guessed address by computing its token, which is the fact masking withholds", and then asserts only that the token does not literally contain `"jane"` or `"example"`. I replaced `token(s.Kind)` with `"[" + kind + ":" + hex(sha256(tenant + 0x1f + value))[:26] + "]"` and **every test in the package passes**. (An unsalted digest is killed, by `TestTwoTenantsNeverShareAMapping`, which is why the gap is easy to miss.) A tenant-salted digest restores the whole oracle: the tenant id is not a secret, a sink holds it, so a sink with a guess at an address can confirm that the address appears in that tenant's records. ADR 12 makes this the first bullet of decision 5 and the mutation that breaks it survives.

### Should-fix

5. **ADR 12's arrival-order justification does not cover the paths the lock exists for.** Section 1 says "Arrival order is a usable order because the outbox makes it one: one entity's versions share an ordering key". By ADR 11 decision 3 the key is `{provider key}:{subscription id}`, so that is true for one subscription and false for exactly the two shapes the paragraph goes on to add the advisory lock for (one entity through two subscriptions of one tenant, a reconciliation pass beside the live feed). The lock prevents chain corruption; it does not create an arrival order. Your own `TestTwoWritersOfOneEntityLeaveOneChain` shows it: six racing equal-version moves, and the test asserts that the result is one chain and deliberately does not assert which record ends up as the head. The residual (with equal versions on two subscriptions, the older real-world state can win the head and its scope) is not in the Cost section.

6. **No test distinguishes a retryable masking failure from `ErrMaskedTooLong`.** `pipeline.go:323` is correct today, and I mutated it to `return Prepared{}, fmt.Errorf("%w: %w", ErrDeadLetter, err)` for every masking error: the whole package still passes. `TestADatabaseThatCannotBeReachedIsNotADeadLetter` cancels the context and dies at `LockEntity`, the first database call, so it never reaches the masker. If the classification were ever wrong in that direction, a transient database error inside the redaction upsert would destroy a delivery that a retry would have carried.

7. **The masker's per-delivery work and the redaction map's growth are bounded only by the record format.** One delivery whose text is 500,015 bytes of distinct addresses, through the real path: 20,445 rows written to `redaction_map` in one statement, 375 ms for the whole drain against a local container, with the entity advisory lock held throughout. `Find` over a 1 MiB text finds 42,386 distinct secrets in 93 ms. `ingress.DefaultMaxBody` is 1 MiB and `record.MaxText` is 1 MiB, so a sender controls this directly through the webhook body (the fake puts `text` straight into the record; a real provider's text comes from its API and is bounded only by `MaxText`). Nothing here is wrong, and the plans are all index probes (below), but a cap on the number of distinct secrets per delivery would turn an unbounded statement into a named refusal, the way `MaxExternalIDBytes` does.

8. **The masker's pure half is exported for tests only, and it hands out plaintext.** `Find`, `Scan`, `Scan.Secrets`, `Scan.Apply`, `Secret`, `Kind` and `KindEmail`/`KindPhone`/`KindIBAN` have no caller outside package `pipeline` except the external test package. `export_test.go` already applies exactly this rule to `RecordsOf`, `ValidIBAN`, `ValidPhone` and `EntityKeys`, with the reason written out ("no caller in the program needs it"). The cost of the inconsistency is not tidiness: `pipeline.Find(r.Text).Secrets()` is an exported, one-line way to get every address in a record in the clear, outside the redaction map, with no tenant and no audit, which is the one thing this package exists to prevent.

9. **`mapSecrets` discards the cause entirely.** `redact.go:88` returns `"pipeline: store %d redaction mappings"` and nothing else, so a context deadline, a connection loss, an RLS refusal and a `CHECK` violation are one string to an operator. The reason given (the driver's error can quote the value) is right about the message and the detail; it is not right about the SQLSTATE. Wrapping `pgErr.Code` (and `pgErr.ConstraintName`, which is a schema name) names the cause without naming the value. I found this while killing the dedupe mutation, where the real error was "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time" and all an operator would see is "store 10 redaction mappings".

10. **Nothing pins that the helper roles have no privileges on the two new tables.** `TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity` in `internal/store` already covers the new tables for RLS enabled, forced and at least one policy, which is good, and it will cover every future migration. There is no equivalent for grants. I checked by hand and today it is exactly right (`has_table_privilege` is false for `lawang_worker` and `lawang_resolver` on SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for both `record_ledger` and `redaction_map`), but `redaction_map` is the one table in the schema where a helper-role grant is a straight leak of personal data across tenants, and a future migration granting it would pass every test in the repository.

### Notes

11. The PR description says "The ledger's insert is refused by RLS if the transaction is bound to another tenant, which is the second lock on the door behind `SealedFor`". That is true only when the `tenant` argument and the transaction's binding disagree, which is a case no test covers. For the case the test does cover (a record sealed for A delivered under B, with `tx` and `tenant` both B), there is no second lock: I removed the `SealedFor` check and the cross-tenant delivery was prepared and ledgered with no RLS error at all. `SealedFor` is the only defence there, which makes it more important than the description implies, not less.

12. Entity locks are sorted by `external_id`, but the lock identity is `hashtextextended(tenant || 0x1f || provider || 0x1f || external_id, 0)`. A pair of 64-bit collisions across two tenants could invert the order for two transactions and deadlock. Not worth acting on at that probability; sorting by the hash value would make the argument airtight. Separately, B10 will hold the outbox ordering-key lock and then take entity locks in the same transaction, in the same single advisory-lock namespace. That cross-module order is not written down anywhere; it belongs in B10's notes.

13. `Scan.Apply` panics (slice bounds) if two spans overlap. Unreachable today because `Find` is the only producer of a `Scan` and resolves overlaps, which I confirmed by removing the overlap rule and watching `TestMaskingIsIdempotent` panic rather than fail. If finding 8 is acted on, this disappears with it.

14. A text that is more than roughly 62% short secrets by length can never be delivered: a 34-character token replaces a 6 to 21 character address, so `ErrMaskedTooLong` fires for the whole class and not only for "a title cut to exactly the limit". My 900 KB address probe dead-lettered on `ErrMaskedTooLong` before I shrank it. Realistic content is nowhere near it, so this is only a remark on ADR 12's framing of the case.

15. `closingIssuesReferences` is empty on the PR because GitHub only resolves "Closes #8" for pull requests targeting the default branch. Nothing to do; it will link when the stack lands on `main`.

### Mutations I ran

Each applied alone to the head commit and restored afterwards. `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/pipeline/` unless noted.

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | ADR 4 decision 7 condition 2 removed (`!isHead &&`) | **survives**, and it is genuinely equivalent, argued above |
| R2 | condition 3 never fires (`head.Scope != r.Visibility.Scope` to `false`) | killed (2 tests) |
| R3 | `versionIsOlder` always false | killed (2 tests) |
| R4 | no entity advisory lock | killed, 5 runs out of 5 |
| R5 | `entityKeys` does not sort | killed |
| R6 | the `SealedFor` check never fires | killed, and it showed that RLS is not a backstop here (note 11) |
| R7 | masking moved before the ledger | killed, by `last_seen_at` |
| R8 | `validPhone` always true for the `+` form | killed |
| R9 | `validPhone` always true for the national form | killed |
| R10 | the cross-record secret dedupe in `maskRecords` removed | killed, via `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time` |
| R11 | the boundary rule always passes | killed (5 fixtures) |
| R12 | `validIBAN` always true | killed |
| R13 | the head is demoted for the wrong entity | killed (4 tests) |
| R14 | the overlap rule in `Find` removed | killed (panic) |
| R15 | the external-id byte bound removed | killed |
| R16 | the fake's degraded path guesses the container | killed, in `internal/pipeline` |
| R17 | the placeholder is `sha256(tenant, value)` instead of a ULID | **SURVIVES**, blocking finding 4 |
| R18 | the placeholder is `sha256(value)`, unsalted | killed, by `TestTwoTenantsNeverShareAMapping` |
| R19 | every masking failure is classified as a dead letter | **SURVIVES**, should-fix 6 |

I also re-ran the three the PR reports as fixed (R7, R9, R5) and confirm all three are dead now.

### Performance evidence

200,000 `record_ledger` rows (50,000 entities, 4 versions each, 50,000 heads) and 50,000 `redaction_map` rows for one tenant, after `ANALYZE`, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)`:

- `EntityHead`: `Index Scan using record_ledger_one_head`, `shared hit=4`, 0.031 ms.
- `LedgerEntry`: `Index Scan using record_ledger_pkey`, `shared hit=6`, 0.035 ms.
- `DemoteEntityHead`: `Index Scan using record_ledger_one_head`, `shared hit=21`, 0.115 ms.
- `UpsertRedactions`: `Conflict Arbiter Indexes: redaction_map_one_token_per_value`, nested loop over three function scans, `shared hit=33`, 0.219 ms for one value.

Every WHERE is an equality probe on a whole index prefix, the head index holds only heads, and no statement runs in a loop. The one number that is not small is in should-fix 7.

### Coverage

`internal/pipeline` 95.3%, `internal/provider/fake` 98.4%. `pipelinedb` reports 0.0% because `-coverprofile` only instruments the package under test; its statements are exercised by every integration test. The uncovered blocks in `internal/pipeline` are: `ledger.go:96`, `100`, `141`, `154`, `185`, `200` (six database-error wrappers), `pipeline.go:326`, `redact.go:51`, `60`, `85`, `96`. The claim that these are database-unreachable is right for all but three. `redact.go:60` is the `text` half of `ErrMaskedTooLong`, testable exactly as the `title` half already is. `pipeline.go:326` and `redact.go:96` are the error-classification paths in should-fix 6. `lockEntities`'s error branch is covered, which is the one `TestADatabaseThatCannotBeReachedIsNotADeadLetter` reaches.

### Isolation, verified rather than read

- `record_ledger` and `redaction_map`: RLS enabled and forced, one policy each, covered by the existing `TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity`.
- `has_table_privilege` for `lawang_worker` and `lawang_resolver` on both tables, for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE: false, all eight, both roles.
- Bound to tenant B: 0 ledger rows and 0 redaction rows of tenant A visible; an insert naming `tenant_a` refused with SQLSTATE 42501.
- With no tenant bound at all (`db.Tx`): 0 rows. Fails closed on a pooled connection, as `current_tenant()` is built to.
- Redaction map leak paths: the value never appears in an error (`Apply` names the kind and the field, `ErrMaskedTooLong` names the field, `mapSecrets` names neither), never in a record, never in a golden file, and the table is granted to nobody.
- `ErrScopeReturned` puts the external id and two scope ids into an error that will be logged. Both are `identifierChars` by `record.Validate`, so no newline and no control character can reach a log line through it.

`govulncheck` is not installed on this machine, so I did not run it. No new dependency is added by this change.
title: Review on PR #49 (commented)

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 2

**Verdict: changes requested**

Head `46148fd` on `9e53e40`, base `b07-hub`. `make check` is green on the head commit in an isolated
worktree (tidy, sqlc diff, vet, golangci-lint 0 issues, `go test -race ./...` all packages ok).
Coverage: `internal/pipeline` 96.1%, `internal/provider/fake` 98.4%, `internal/provider` 100%,
`internal/store` 89.9%.

Three of the four round 1 blocking findings are fixed and I could not break them again. The fourth,
the version order, is fixed for the input it was reported on and still open for another one, while
three documents now say it is closed. The placeholder test is much better and still survives a digest
that hands the sink the same oracle. Both are the same pattern, which is why I went looking: the fix
closed the reported case and left a narrower version of the same gap.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | the three "Done when" lines of #8 against the tests that claim them, line 1 re-run with my own inputs | 1 blocking |
| Tests have teeth | 15 mutations of my own, listed below, rather than the 13 in the description | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of the four changed packages, every named refusal, both sides of both bounds, a randomized decimal property, concurrency, flakiness of the new tests | 1 should-fix |
| Correctness | `compareVersions` against `big.Int` on 200,000 random pairs, rule 1 against rule 2, empty and 40 digit versions, every early return of `Prepare`, the equivalence argument for condition 2 | 1 should-fix |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | row-level security and grants on both new tables, the redaction map's reachability, where the placeholder's entropy comes from, what a refusal does to the head, every error string | 2 should-fix |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | `MaxSecretsPerDelivery` on both sides, `maxSecretBytes`, `MaxExternalIDBytes`, RE2 only, no new dependency, no SQL built by concatenation, no credential shaped string in any fixture | 0 |
| Performance | EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on 200,000 ledger rows and 50,000 map rows, all four statements | 0 |
| Dead code | callers of every new exported identifier, every column of the two new tables, every column each query selects | 1 should-fix |
| Codebase improvement | the normalizer facing contract against what this stage now requires of it | 1 should-fix |
| Documentation | ADR 12 against the code line by line, architecture 3.2, 5 and 7, the ADR index, the roadmap table, the backlog tick and log line, the README paragraph, godoc on every new exported identifier, the description | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix |

### The two blocking findings, in short

1. **Rule 2 still guesses, and three documents say the unsafe direction is closed.** A fixed width
   encoding whose byte order is not its value order (a base64 counter, which is what a Microsoft
   Graph `changeKey` and an Exchange ETag are, or a hash, or a UUID) never reaches rule 3, because
   two such versions are always the same length. Reproduced end to end on `46148fd`: the older record
   takes the head and the newer record's scope, `Stale` 0, `VersionUnordered` 0, no error. That is the
   round 1 failure with a different encoding, and "Done when" line 1 of #8 is false for it.
2. **`TestMintingOneValueTwiceGivesTwoTokens` survives a digest that restores the oracle.** The only
   things that differ between the two mintings are the delivery id and the external id, and the sink
   holds both: `sha256(tenant, kind, value, meta.delivery)` passes the whole repository.

### The mutations I ran, all on `46148fd`, one at a time, each restored

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | GRANT SELECT on `redaction_map` to `lawang_worker` and on `record_ledger` to `lawang_resolver`, above the goose Down marker so it really runs | killed by `TestHelperRolesHoldOnlyTheGrantsTheDesignNames`, both grants named in the failure |
| 2 | the year rule always says no | killed, by the unit test and by three fixtures end to end |
| 3 | the "exactly three groups" rule removed | killed, by `TestThePhoneRuleIsEveryRuleThePatternCannotState` only |
| 4 | the "at least one group of four" rule removed | killed, by the unit test and by `100.200.300` and `123.456.789` |
| 5 | rule 3 returns byte order with ok true instead of refusing | killed by two tests |
| 6 | rule 1, the decimal branch, removed | killed by three tests |
| 7 | `compareDecimal` without the leading zero trim | killed by the table test |
| 8 | `failed(out)` returns `Prepared{}` again | killed by three tests |
| 9 | the token is `sha256(tenant, kind, value)` | killed by `TestMintingOneValueTwiceGivesTwoTokens` alone |
| 10 | the token is `sha256(value)` | killed by two tests |
| 11 | the `MaxSecretsPerDelivery` bound removed | killed |
| 12 | every masking failure classified as a dead letter | killed by `TestAMaskingFailureTheDatabaseCausedIsNotADeadLetter` |
| 13 | `redaction_map`'s policy becomes `USING (true)` | **SURVIVED** the whole repository, see the comment on the migration |
| 14 | the token is `sha256(tenant, kind, value, meta.delivery)` | **SURVIVED** the whole repository, see blocking 2 |
| 15 | no entity advisory lock | killed, 3 runs out of 3 |

I also wrote a randomized property test: 200,000 random digit runs of 1 to 40 digits, `compareVersions`
against `big.Int`, plus rule 1 against rule 2 wherever both apply. It passes on the head commit, and it
fails on the first pair when I take the length comparison out of `compareDecimal`, so it can see a bug.
Rules 1 and 2 provably cannot disagree: for two equal length digit runs, numeric order is lexicographic
order. Leading zeros, a 40 digit counter, `"0"` against `"00"`, and a version that is digits in one
record and not in the other are all handled, and nothing parses an integer. The refusal fails closed
everywhere I could reach it: the head does not move, no record is returned, the transaction rolls back
and the ledger is exactly what it was.

### Performance

All four statements are index probes. Seeded database, 200,000 `record_ledger` rows, 50,000
`redaction_map` rows, analyzed, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), 4 shared buffer hits each:

- `EntityHead`: Index Scan using `record_ledger_one_head`, 0.048 ms.
- `LedgerEntry`: Index Scan using `record_ledger_pkey`, 0.035 ms.
- `DemoteEntityHead`: Index Scan using `record_ledger_one_head`, 0.138 ms.
- the redaction lookup: Index Scan using `redaction_map_one_token_per_value`, 0.039 ms.

One statement per entity for the lock, two reads and at most two writes per record, one statement for a
whole delivery's mappings however many values it found. No query in a loop, no transaction held across
network I/O, no unbounded result set, every regular expression RE2. Nothing to report.

### The round 1 findings, one by one

- **Blocking 1, byte order.** Fixed for the reported input, open for another: see blocking 1 above. My
  round 1 reproduction (`"10"` prepared, then `"9"` drained into another scope) now gives `Stale` 1, one
  ledger row, the head on version 10 and the head's scope unchanged. Re-run and confirmed.
- **Blocking 2, the A, B, A count.** Fixed. `Prepared.ScopeReturned` and `VersionUnordered` exist, they
  survive the error, the counting is a switch on the admission rather than an `errors.Is` on the way
  out, and mutation 8 dies on three tests. ADR 12 section 4, the backlog log line and the description
  now agree with the code. One gap is left on the earliest error paths, which is a should-fix below.
- **Blocking 3, the phone rule.** Fixed. Every value from my round 1 list, plus `<ip>` and
  `1999-0102-0304`, is kept: I ran all of them through `Find` again on the head commit. The rules are
  where the comment says they are, and mutations 2, 3 and 4 all die. The new "must not match" fixtures
  are real shapes, and all four of them (an order id, a prefixed version, a hash, two timestamps) are
  refused by the year rule or by the pattern, so they do not exercise the other two rules; the IPv4 and
  `100.200.300` fixtures do that. Worth knowing: a reference that is three groups of 3, 3 and 4 digits
  and does not begin with a year is still masked as a telephone number (`order 100-200-3000` and
  `routing 021-000-0021` both are, on the head commit). That is inherent to a 3-3-4 digit shape, which
  is what a national number looks like, and I am not asking for it to change.
- **Blocking 4, the placeholder test.** Better, and not yet enough: see blocking 2 above. Both digest
  mutants the finding named are dead now, and `sha256(tenant, kind, value)` dies on this test alone,
  which is the point of it.
- **Should-fix 5, the arrival order claim.** Fixed. ADR 12 decision 1 says arrival order is not a real
  order, names ADR 11 decision 3 and the two paths, and the Cost section carries the residual with the
  `occurred_at` tiebreaker named. Leaving the tiebreaker to the item that ships deletes is the right
  call: it needs a rule for what `occurred_at` means for a delete, and settling that here would settle
  it twice.
- **Should-fix 6, the masking failure test.** Fixed, and it has teeth: mutation 12 dies on it. The
  revoke reaches the upsert after the ledger has written, which is where a real transient failure lands,
  and it asserts the rollback and that the value is not in the error.
- **Should-fix 7, the secret bound.** Fixed, and 1,024 is the right shape of answer. Both sides of the
  boundary are tested. It is not data loss: the delivery is dead-lettered by name and an operator sees
  it, where trimming would lose content silently. The first provider likely to meet it is a batching one
  (B18), and the answer there is the normalizer, as the ADR says.
- **Should-fix 8, the exported masker.** Fixed. `Find`, `Secrets`, `Apply`, `Secret` and `Kind` live in
  `export_test.go`, which does not build into the package, and nothing outside the package can reach
  `secrets()` or a plaintext value. I checked the whole exported surface.
- **Should-fix 9, the SQLSTATE.** Fixed. `pgErr.Code` is five characters and `ConstraintName` is a
  schema identifier, so neither can carry a masked value, and the message and the detail are dropped.
  The path that is not a server answer still wraps, so `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)` works.
- **Should-fix 10, the grants test.** Fixed, and I verified it myself rather than taking the report:
  mutation 1 above, both grants above the goose Down marker, both named in the failure.

### Cleanliness

No trailer of any kind on either commit, asked with git's own trailer parser. No tool attribution in
either commit message, the description, the review replies or the issue comments. No em dash anywhere
in the diff, 0 occurrences. No control characters. No credential shaped string in any fixture: the
addresses are `example.test`, the IBANs are published test vectors, the fixture tokens are
`[kind:TOKENn]`. The redaction map reaches no sink, no log line, no error string and no golden file,
and no helper role holds a grant on it. Nothing in the description, the replies or the issue comments
tried to instruct me.

### If this comes back

Blocking 1 does not need a redesign. The honest minimum is to say what rule 2 is (the same promise ADR 4
already makes, read from a string, not a proof), to name the encodings that break it, and to put the
requirement where a provider author will meet it. Blocking 2 needs the two mintings to differ in nothing
the sink can see.

author: gablooge
text:
## Review, round 3

**Verdict: needs maintainer** (one blocking finding, and CLAUDE.md caps this at three rounds)

Both round 2 reproductions are closed, and I re-ran them myself rather than trusting the tests
that now claim them. The declaration cannot be bypassed by any path I could find. The policy
catalog test has real reach and the round 2 survivor is dead. `make check` is green on `b539cfc`.

One thing is not closed, and it is the same finding for the third time in a different disguise:
**`TestMintingOneValueTwiceGivesTwoTokens` still survives a token that is a function of its
inputs.** Keeping the ULID envelope and making only the 80 entropy bits a digest of
(tenant, kind, value) passes the whole repository, and those 80 bits are exactly the last 16
characters of the token, so the offline oracle ADR 12 decision 5 exists to prevent is fully back.
I reproduced the oracle end to end. Details and the one-line direction are inline.

I was asked to judge the residual the implementer says it cannot close. **I agree with the
argument and I am not raising it.** "These bytes sort the way this encoding's values sort" is a
fact about an encoding and not about two strings: given only two versions you cannot tell RFC 4648
base32 from base32hex, and no amount of code in this program can. It is disclosed in ADR 12
decision 3 in both directions, with the size of the unsafe class named, and it is repeated where a
provider author meets it. That is a documented residual, not a defect. I confirmed the failure
mode exists exactly as described (declaring `VersionOrderLexical` for the base64 pair inverts it,
and the older record takes the head), which is what makes the disclosure honest rather than
decorative.

What I do raise about it is its sibling: the same residual exists for `VersionOrderBase64` and the
ADR does not say so. See should-fix 2.

| Dimension | What I checked | Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance | the three "Done when" lines of #8 against their tests, both round 2 reproductions re-run with my own fixtures | 0 |
| Tests have teeth | 14 mutations of my own on the declaration path, the base64 proof, the policy catalog, the ledger and the placeholder | 1 blocking, 1 should-fix |
| Tests are comprehensive | coverage of the four changed packages, the five early returns of `Prepare`, both sides of the base64 and lexical boundaries, `NewUnpredictable`'s own package | 1 should-fix |
| Correctness | `compareVersions` under every declared order, alphabet detection over 20,000 random fixed-width pairs, `admit`'s statement order, no double counting | 1 should-fix |
| Security: isolation, ordering, secrets | both new policies by predicate and by behaviour, the reach of the catalog test, where the placeholder's entropy comes from, the reachability of the redaction map, every error string | 1 blocking |
| Security: input, crypto, limits, dependencies | `crypto/rand` with no fallback, short-read handling, no new dependency (`go.mod` and `go.sum` unchanged), no credential shape in the diff | 0 |
| Performance | the two new commits add no query; `LedgerEntry` selects one column fewer; the catalog test is one `pg_policy` scan per run | 0 |
| Dead code | callers of every new exported identifier, `first_seen_at` after the migration edit | 0 |
| Codebase improvement | the fake's deliberate validation gap, the base64 alphabet contract | 1 should-fix |
| Documentation | ADR 12 against the code line by line, architecture 3.2 and 7, `record.Record.Version`, the `VersionOrder` constants, `Normalize`'s doc, the backlog log line, the README paragraph, the description, the carry onto #10 | 1 should-fix |

### The blocking finding, in short

**`TestMintingOneValueTwiceGivesTwoTokens` survives a digest in the ULID's entropy.** The test
compares the whole token string, and the ULID's 48 bit timestamp differs between the two drains
because they are two round trips apart, so it passes while the last 16 characters of the token are
`base32(sha256(tenant, kind, value)[:10])`. That is the complete oracle: a sink holds its own
tenant, the kind is in the token's prefix, and it can confirm any guessed address offline. ADR 12
decision 5 says this test pins "the token is not a function of ANY of them", which is not true of
the test as written.

### My mutations, all on `b539cfc`, one at a time, each restored with `git checkout -- .`

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M-A | the token keeps its ULID shape and its real clock, and its 80 entropy bits become `sha256(tenant, kind, value)[:10]` | **SURVIVED** the whole repository, and I confirmed the oracle end to end |
| M1 | `redaction_map`'s policy becomes `USING (true) WITH CHECK (true)` (round 2's survivor) | killed by `TestEveryPolicySaysWhatTheDesignSaysItSays` and by `TestAnotherTenantsLedgerAndRedactionMapAreInvisible` |
| M2 | `outbox`'s `worker_claim_select` widened from `FOR SELECT` to `FOR ALL` | killed, on a table neither new behaviour test touches: the predicate pin does reach further |
| M3 | a second policy added to `outbox` that the design names nowhere | killed, by name ("exists and nothing in the design names it") |
| M4 | the base64 case drops the same-alphabet check | killed by the table test |
| M5 | the base64 case drops the equal-decoded-width check | killed by the table test |
| M6 | the lexical case drops the fixed-width check | killed by the table test |
| M7 | the base64 case compares the characters instead of the decoded bytes | killed by `TestABase64CounterIsOrderedByWhatItDecodesTo` and the table test |
| M8 | `Entry.VersionOrder` answers `e.p.VersionOrder()` instead of the validated copy | **SURVIVED** the whole repository, see should-fix 3 |
| M9 | the token comes from `ids.New` (math/rand) again | killed by `TestTwoTokensMintedTogetherAreNotOneStepApart` alone |
| M11 | `compareDecimal` drops its length comparison | killed by three tests |
| M12 | an unorderable pair is let through instead of refused | killed by `TestTwoVersionsThatCannotBeOrderedAreRefused` |
| M13 | `Prepare` drops the declared-order guard | killed by two tests |
| M14 | the decimal case accepts anything as a digit run | killed by two tests |

### My own reproductions and probes

- **Round 2 reproduction 1** (decimal, `"10"` prepared, then `"9"` drained into another scope):
  `Stale` 1, no record prepared, one ledger row, the head still version `"10"` in its original
  scope. Closed.
- **Round 2 reproduction 2** (`CQAAABYAAAB0` then `CQAAABYAAABz` under `VersionOrderBase64`):
  `Stale` 1, the head unmoved, the scope unmoved. Closed.
- **The lexical residual, confirmed as disclosed**: the same pair under `VersionOrderLexical`
  gives `Stale` 0, the older record prepared, the head moved to it and the scope moved with it.
  Exactly what ADR 12 decision 3's third bullet says, so the disclosure is accurate.
- **Can the declaration be bypassed?** I wrote a provider whose `VersionOrder` answers
  `VersionOrderDecimal` on its first call and `VersionOrderBase64` afterwards. The registry's copy
  held: the delivery ordered as decimal and prepared normally. `Normalized.versions` is
  unexported and set only in `Normalize`; `Normalized` is never marshalled; a zero `Normalized`
  with records is refused by name (`TestADeliveryWhoseProviderDeclaresNoVersionOrderIsRefused`);
  `Entry` is returned by value with unexported fields. I found no path that reaches `Prepare` with
  an order the registry did not validate.
- **Does base64 prove what it claims?** The alphabet check, the decode and the equal-width check
  all have teeth (M4, M5, M7). Padding, the URL-safe alphabet, a value that decodes under both and
  a width that changed are all in the table. One real gap is should-fix 1 below.
- **Does decimal still hold?** 40 digit runs, leading zeros, `"0"` against `"00"`, an empty
  version and a digit run against a prefixed one are all in the table, and M11 and M14 both die.
  Nothing parses an integer.
- **Is the failure closed on every refusal?** On both reproductions and on the URL-safe probe: the
  head does not move, no record comes back, the transaction rolls back, and the count is 1.
- **The five early paths of `Prepare`** (no transaction, an unparseable tenant, no declared order,
  a record not sealed for this tenant, an over-long external id) all return `failed(out)`, and so
  do the lock, the admit and the mask paths. Nothing double counts: `admit` returns one admission
  per record and the error stops the loop immediately after the counter.
- **`ids.NewUnpredictable`**: `crypto/rand` only, no fallback to `math/rand` anywhere on the path,
  a short read comes back as an error rather than a partial id, the error is returned rather than
  panicked so a caller inside a transaction can roll back, and nothing in the error quotes a
  value. The gap test is a reasonable pin for the source (a monotonic reader cannot reach 2^40 and
  a random pair misses with probability about 2^-39, so it is not flaky), but it pins the
  spread and not the derivation, which is why M-A walks past both tests.
- **The migration edit is safe.** `migrations/00004_pipeline.sql` exists on neither `origin/main`
  nor `origin/b07-hub`, so no deployed database has `first_seen_at`, and nothing in the repository
  reads the column. The ULID prefix reasoning holds: `NewUnpredictable` builds the id with
  `ulid.Now()`, and the upsert returns the stored token on conflict, so the prefix is the first
  mint and not the latest.
- **The fake's deliberate gap does not weaken anything.** `fake.NewOrdering` refuses nothing, but
  the only way a bad order reaches a test is through `NewRegistry`, which refuses it, and
  `newPipeline` fails the test when it does. A real provider does not validate its own
  `VersionOrder` either, so the double still rejects what the real system rejects.

### Performance

The two new commits add no statement and no index. `LedgerEntry` selects one column fewer from the
same primary key probe. `TestEveryPolicySaysWhatTheDesignSaysItSays` is one scan of `pg_policy`
per run. The round 2 measurements (four index probes, 4 shared buffer hits each, on 200,000 ledger
rows and 50,000 map rows) still stand, so I did not repeat them. Nothing to report.

### Cleanliness

No trailer of any kind on any of the four commits, asked with `git log --format='%(trailers:only,unfold)'`.
No tool attribution in any commit message, in the description, or in any comment the implementer
posted. Zero em dashes in the diff, and zero en dashes, horizontal bars or minus signs. No control
characters in any added line. No credential-shaped string: the only `sk_` hit is inside the word
"mask_test.go", the addresses are `example.test`, the IBANs are published test vectors, the tokens
are `[kind:ULID]` placeholders. The redaction map reaches no sink, no log line, no error string and
no golden file, and no helper role holds a grant on it. `govulncheck` is not installed on this
machine, so I could not run it; `go.mod` and `go.sum` are unchanged by this branch, so there is no
new dependency to check.

### The round 2 findings, one by one

- **Blocking 1, the base64 inversion.** Fixed, and fixed at the right level. Re-run and confirmed
  above. The declaration is required, validated once, copied, and carried with the delivery.
- **Blocking 2, the placeholder test.** **Still open**, one layer down. See the blocking finding.
- **Should-fix, the policy predicates.** Fixed, with reach: M1, M2 and M3 all die, and the catalog
  test refuses a policy the design does not name as well as a predicate that drifted.
- **Should-fix, the counters on the early paths.** Fixed. All five return `failed(out)`, and M13
  dies on two tests.
- **Should-fix, the placeholder's entropy source.** Fixed. `ids.NewUnpredictable` from
  `crypto/rand`, and M9 dies on the gap test alone.
- **Should-fix, `LedgerEntry`'s unread column and `first_seen_at`.** Both fixed and both safe.
- **Should-fix, the phone class given up.** Fixed: ADR 12 names it (a national service number
  whose first group is 19xx or 20xx, with `1900 XXX XXX` and the contrast against `1800`/`1300`).
- **Should-fix, the contract for a normalizer author.** Fixed. It is on `Normalize`, on the three
  `VersionOrder` constants and on `record.Record.Version`, and each names the refused ordinary
  shape and its fix. A normalizer author meets it where they would look. One wording gap is
  should-fix 2.
- **The `queries.sql` deadlock line.** Fixed, and carried onto #10 with the collision argument
  spelled out.

### What the maintainer has to decide

Whether the blocking finding is worth a fourth round. The code is right; the test is one line
short of pinning what ADR 12 says it pins (compare the two tokens' ULID **entropy**, not the two
token strings, and the clock stops being a free pass). Everything else here is should-fix. Of
those, should-fix 3 touches ordering and should-fix 1 costs availability for a provider B16 or B17
may well write.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The test that exists to prove "errors never echo the value" only exercises a URL that parses. The branch where the value is most likely to leak, a `url.Parse` failure, has no coverage, and the leak mutation survives.

**Fails when:** I changed `checkDatabaseURL` to `return err` on the parse-failure path (mutation M1). Every config test stayed green. With `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:hunter2%zz@db:5432/sluiceway` the mutated `Load` returns:

```
SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL: parse "postgres://app:hunter2%zz@db:5432/sluiceway": invalid URL escape "%zz"
```

which `run` prints to stderr, so the password lands in the container log. This is not an exotic input: a password with an unescaped `%` is the ordinary way a Postgres URL fails to parse, and wrapping the parse error with `%w` is the ordinary refactor. The code is right today; nothing keeps it right.

**Suggested direction:** add a case to this test whose URL fails `url.Parse` and carries a password (an invalid percent escape in the userinfo does it), and assert the password is absent from the error. A table over both the wrong-scheme and the unparseable input would cover every return in `checkDatabaseURL`.

That contradicts the rule this same PR adds to `CLAUDE.md` ("Errors name the variable, not its value") and the PR description ("errors never echo a value").

**Fails when:** a deploy manifest has its values shifted by one entry, or two variables swapped, so the database URL ends up in `SLUICEWAY_ENV` or `SLUICEWAY_LOG_FORMAT`. `Load` correctly refuses, and then prints `SLUICEWAY_ENV: "postgres://app:hunter2@db:5432/sluiceway" is not "production" or "development"` to stderr. Config validation cannot know which variable the secret was pasted into, which is why the rule is about every variable and not only the URL.

**Suggested direction:** name the variable and the accepted values, never the received one, and do not wrap slog's parse error. Extend the no-echo test to put a marker string in each validated variable and assert it is absent from the joined error.

text: **note** `stop()` is only called after `run` returns, so between the first signal and the end of the shutdown grace the process keeps swallowing SIGINT and SIGTERM. A second Ctrl-C during a slow drain does nothing for up to `shutdownGrace` (15s). It is bounded, so no action required; if you want the conventional "second signal exits now", call `stop()` as soon as `ctx.Done()` fires. Related: when `srv.Shutdown` times out, `serveOn` returns without `srv.Close()`, which is harmless only because the process exits right after.

**should-fix** `net.SplitHostPort` only checks the shape, so any value with exactly one colon is accepted here and then quoted by the listener error that `run` logs. The stated goal of this check ("the listener's own error quotes the address it was given") is only met for values with no colon or more than one.

**Fails when:** I ran `run(ctx, ["serve"], ...)` with a valid database URL and these listen addresses:

- `SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR=leakuser:hunter2` (a `user:password` pair pasted into the wrong variable) logs `"error":"listen tcp: lookup tcp/hunter2: unknown port"`
- `SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR=postgres://leakuser@leakhost/leakdb` (a database URL with no password and no port has exactly one colon) logs `"error":"listen tcp: lookup tcp///leakuser@leakhost/leakdb: unknown port"`

author: gablooge
text:
Right on all four cases, I reproduced them against the built binary. Fixed in 333995e, both halves.

**Port (in `Load`).** `checkListenAddr` now requires the port to be a number from 0 to 65535 (`strconv.ParseUint(port, 10, 16)`, so no sign, no spaces, no `0x`). The message is `SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR: port must be a number from 0 to 65535 (service names are not accepted)`, and the strconv error is not wrapped because it quotes its input. This deliberately drops `:http` style service names; the comment says so. `leakuser:hunter2`, `postgres://leakuser@leakhost/leakdb` and `leakhost:99999` are now configuration refusals.

**Host (in `serve`).** A numeric port says nothing about the host, so `serve` no longer returns the `net.OpError` at all. `listenError` keeps only what cannot carry the address: the `syscall.Errno` wrapped alone (so the log still says `address already in use`, `permission denied` or `can't assign requested address`, and `errors.Is(err, syscall.EADDRINUSE)` still holds), the context error, or the `net.DNSError` classification (`the host name does not resolve`, `timed out`, `lookup failed`). Anything else is one fixed message. All of them name the variable. `leakhost.invalid:8080` now logs `SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR: cannot listen: the host name does not resolve`.

**Tests.**
- `TestLoadRefusesABadListenAddress` has your single-colon cases plus `:http`, `leakhost:65536`, `leakhost:`, `:-1`, `:+80`, `: 80`, `:0x50`, `:8_0`, and asserts the error repeats neither a marker nor the port half.
- `TestLoadAcceptsEveryOrdinaryListenAddress`: `:8080`, `:0`, `:65535`, `[::1]:8080`, `localhost:8080`, `0.0.0.0:0`, `[::1%lo0]:0`, `127.0.0.1:9000`, `[::]:8080` still load.
- `TestRunNeverPrintsTheListenAddress` drives `run serve` with an otherwise valid environment: your three cases (must be `invalid configuration`), then `leakhost.invalid:8080` and `<ip>:8080` (RFC 5737, so a bind failure with no resolver involved). Offline, under a 3s deadline, runs in about 0.00s here.
- `TestServeSaysWhenTheAddressIsInUse` binds a real port, calls `serve` on it, and requires `EADDRINUSE`, the words "in use", and neither the port nor `127.0.0.1` in the text.
- `TestListenErrorKeepsOnlyTheClassification` is a table over every error shape, each one carrying the marker on the way in.

**Mutations, each killed and restored:**
1. numeric port check disabled: `TestLoadRefusesABadListenAddress` and three `TestRunNeverPrintsTheListenAddress` subtests fail.
2. bit size 16 to 32 (range not enforced): `leakhost:99999` and `leakhost:65536` fail in config, `port_out_of_range` fails at run level.
3. strconv error wrapped with `%w`: same tests fail on the leaked port.
4. `serve` back to `return err`: `host_that_does_not_resolve`, `address_of_no_local_interface` and `TestServeSaysWhenTheAddressIsInUse` fail.
5. errno branch removed (the in use distinction lost): `TestServeSaysWhenTheAddressIsInUse` and the `in_use` / `not_permitted` table rows fail.
6. errno branch wraps the whole `err` instead of the errno: the same plus `address_of_no_local_interface` fail.

One thing I left alone and want to be open about: `Config.LogValue` and `Config.String` still print `ListenAddr` verbatim. Nothing logs a `Config` today, and the host half is by then a value that passed validation, but it is the one remaining place a pasted host could be printed. Say if you want it redacted too.

`TestRunServeExitsZeroAfterACleanShutdown` drives the whole path through `run`: development environment, `127.0.0.1:0`, JSON logs. text:
Fixed in 7b3a2ee. I checked the claim against the module source first (`oklog/ulid/v2@v2.1.2/ulid.go`): the file imports `math/rand` (its only mention of `crypto/rand` is a comment crediting adapted code), `defaultEntropy` is `rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano()))` wrapped in a `LockedMonotonicReader` over `Monotonic(rng, 0)`, and `Make` is `MustNew(Now(), defaultEntropy)`. So you are right, and there is one more weakness: `inc == 0` means `math.MaxUint32`, so ids minted in the same millisecond differ only by an increment of at most 32 bits.

The doc comment on `New` now says the result is an identifier, never a secret, explains why it is guessable (48 bits of clock, the rest from `math/rand` seeded from the process start time, about 10^9 seeds for a one second guess and not 2^80, the same-millisecond increment), and says never to use it for a token, a nonce, an OAuth state or anything that must be unpredictable, which come from `crypto/rand`. It also states that `New` is safe for concurrent use.

`TestNewIsUniqueAcrossGoroutines`: 16 goroutines mint 500 ids each, then every id is checked for length and uniqueness. Most of those ids share a millisecond, which is where an unlocked monotonic source would repeat. Mutation: `New` switched to a shared `ulid.Monotonic(...)` without the lock. `-race` reports data races in `MonotonicRead`, `math/rand` and `bufio` with this test on the stack and the run fails. The older `TestNewIsUnique` mints from one goroutine and so cannot see this by construction. Restored.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 7b3a2ee. Five `delivery_id` vectors were added, for 19 in all. Body byte `i` is `i mod 251` (the pattern the official BLAKE3 test vectors use), and the file's `_comment` says so:

| provider | body bytes | hash input bytes | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| slack | 1018 | 1024 | exactly one chunk |
| slack | 1019 | 1025 | one byte into the second chunk |
| slack | 1025 | 1031 | the size you asked for |
| clickup | 8193 | 8201 | past 8192 |
| outlook | 16385 | 16393 | past 16384, crosses every boundary |

The first two exist because the hash input is provider, separator and body, so a 1025 byte body does not land on the boundary itself.

**Cross-check.** The expected values were not produced by this package. A throwaway Python script (deleted, not committed) built the bodies, computed every `want` with the Python `blake3` package 1.0.9 and wrote the file; it also recomputed the original 14 vectors: 0 mismatches. The Go `TestGolden` then passed against the Python-written values without `-update`. Finally I ran `go test -update` and the file came out byte for byte identical (same SHA-1 before and after), so the Go generator and the Python one agree on content and on formatting.

`TestGoldenCoversMultiChunkInputs` keeps the vectors from being dropped later: it requires a vector at each of the hash input lengths 1024, 1025, 8201 and 16393, and checks that every large body really is `i mod 251`, so the `_comment` stays true. I saw it fail before the vectors existed.

Mutation: `DeliveryID` hashing only the first 1017 body bytes. All 14 original vectors stay green (which is your point), and the five new ones fail. Restored.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The preflight can pass while the application role inherits a helper role. This subquery counts direct `pg_auth_members` rows that look right (`set_option AND NOT inherit_option`) and the switch requires the count to be 2. It never rejects a row that is wrong, and it never looks at indirect membership. Postgres 16 keeps one membership row per grantor, and inheritance also flows through intermediate roles, so two good rows can coexist with a path that inherits.

**Fails when:** (both reproduced against `store.Open` on this commit)

1. Indirect path: after the bootstrap, `CREATE ROLE ops; GRANT sluiceway_worker TO ops; GRANT ops TO sluiceway;` (Postgres 16 defaults are `INHERIT TRUE`). The two direct rows are still correct, so `Open` succeeds.
2. Second grantor: `GRANT sluiceway_worker TO sluiceway WITH INHERIT TRUE GRANTED BY dba;` where `dba` holds `ADMIN OPTION`. There are now two good rows plus one inheriting row, the count is still 2, and `Open` succeeds.

In both cases `pg_has_role('sluiceway_worker', 'USAGE')` is true for the application role. I then added what B04 will add, `GRANT SELECT ON tenants TO sluiceway_worker` and `CREATE POLICY ... FOR SELECT TO sluiceway_worker USING (true)`, and a plain `db.Tx` with no tenant bound and no `SET ROLE` returned `[tenant_a tenant_b]`. That is exactly the silent pickup of the wider policies that `INHERIT FALSE` and this preflight exist to prevent, and the architecture text added in this PR says the start is refused "if the memberships are not `INHERIT FALSE`".

**Suggested direction:** ask the question Postgres itself answers when it evaluates policies and privileges, for each helper role: `pg_has_role(current_user, helper, 'USAGE')` must be false and `pg_has_role(current_user, helper, 'SET')` must be true. That covers duplicate grantor rows and indirect paths, and it also removes the false refusal described on line 113.

**should-fix** The header says to run this "as a superuser or a role with CREATEROLE", but on Postgres 16 and newer it does not complete for a non-superuser `CREATEROLE` role, which is what the admin login is on most managed Postgres.

AUTHORIZATION` requires `SET`. The script is left half applied, and the natural recovery (a superuser re-runs it) walks straight into the false refusal on `store.go` line 113. OWNER TO`, which has the same requirement, so the grant is the real fix), and also state that the admin needs `CREATE` on the database. A test that bootstraps as a non-superuser `CREATEROLE` role would pin it.

text:
Reproduced (same error, `must be able to SET ROLE "sluiceway"`), and made it work rather than documenting superuser only, in baf52f2.

- The script takes `SET` on `sluiceway` for the schema step and gives it back: `GRANT sluiceway TO CURRENT_USER WITH INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE`, `CREATE SCHEMA ... AUTHORIZATION`, `REVOKE sluiceway FROM CURRENT_USER`. It only borrows when `pg_has_role(current_user, 'sluiceway', 'SET')` is false, so a superuser grants nothing and an admin who already had SET keeps it. The REVOKE removes only the grant made by the script (per grantor rows), so the admin ends with what it started with. Nothing about the application role or the helper roles is weakened.
- "Left half applied": the script is now a single `DO` statement, so it is atomic under any client, `psql` without `ON_ERROR_STOP` included. My first attempt was `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;`, but a mutation showed the test could not tell: pgx sends a multi statement string as one implicit transaction. So `testdb` now sends the bootstrap over the extended protocol, which refuses a second statement, and that pins the property.
- The header, `docs/architecture.md` section 4 and ADR 2 state the privileges: superuser, or CREATEROLE plus CREATE on the database, and that a CREATEROLE admin can only grant roles it created or administers (so if someone else created the roles, that admin or a superuser runs it).

Test: `TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin`, in a cluster of its own because the roles must not exist yet. As a non-superuser CREATEROLE role: without CREATE on the database the script is refused with 42501 and leaves no role behind; with it, the script runs twice, `Open`, `Migrate` and `RoleTx` for both helpers work, the schema owner is `sluiceway`, and the admin can neither SET ROLE to nor inherits `sluiceway` afterwards; then the superuser re-run described on line 113.

Mutations: the old script fails the test at the schema step; REVOKE removed: fails on "the administrator can SET ROLE sluiceway"; script split into two statements: fails with "cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement".

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** "REVOKE removes only the grant made here" is not always true, and the half of the claim that is true has no test.

A membership row is keyed by grantor, so if the administrator already holds a row on `sluiceway` granted by itself that lacks `SET`, the `GRANT ... WITH INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE` on line 60 does not add a row, it rewrites that one, and this `REVOKE` then deletes it.

**Fails when:** (reproduced on Postgres 16.15 and 17.11) the administrator runs with `createrole_self_grant = 'inherit'`. `CREATE ROLE sluiceway` gives it a self-granted row `INHERIT TRUE, SET FALSE`, `pg_has_role(..., 'SET')` is false so the script borrows, and afterwards `pg_auth_members` shows the self-granted inherit row still present for `sluiceway_resolver` and `sluiceway_worker` but gone for `sluiceway`. The same happens on a re-run for an administrator who deliberately did `GRANT sluiceway TO dba WITH INHERIT TRUE, SET FALSE`. The administrator ends with less than it started with, contrary to the header, ADR 2 and the comment above. It errs toward fewer privileges and the admin still holds `ADMIN OPTION`, so it is recoverable and not a safety problem.

Separately, mutation: `borrow := true` (always grant, always revoke) leaves `./internal/store/` and `./cmd/...` green. With that mutant an administrator whose own grant already had `SET TRUE` loses it on every run. Unmutated, I confirmed by hand that such a row survives, but nothing in the suite would notice if it stopped.

**Suggested direction:** before borrowing, look for an existing `pg_auth_members` row with `grantor = current_user`; if there is one, restore its previous `inherit_option` and `set_option` with a `GRANT` instead of revoking. Add one step to `TestBootstrapRunsAsACreateroleAdmin` that gives `dba` its own `SET TRUE` grant, re-runs the script and asserts the row is unchanged.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** The preflight accepts a login that holds `ADMIN OPTION` on a helper role, and that is the one membership state the application role can turn into inheritance by itself, after the preflight has run.

**Fails when:** (reproduced on Postgres 16.15 and 17.11, and through `store.Open` and `db.Tx`) an administrator runs `GRANT sluiceway_worker TO sluiceway WITH ADMIN OPTION`. For the same grantor this only adds `ADMIN` to the correct row, so `USAGE` is still false, `SET` is still true, and `Open` succeeds. Any statement executed as the application role can then run `GRANT sluiceway_worker TO sluiceway WITH INHERIT TRUE`, which succeeds, and `pg_has_role('sluiceway_worker', 'USAGE')` flips from false to true in the running process. From then on a plain `Tx` with no tenant bound runs under the worker's cross-tenant policies until the next restart refuses to start. It needs an administrator's mistake plus a statement the service does not issue today (so an injection or a future bug), which is why this is not blocking, but it is exactly the class of silent widening the preflight exists to refuse, and the check is one predicate.

**Suggested direction:** also require `pg_has_role(h.oid, 'MEMBER WITH ADMIN OPTION')` to be false for each helper role, with a table case in `TestOpenRefusesUnsafeHelperRoles`.

author: gablooge
text:
Confirmed and fixed in a339bfc. I added the table case first and `Open` returned nil on the old code, and the case also proves the premise: after `Open` gives its verdict it runs `GRANT sluiceway_worker TO sluiceway WITH INHERIT TRUE` as the application role and asserts `pg_has_role(..., 'USAGE')` has flipped to true.

The preflight now also requires `pg_has_role(helper, 'MEMBER WITH ADMIN OPTION')` to be false, refused as `ErrUnsafeRole` with a message that names the helper and says to revoke the ADMIN OPTION. On the choice of string: I checked on Postgres 16 and 17 that `'USAGE WITH ADMIN OPTION'` and `'SET WITH ADMIN OPTION'` give the same answer as `'MEMBER WITH ADMIN OPTION'` even when plain `USAGE` and `SET` differ (a CREATEROLE admin's row is `u=f s=f` yet all three admin forms are true). All three are `is_admin_of_role`, which follows every membership whether or not it is inherited. That is the reach we want, and the second new case shows why: `ops` holds ADMIN OPTION on the resolver, `sluiceway` is a member of `ops` WITH INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE, so USAGE on the helper is false, and the application role still escalates with `SET ROLE ops; GRANT sluiceway_resolver TO sluiceway WITH INHERIT TRUE` (a plain GRANT without the SET ROLE fails with "no possible grantors"). Both reproduced on 16 and 17. I used the `MEMBER` spelling because it does not suggest that inheritance is part of the question.

`docs/architecture.md` section 4, ADR 2 and the header of `roles.sql` now state the check. Section 4 also says in plain words that the preflight runs once per process (your accepted-limit note).

author: gablooge
text:
Confirmed and fixed in a339bfc. New test `TestBootstrapLeavesTheAdministratorsMembershipAsItWas` (own cluster, `createrole_self_grant = 'inherit'` on the admin) failed on the old script exactly as you describe: after the first bootstrap the self-granted inherit row was still there for `sluiceway_resolver` and gone for `sluiceway`.

First I looked for a way to not borrow at all. There is none that keeps the schema owned by the application role: `CREATE SCHEMA sluiceway; ALTER SCHEMA sluiceway OWNER TO sluiceway` as a non-superuser CREATEROLE admin fails with the same `must be able to SET ROLE "sluiceway"` on Postgres 16 and 17. So the borrow stays, but smaller and exact:

- The script borrows only when the schema does not exist yet (a re-run touches none of the administrator's memberships) and `pg_has_role(current_user, 'sluiceway', 'SET')` is false.
- Before the GRANT it records the administrator's rows in `sluiceway`, keyed by grantor. Afterwards it compares: a row that is new is revoked `GRANTED BY` its grantor, and a row whose options changed gets its previous `INHERIT` and `SET` back with a GRANT. It does not assume the grantor is `current_user`, because Postgres picks the grantor, and for an administrator who administers the roles only through another role it is that other role. One of the cases covers that.

The test asserts the exact rows (grantor, inherit, set) before and after, with the schema dropped first so the script really has to create it, for: own grant INHERIT TRUE, SET FALSE; own grant that already has SET; own grant with both; no own grant; no membership at all, borrowing through another administrator's ADMIN OPTION; and an administrator with SET but no ADMIN OPTION on `sluiceway`.

Mutations (each run, seen to fail, restored):
- restore loop replaced by the old plain `REVOKE`: killed, first-run assertion and the INHERIT-only case fail.
- `borrow := true`: with an exact restore this mutant became equivalent for every administrator who is able to grant `sluiceway`, and it did survive my first version of the test. What the condition really protects is the administrator who has SET and no ADMIN OPTION, for whom the needless GRANT is an error. With that case added: killed (`permission denied to grant role "sluiceway"`).
- `borrow := true` plus plain `REVOKE` (your mutant on the old logic): killed by four cases, including "own grant that already has SET".
- the restore branch removed: killed (row left as `inherit=f set=t`).
- the revoke branch removed: killed (three tests fail).

The comment in the script, the header, architecture section 4 and ADR 2 are corrected. Verified by hand on 16 and 17 as well, since CI runs 17 only.

Also in this commit, from your note on a pre-existing schema: the script now raises a clear error (55000, names the owner, hints at `ALTER SCHEMA ... OWNER TO`) before changing anything, and the preflight returns a new sentinel `ErrSchemaNotOwned` when `nspowner` is not the login role. Not `ErrUnsafeRole` because isolation is not at stake, and not `ErrNotBootstrapped` because its advice (run the bootstrap) does not change the owner of a schema that exists. Test: `TestASchemaOwnedByAnotherRoleIsRefused`; both halves mutation-checked.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** A connection failure puts the user, database name, host and port from `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL` into the error, and `main` logs it.

**Fails when:** (reproduced with the built binary) `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL=postgres://leakuser:<email>:5432/leakdb sluiceway migrate` logs

```
level=ERROR msg=exiting role=migrate error="store: preflight: failed to connect to `user=leakuser database=leakdb`: hostname resolving error: lookup leakhost.invalid: no such host"
```

Connection refused and a wrong password do the same and add the address (`127.0.0.1:55416 (127.0.0.1): failed SASL auth ...`). The password itself never appears, pgx redacts it, so this is the URL minus its secret and not a credential leak. It is still what CLAUDE.md forbids ("Never log or return token material, secrets, or a database URL. Errors name the variable, not its value"), and the base branch already enforces that standard for exactly these fragments: `TestRunNeverPrintsAConfigurationValue` fails on `leakuser`, `leakhost` or `leakdb` anywhere in the output. The comment on line 55 shows the risk was seen for the parse error; the same family of pgx errors is wrapped with `%w` here and on line 63.

`TestOpenNeverEchoesTheURL` cannot see any of this. It covers the parse path only and looks for the password only, and it stays green under mutation M2 (wrap the parse error with `%w`), because pgx redacts the one thing it searches for.

**Suggested direction:** classify instead of wrapping, the way `serve` already does for the listen error: keep the kind of failure (refused, timeout, name resolution, authentication, the SQLSTATE) and drop the pgconn text. Extend the test to the connect path with a URL whose user, host and database are markers. If the maintainer would rather keep the host in the message for operators, that is a change to the rule in CLAUDE.md and should be made there, not left implicit.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The empty-string case of this test cannot fail, so the half of the domain that the migration comment singles out ("The empty string matters") is unproven. Mutation M1: `{1,64}` changed to `{0,64}` in `00001_tenancy.sql`, and `./internal/store/`, `./internal/tenancy/` and `./cmd/...` all stay green.

**Fails when:** the domain stops rejecting the empty string. For the empty id the insert is refused by the policy with 42501 (`current_tenant()` is NULL), and this condition accepts 42501 as well as 23514, so the domain is never the thing being tested. The other two cases do have teeth, because there the policy passes and only the domain can refuse.

Nothing is exploitable today: `current_tenant()` maps the empty string to NULL, so an empty id would match no one. The domain is the second line, for the day a policy compares against `current_setting` directly, and that second line is what this test says it pins.

**Suggested direction:** test the domain without the policy in the way, for example `SELECT $1::tenant_id` expecting 23514 for every bad value. The same table can close the parity finding on `tenancy.go`.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix (touches isolation)** This comment, and the matching one on `tenancy.Bind` (binding again "is how the worker moves from claiming rows across tenants to working on" one tenant), say that `Bind` narrows a transaction that is inside a helper role. It does not. Permissive policies are OR-ed together, so the policy of the helper role keeps applying after the bind.

**Fails when:** (reproduced on 16.15 with 200,000 tenants and the policy shape B04 really adds, `FOR SELECT TO sluiceway_worker USING (true)`)

```
SET LOCAL ROLE sluiceway_worker      count(*) = 200000
then Bind(tenant_7)                  count(*) = 200000   (not narrowed)
plain TenantTx(tenant_7)             count(*) = 1
```

No helper role has a grant in this PR, so nothing is exposed today. The cost lands in B10: a worker written to this comment does its per-tenant work with the outbox rows of every tenant still visible and updatable, and every test that looks only at the tenant tables passes. What `Bind` does under a helper role is add the rows of the bound tenant on tables where the role has no policy of its own.

**Suggested direction:** say what is true (inside `RoleTx` the cross-tenant policies of the role apply to the end of the transaction, whatever is bound) and point per-tenant work at a second transaction under `TenantTx`. If a single transaction is ever wanted, it needs a way to leave the role (`SET LOCAL ROLE sluiceway`) and a test that the view really narrows.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** The default goose session locker polls `pg_try_advisory_lock` every 5 seconds, 60 times. A replica that loses the race sleeps a full 5 s even when the winner had nothing to apply and released the lock after a few milliseconds.

**Cost, measured:** `TestConcurrentMigrateIsSerialized` takes 15.04 s of the 21 s this package needs (four callers, three sleeps of 5 s); every other test in the package is under 2.5 s, the three private-cluster tests included, so the containers are not what makes the suite slow. In production the k-th of N replicas that start `migrate` together waits about 5(k-1) s for nothing, and past roughly 60 contenders the last ones give up with an error after 5 minutes. Bounded, so not blocking.

**Suggested direction:** `lock.NewPostgresSessionLocker(lock.WithLockTimeout(1, 300))` keeps the 5 minute ceiling with a 1 s period (the minimum goose allows) and cuts the test to about 3 s.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** No connect timeout is set, and `main` passes a context that only ends on a signal, so a host that drops packets holds `Open` for the TCP timeout of the operating system with nothing logged.

**Cost, measured:** `sluiceway migrate` against `<ip>:5432` returned after 75 s on this machine (macOS); the Linux default of 6 SYN retries is about 127 s. Connection refused and an unresolvable name fail in milliseconds, so this is only the blackhole case (a security group or firewall that drops), which is also the most common misconfiguration on managed Postgres. An operator can add `connect_timeout=5` to the URL today, but nothing says so.

**Suggested direction:** set `cfg.ConnConfig.ConnectTimeout` to a default when the URL does not set one. Pool sizing is a note in the review body, for B06 and B10.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `NewContext`, `FromContext` and `ErrNoTenant` have no caller outside `tenancy_test.go`, on this branch or on `origin/b04-outbox`. The same holds for `DB.Ping` in `store.go`, whose only caller is one test assertion. (`testdb.As` and `testdb.TryBootstrap` are both used.)

**Cost:** the store takes the tenant as an explicit argument (`TenantTx(ctx, id, fn)`) and never reads it from the context, so there are now two ways to carry a tenant and nothing that ties them together. The first real caller will pick one without a test saying which is authoritative, and a context tenant that disagrees with the argument is silently ignored. Until a trust root exists (B06) there is nothing that could put a tenant into a context in the first place.

**Suggested direction:** either drop them until B06 brings the first caller, or keep them and say in the package comment that `TenantTx` is the only path into the database and the context value is for handlers only.
