author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in edeba03. Nothing disputed: the rule answers the question (no part of the URL), so I did not keep the host.

`Open`, `preflight` and `helperStates` no longer return, wrap or format the pgx error. `connError` (new file `internal/store/connerr.go`, modelled on `listenError`) keeps only a classification, prefixed with `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL`: host name does not resolve, lookup timed out or failed, connection refused (the errno is wrapped, so `errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED)` still works), timed out, authentication failed (SQLSTATE class 28), database does not exist (3D000), a few other SQLSTATEs, TLS failure, other. For a server error only the SQLSTATE is printed, never Message, Detail or Hint, since at connection time those quote the role, the database and the client address; the code is printed only after checking it is five characters of 0-9A-Z. The server verdict is checked first, because under `sslmode=prefer` pgx joins the TLS attempt to the plain one.

Two things beyond the finding, both from the same rule:
- The pool connects lazily, so any later transaction or a migration can be the first to meet an unreachable server. `Tx`, `TenantTx`, `RoleTx` and `Migrate` go through `scrub`, which replaces an error only when it carries the connection target (`pgconn.ConnectError`, `net.OpError`, `net.DNSError`) and leaves everything else, a 23505 for example, exactly as the server sent it.
- Preflight refusals quoted the login role (`"leakuser" is SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS`). That name is the user half of the URL, so they now say "the login role". This is a change to documented messages; it is called out in the PR description.

Tests: `TestOpenConnectFailuresNeverEchoTheURL` drives `store.Open` against an `.invalid` host, a closed local port, a wrong login and a missing database on the test container, with markers in user, password, host and database, plus the real port and database name; `TestOpenNeverEchoesTheURL` now checks user, host and database too; `TestConnErrorKeepsOnlyTheClassification` is the table of synthetic errors (23 cases); `TestMigrateNeverLogsAPartOfTheDatabaseURL` checks the log of the real command. All have deadlines and need no network.

Mutations: run against the unfixed code, every one of those tests failed with the exact message from your reproduction. M2 (parse error wrapped with `%w`), which survived in your round, is now killed by `TestOpenNeverEchoesTheURL` on `leakuser`, `leakhost`, `leakdb` and `banana`.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in edeba03. The comments were wrong and you are right about Postgres: permissive policies are ORed, so a bind under a helper role takes nothing away.

- The doc comments on `RoleTx` and `tenancy.Bind` now say the truth: a helper-role transaction is cross-tenant for its whole life, a bind could only ever add rows, and per-tenant work happens in a second transaction under `TenantTx`.
- I went one step past documenting it, because the refusal turned out to be clean. `RoleTx` hands `fn` a thin wrapper (`crossTenantTx`, embedding `pgx.Tx`) that carries a marker, and `tenancy.Bind` refuses a marked transaction with the new `tenancy.ErrCrossTenantTx` before it touches the database. The wrapper overrides `Begin`, so a savepoint is marked too. A later item that really wants a role and a tenant in one transaction has to add that on purpose, along the lines you describe (leave the role, and a test that the view narrows). I checked `origin/b04-outbox` first: it never binds inside `RoleTx`, and the wrapper still satisfies what sqlc takes.
- `TestAHelperRoleTransactionIsCrossTenantWhateverIsBound` pins the behaviour with the policy shape B04 really adds: a scratch table with the tenant policy plus `FOR SELECT TO sluiceway_worker USING (true)`. Inside `RoleTx(worker)`: both tenants visible; `Bind` refused, on the transaction and on a savepoint; then, going around `Bind` with a raw `set_config`, both tenants are **still** visible (the reason for the refusal); in `TenantTx`, one.
- `docs/architecture.md` sections 3.2 (step 2) and 4 (the `sluiceway_worker` row, plus a new paragraph) say the same thing, and the B10 backlog line no longer says "re-bind per row".

The cases include a trailing, a leading and a lone newline, CR, tab, the `0x1F` separator of the id recipes, 64 and 65 characters, 64 characters that are 128 bytes, empty, an accented letter, fullwidth letters, a digit from another script, quote, backslash, dot, semicolon, and the two values Postgres cannot hold as text at all (invalid UTF-8 and NUL, which may answer 22021 and nothing else may).

author: gablooge

Fixed in edeba03 with `lock.WithLockTimeout(1, 300)`. I read the goose v3.28.0 source first (`lock/session_locker_options.go`, `lock/postgres.go`): the two arguments are the period in seconds and the failure threshold, they become `retry.WithMaxRetries(threshold, retry.NewConstant(period))`, the minimum for each is 1, and the default is 5 and 60. So 1 and 300 keeps the five minute ceiling at the shortest period goose accepts, as you said. The numbers are named constants with the reason in the comment on `Migrate`, and ADR 2 records it.

Measured on this machine, same command both times (`go test -count=1 ./internal/store/`): **20.8 s before, 9.4 s after**, and the after figure includes the 12 tests this round added. `TestConcurrentMigrateIsSerialized` alone went from about 15 s to 3.05 s.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in edeba03. `poolConfig` sets `ConnConfig.ConnectTimeout` to 10 seconds when the URL has no `connect_timeout`, and leaves the operator's value alone when it has one. I read pgconn to see what the timeout covers: it bounds the whole attempt per address, and the TLS and plain attempts under `sslmode=prefer` share it, so 10 s is 10 s and not 20. Architecture section 4 now tells the operator about the default and the URL parameter.

Two tests, split on purpose so the suite does not pay 10 s:
- `TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout` (no network): 10 s with no parameter, 3 s with `connect_timeout=3`. Removing the default fails it.
- `TestOpenGivesUpOnAHostThatDropsPackets`: `store.Open` against `<ip>` (RFC 5737) with `connect_timeout=1` must come back classified as timed out, inside 5 s, without leaking the address. It ran for real here (1.00 s, not skipped). If an environment answers for that range at once instead of dropping the packets, it skips with a message saying so, since the point is only that `Open` does not hang. The context has an 8 s deadline, so it cannot stall the package either way.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix (touches secrets; a mutation survives)** Nothing proves that this call, or the two in `Migrate` (`migrate.go` lines 54 and 62), is there. Mutation M4 (return `pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, db.pool, fn)` without `scrub`) and M5 (both `scrub` calls removed from `Migrate`) leave `./internal/store/` and `./cmd/...` green. `TestScrubReplacesOnlyWhatCarriesTheConnectionTarget` tests the function by itself, and every leak test goes through `Open`, which never reaches `begin` or `Migrate` because the preflight fails first.

**Fails when:** someone rewrites `begin` (the comment on the panic tests already expects "a move away from BeginFunc") or adds a fourth entry point and forgets the wrapper. The pool connects lazily, so after a database restart the first `Tx` returns pgx's ``failed to connect to `user=... database=...`: dial tcp host:port`` again and the worker logs it, with a green suite. The code is correct today: I drove it through a TCP proxy that I cut after `Open`, and `Tx`, `TenantTx`, `RoleTx` and `Migrate` all came back as `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL: cannot use the database: connection refused` with no marker at any depth.

It kills M4 and M5 and takes about a second.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `connect_timeout=0` is treated as "not set" and replaced by 10 s, and nothing says that this is on purpose. In libpq, and in pgx, 0 means wait indefinitely, and pgx parses an explicit `connect_timeout=0` to the same zero value as an absent parameter, so this condition cannot tell them apart.

**Fails when:** (measured) `store.Open` with `...?connect_timeout=0` against a listener that accepts and never answers returns "the connection attempt timed out" after 10.00 s. An operator who wrote 0 to get libpq's behaviour (a slow failover proxy, a debugger on the server) gets a 10 s limit instead, and the message suggests "connect_timeout is too short" while the URL says unlimited. Architecture section 4 and the comment on `defaultConnectTimeout` both say the bound holds "unless the URL sets `connect_timeout`", which is not true for this one value. The direction is the safe one (a bounded start), which is why this is not blocking.

**Suggested direction:** keep the behaviour, and make it deliberate: say in the comment and in section 4 that 0 does not disable the bound here, and add the `connect_timeout=0` row to `TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout`.
title: Review comment on PR #31, internal/store/store.go

author: gablooge
text:
**note** `scrub` looks at the whole error that comes out of `BeginFunc`, which includes whatever `fn` returned, not only what the pool or the connection produced. An error from `fn` that wraps a `*net.OpError` or a `*net.DNSError` of its own is replaced as if the database had failed.

**Measured:** `db.Tx(ctx, func(pgx.Tx) error { return fmt.Errorf("%w: %w", sentinel, &net.OpError{...ECONNRESET}) })` returns `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL: cannot use the database: connection reset by peer`, and `errors.Is(err, sentinel)` is false. The operator is pointed at the database URL for a failure that was somewhere else, and the caller's sentinel is gone.

No caller does this today, and architecture principle 6 (no network I/O inside an open transaction) says none should, so there is nothing to fix here. It is worth one sentence in the doc comment of `begin` ("fn must not return a net error of its own"), and it is worth knowing for B10 and B12, where a hydration or sink call placed inside a transaction by mistake would show up as a database outage in the log.
title: Review comment on PR #31, internal/store/connerr.go

author: gablooge
text:
**note** The refusal is opt-out by construction: `Bind` refuses what carries the marker and accepts everything else, so anything that hides the marker gets the old behaviour back without an error.

**Measured inside `RoleTx`:** `tenancy.Bind(ctx, struct{ pgx.Tx }{tx}, id)` returns nil and binds, because a struct that embeds the `pgx.Tx` interface promotes only the methods of `pgx.Tx`, and `CrossTenant()` is not one of them. The same holds for `tx.Conn()`, which hands out the raw connection. Savepoints, `pgx.BeginFunc` on the wrapper, nested savepoints, batches and the sqlc `DBTX` shape all behave (refused or working, as they should).

This matches what the doc comment promises ("to keep that from being forgotten", a guard against accident and not a boundary), and the real boundary is still the policy set, so no action here. For whoever first wraps a transaction (tracing, metrics, a retry helper, most likely B25): the wrapper has to forward the marker, or `Bind` should be turned around to accept only what `TenantTx` hands out. The pinned truth test is sound: it builds the policy shape B04 really adds, proves both tenants are visible before anything is bound, goes around `Bind` with a raw `set_config` to show both are still visible, and shows the narrow view in a second `TenantTx`.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 2e6699d. `TestALostDatabaseNeverEchoesTheURL` (new file `internal/store/connlost_test.go`) opens a pool with `pool_max_conns=1` through an in-process TCP forwarder in front of the test database, lets `Open` succeed, then cuts the forwarder (listener closed, both halves of every relayed connection closed, relays awaited with a 10 s bound, also in `t.Cleanup`). The first `Tx` after the cut meets the dead pooled connection ("conn closed") and is checked for leaks too; a bounded loop of at most 5 calls, no sleep, waits for the pool to be empty, which takes one call. Then `Tx`, `TenantTx`, `RoleTx` and `Migrate` are each asserted to: name `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL` and "refused", match `errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED)`, never run their function, return within a 20 s deadline of their own, and carry no marker at any depth (walks `Unwrap() error` and `Unwrap() []error`, prints each node with `%v` and `%+v`). Markers: the role name, the password, the database name, the forwarder address, host and port, the real host and port, and the labels `user=`, `database=`, `dial tcp`. `%#v` is left out on purpose, it prints pointer values and a five digit port can turn up inside one by chance.

Mutations, each restored: M4 (`begin` returns `pgx.BeginFunc` without `scrub`) is **killed**, `Tx`, `TenantTx` and `RoleTx` all fail with the pgx text in the message. M5 (both `scrub` calls out of `Migrate`) is **killed**, the `Migrate` row fails on `store: migrate: failed to initialize: failed to connect to ...`. The test takes about a second.

One thing the mutation showed that I would rather say than hide: M5 is killed by the second call alone. The first one (the `provider` error path, line 54) cannot be reached today, because goose v3.28.0 does not touch the database in `NewProvider` (its first `db.Conn` is in `initialize`, called from `Up`), so removing only that call still leaves the suite green and no test can change that. I kept it as a guard against a goose release that does connect there, and a comment at that line now says exactly this.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 2e6699d, behaviour kept and made deliberate. The comment on `defaultConnectTimeout` now says that `connect_timeout=N` overrides the bound for N of 1 or more, that `connect_timeout=0` does NOT lift it, why (pgx parses an explicit 0 to the same zero as a missing parameter, and of the two readings the bounded start is the safe one), and what an operator who needs a long wait writes instead (a large number). A line at the condition in `poolConfig` points there. Architecture section 4 no longer says "unless the URL sets `connect_timeout`": it says 1 or more, and states the 0 case. `TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout` has the row: `connect_timeout=0` yields 10 s, next to the existing rows for unset (10 s) and `connect_timeout=3` (3 s). Mutation: applying the default only when the URL does not mention `connect_timeout` at all (the rewrite that would turn 0 into "unbounded") is **killed** by the new row, restored.

I left the timeout message ("the host drops packets, or connect_timeout is too short") as it is: with 0 meaning 10 s it is still true, and the comment and section 4 are where an operator who wrote 0 finds out why.
title: Review comment on PR #31, internal/store/store.go

author: gablooge
text:
Decided in 2e6699d: the current behaviour stays, and it is now stated and pinned instead of being an accident.

Why not scrub only what the pool and the transaction machinery return: the error that matters most is returned BY `fn`. A statement that `fn` runs on a connection that has just died fails with a `*net.OpError` carrying the address, and `fn` hands it back. To let a net error of the caller through while still replacing that one, `begin` would have to tell them apart, and the only handle is a side channel (is the pgx connection marked closed after `fn` returned?). That has to hold on every failure path of pgx (write error, read error, cancel during a statement, a savepoint inside `RoleTx`), this package cannot pin all of them with tests, and a miss puts user, database and host:port back into the log. The other side of the scale is a wrong label and a lost sentinel in a case the architecture forbids anyway. Failing closed on the secret is the cheaper mistake.

What changed: the doc comment of `begin` explains this in full, and `Tx`, `TenantTx` and `RoleTx` each say that `fn` does database work only, that a net error it returns comes back as a database connection error without whatever was wrapped around it, and that network I/O inside the function is forbidden for this reason and because it holds a pooled connection and its row locks for as long as the far end takes (section 10, principle 6). `scrub` has a sentence pointing at `begin`, and architecture section 4 has a paragraph. `TestANetErrorFromTheTransactionFunctionIsReplacedToo` documents it on all three entry points with your case (a sentinel joined with a `*net.OpError` of its own, ECONNRESET): the prefix is there, `errors.Is(err, sentinel)` is false, `ECONNRESET` survives, the far end address appears at no depth, and a plain wrapped sentinel comes back untouched, text and all. Its failure message tells whoever changes this which comments and which section to update. It fails under M4, as it should.

Agreed that B10 and B12 are where this bites if a hydration or sink call lands inside a transaction by mistake. That is for the orchestrator to copy onto those issues.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The head rule only looks at the earliest unfinished row of a key. It never asks whether a *later* row of the same key is already leased. So two versions of one entity can be in flight together, and the later one can be delivered first. That is the property this query, the architecture text and `TestConcurrentWorkersDeliverEachEntityInOrder` ("no two versions of one entity are ever in flight together") all claim.

**Fails when (no operator involved):** `seq` is assigned at INSERT, not at COMMIT. Two ingress handlers accept v1 and v2 of one entity at the same moment. T1 inserts v1 (seq 10) and has not committed. T2 inserts v2 (seq 11) and commits. A claimer's snapshot sees only v2, so v2 is the head and is leased. T1 commits. The next claim sees v1 as the head (lower seq, pending, no lease) and leases it while v2 is still in flight. Reproduced deterministically: hold an INSERT open in a `TenantTx`, `Accept` v2, `Claim` (gets v2), release the INSERT, `Claim` again: it returns the late v1.

**Also fails when:** v1 is dead, v2 is claimed and in flight, the operator calls `Replay(v1)`. The next `Claim` returns v1 while v2's lease is running. Reproduced the same way. The comment on `Replay` only considers newer versions that were already *delivered*, where the forward-only supersede chain does cover it. It does not cover two workers running step 5 for the same entity at once, each reading the ledger before the other commits and both linking `supersedes` to the same predecessor.

**Suggested direction:** make commit order equal `seq` order per key, for example a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` on (tenant, ordering key) taken in `Accept` as its own statement before the INSERT, and make a key ineligible while *any* unfinished row of it holds a live lease, not only its head. Note that the second check alone is evaluated on the snapshot and is not re-checked for the other row under the lock, so on its own it still races. Whichever you choose, add the two interleavings above as tests.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `clip` cuts on a byte index, and the result goes into a `text` column. A cut that lands inside a multibyte rune, or a NUL anywhere in the cause, makes Postgres reject the whole statement, so `Fail` and `MarkDead` return an error instead of recording the failure.

**Fails when:** `Fail(ctx, c, DefaultLadder, "a"+strings.Repeat("é", 600))` returns `invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0xc3 (SQLSTATE 22021)`. `Fail(..., "bad\x00byte")` returns the same for `0x00`. Both reproduced. A sink that answers 503 with a long non-ASCII body is enough. The row is then neither backed off nor parked: its lease simply runs out, it is taken over, fails the same way, and loops at lease cadence with no backoff and no dead letter, while holding every later version of that entity behind it.

**Suggested direction:** sanitize before clipping (`strings.ToValidUTF8`, strip NUL) and cut on a rune boundary. Add both inputs to a test.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `Replay` always sets `state = 'pending'`, so it forgets that a row was already prepared. `Retry` is careful about exactly this ("a prepared row retries its delivery, it does not prepare again"), and `MarkPrepared`'s doc promises a re-drain goes into delivery, not into preparing again. That promise does not survive a dead letter.

**Fails when:** the commonest dead letter there is. A row is prepared (ledger rows and prepared records committed), the sink stays down until the ladder is used up, `Fail` parks it as dead from state `prepared`. The operator fixes the sink and replays. Reproduced: after the replay `Get` shows `pending`, which is the one state `MarkPrepared` accepts, so the row will be prepared a second time. The worker will run steps 3 to 6 again for a delivery whose ledger rows already exist, where step 5 skips ids already in the ledger, so whether anything is delivered at all now depends on pipeline code that has to know about this case.

**Suggested direction:** keep the information. Either remember the pre-death state (a column, or `dead` split by origin) and have `Replay` restore it, or state in the architecture that replay always re-prepares and that prepare must therefore be a safe no-op over existing ledger rows while still re-delivering.

**Fails when (with the clause gone):** v1's lease has expired and the slow holder A is about to finish. Claimer B's snapshot sees v1 as the head with an expired lease. A's `MarkDelivered` commits before B reaches the row lock. B re-checks the new row version: lease is NULL, `next_attempt_at` is in the past, so without the state clause B leases a *delivered* row and hands it to a worker, which delivers it to the sink a second time. The head subquery does not save it: on that re-check Postgres reuses the subquery row it already joined, it does not run the subquery again.

**Suggested direction:** this window cannot be hit deterministically from Go, so a stress test is the honest option: short leases forced to expire, finishers racing claimers, asserting that `Claim` never returns a row whose state is `delivered` or `dead`. If that is judged not worth the runtime, say so in the test file so the next reader knows the clause is unguarded.

author: gablooge
text:
**Fixed in 1417501.** You are right on both. The replay case I reproduced against e845b2f before changing anything; the late commit is shown by mutation (without the lock, the new test fails because T2's Accept does not wait). Fixed with three changes that work together, plus the defensive condition you asked for.

**What changed**
1. `LockOrderingKey`: `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(tenant || chr(31) || ordering_key, 0))`, its own statement, taken by `Accept` before the INSERT. Within one key, `seq` order is now commit order. A hash collision only makes two keys wait for each other.
2. `Replay` takes the same lock (`LockOrderingKeyOf`, by row id) and then sets `seq = DEFAULT`: the replayed row goes to the BACK of its key's queue, as if it had just been accepted. I chose this over "restore the old place and check leases" because of exactly the race you warned about: a lease check runs on the claim's snapshot, and a claimer of v2 that has not committed yet is invisible to it. A row that is behind v2 cannot be the head while v2 is unfinished, and that needs no snapshot luck. The cost is that a replayed v1 is always delivered after versions accepted before the replay. That was already the normal case (a dead row does not hold back newer versions, so by replay time they are usually delivered), and the forward-only supersede chain handles it. Documented on the query, on `Outbox.Replay`, and in architecture 3.2 ("Replay goes to the back").
3. The claim re-checks `c.seq = head.seq` on the locked row. On the re-check Postgres reuses the head row it joined on the snapshot, so a row that died, was replayed and is pending/unleased/due again would pass every other condition while v2 is in flight.
4. The defensive condition: `NOT EXISTS` another unfinished row of the key with a live lease. It is evaluated on the snapshot, so it is a second line of defense only (for a row that reached the table without the lock), not part of the argument below.

**Why no interleaving is left (READ COMMITTED).** Lemma: all seq values of one key are assigned under the key's lock, which is held to commit. So if row x has a lower seq than row y, x's transaction ended before y's got the lock, and any snapshot that sees y's seq also sees x's. A successful claim of h means: on the snapshot h had the lowest seq among unfinished rows of its key, and on the locked latest version h is unfinished, unleased (or expired), and has the same seq. Any row with a lower seq was visible and finished on the snapshot; `delivered` is terminal, and `dead` leaves only through Replay, which moves the row to a higher seq. So h is the true head at lock time. If another row r of the key held a live lease at that moment, r was the true head when it was locked, so h (lower seq, committed earlier by the lemma) was finished then, and could only be unfinished now by a replay, which would have given it a seq above r's. Contradiction.
- Two claimers: same head on both snapshots. The second either skips the locked row, or, if the first committed, re-checks the new version and drops it on the lease condition. It cannot fall through to the row behind: that was not a head on its snapshot.
- Claimer versus Accept: a new row has the highest seq of its key and can only become a head when nothing is unfinished ahead of it. The late commit is gone by the lemma.
- Claimer versus Replay: the replayed row is behind everything accepted before it. A claimer whose snapshot predates the death and replay is stopped by the seq re-check (and usually already by `next_attempt_at`, which the replay sets to its own transaction start).
- Claimer versus expiry and takeover: a takeover leases the SAME row, so it is never a second version. If the old holder finishes between the snapshot and the row lock, the state re-check drops the row. If the takeover locks first, the old holder's transition blocks on the row lock, re-checks the token and changes nothing.
- Not covered by any of this, by design: a holder whose lease has expired may still be talking to the sink while the takeover (or, after it, the next version) runs. The token stops it from committing anything, and sink idempotency covers the repeat. The worker (B10) should stop work at lease expiry.
- Lock ordering: Accept and Replay take the advisory lock before any row lock, and the claim and the transitions never take it, so no cycle. A future transaction that accepts several keys at once holds several locks and should order them or retry a deadlock; architecture 3.2 now says so.

**Tests** (`internal/outbox/interleaving_test.go`, all deterministic, no sleeps as assertions: they poll `pg_locks` for an ungranted advisory lock)
- `TestAcceptsOfOneKeyCommitInQueueOrder`: T1 accepts v1 and stays open (through the real `acceptIn`, exported to tests only). T2's `Accept` of v2 is observed waiting on the lock. Meanwhile another key is accepted and claimed without waiting, and it is all a claim sees. T1 commits, T2 completes, claims come out v1, nothing, (deliver), v2.
- `TestReplayNeverOvertakesAVersionInFlight`: your replay case. Failed before the fix ("Claim = [v1], want nothing"). Also asserts the replayed seq is above v2's.
- `TestReplayWaitsForAnOpenAcceptOfItsKey`: a replay assigns a seq too, so it must queue behind an open Accept of its key.
- `TestClaimRechecksARowReplayedAfterItsSnapshot`: pins the seq re-check (see the reply on line 28 for the pausing technique).
- `TestAKeyWithAnyLeasedRowIsNotClaimable`: pins the defensive condition with a row inserted as superuser ahead of a version in flight.

**Mutations, each killed and restored:** Accept without the lock (`TestAcceptsOfOneKeyCommitInQueueOrder`), Replay without the lock (`TestReplayWaitsForAnOpenAcceptOfItsKey`), Replay keeps its seq (`TestReplayNeverOvertakes...` and `TestClaimRechecksARowReplayed...`), seq re-check removed (`TestClaimRechecksARowReplayed...`), defensive `NOT EXISTS` neutralized (`TestAKeyWithAnyLeasedRowIsNotClaimable`). Interleaving tests run 15 times and the concurrent ones 5 times under `-race`, all green.

text:
**Fixed in 1417501, and deterministically.** I disagree with one sentence only: the window can be hit on purpose from Go, just not by timing.

The claim's plan locks its rows one at a time, in `seq` order, as the UPDATE consumes them (LockRows sits above the Sort and Limit and is pulled row by row). So a test-only `BEFORE UPDATE` row trigger, created as superuser, that calls `pg_advisory_xact_lock` when a chosen "gate" row with a lower seq is being leased, stops the claim after it has taken its snapshot and chosen its heads, and before it locks the rows behind the gate. The test holds that advisory lock from an admin session, waits until `pg_locks` shows the claim waiting, changes the row behind the gate, and releases. See `gateClaimOf` in `internal/outbox/interleaving_test.go`.

`TestClaimRechecksARowFinishedAfterItsSnapshot` is your interleaving exactly: v1's lease has expired, the paused claim's snapshot sees it as a head, the slow holder's `MarkDelivered` commits inside the window, the claim resumes. It must return only the gate row, and v1 must be `delivered` and unleased.

The test cannot lose its teeth silently. If a future plan locked all rows up front, the claim would hold v1's row lock while paused, the holder's `MarkDelivered` would block, and the test fails on a 30 second timeout with a message that says the window is gone.

Mutation: `c.state IN ('pending', 'prepared')` removed from the locked row's conditions. Killed by that test (the claim returns the delivered row), 1 run out of 1, and the test passed 15 out of 15 runs under `-race` with the clause in place. Restored.

author: gablooge
text:
**note** On the statement you flagged as unverified. I ran EXPLAIN as the worker role. The locking is row by row because the top of the plan is `Nested Loop` with `Subquery Scan on claimed` (`Limit -> LockRows -> ...`) as its outer side and an index scan on `outbox_pkey` for `o` as its inner side, so each row is locked, then updated (your trigger fires), then the next is locked. That is the plan on the tiny test table and also on 36,000 rows after ANALYZE, which is expected with `LIMIT` capping `claimed` at the batch size.

It is a property of that join choice, though. With `enable_nestloop = off`, or with index scans off, the top becomes a Hash or Merge Join with `claimed` built first, every row is locked before the first update, and the window is gone. I ran `TestClaimRechecksARowFinishedAfterItsSnapshot`'s scenario under those settings: it fails on the `MarkDelivered` timeout exactly as your message predicts, never silently green, so the guard works. Only the test depends on the plan, not the claim: see the review body, both re-checks hold under every plan I could force.

If the plan ever does change, a pause that does not depend on it: replace the worker's SELECT policy in the test database with `USING (gate_fn(id))`, where the function takes the advisory lock when it sees the gate row. Every plan scans before it locks, so that stops the statement after its snapshot and before its first row lock. It needs a `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock` on a second key so that only the first claim stops and the claims made inside the window pass through.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The claim costs O(backlog) on every poll, not O(batch). This subquery computes the head of EVERY unfinished key in the table (scan, sort, unique), the outer query scans every unfinished row a second time to join against it, the `NOT EXISTS` runs once per head, and the result is sorted by `seq` again, all before `LIMIT` discards everything but the batch.

**Measured** (real schema and roles, as `sluiceway_worker`, 5,000,000 delivered rows present, full table in the review body):
- 100,000 unfinished: 331 ms and 378,196 buffers to return 10 rows. Batch 100 costs the same (299 ms). 90,000 anti-join probes, two disk-spilling sorts.
- 1,000,000 unfinished: 4.5 s and 4.37M buffers to return 10 rows, and the planner drops `outbox_unfinished` for two sequential scans of the whole heap (`Rows Removed by Filter: 5000000`, twice), so the partial index stops keeping finished rows out exactly when it matters.
- 1,000,000 unfinished, all in backoff: 520 ms and 1.8 GB of buffers read to return nothing.

**Fails when:** a sink is down for a few hours, or a backfill or reconcile pass lands, on an instance with 8 drain goroutines polling once a second. At 100,000 unfinished rows the pollers alone keep two and a half to five cores of Postgres busy. At 1,000,000 a poll takes longer than the poll interval, so all 8 backends are permanently occupied, the default pool is exhausted and `Accept` (target under 200 ms) waits for a connection. Adding worker replicas, which architecture section 9 offers as the way to add drain capacity, multiplies the scans. The backlog is controlled by senders and by the health of a sink someone else runs, so this is unbounded growth on a per-poll path.

**Suggested direction:** make the claim walk candidates in `seq` order and stop at the batch, so that being the head is a per-candidate index probe ("no unfinished row of this key has a lower seq") instead of a table-wide `DISTINCT ON`. A throwaway probe of that shape with a partial index on `(seq)` returned the same 10 heads in 0.10 ms and 35 buffers on the hot-key table. Alternatives: a recursive skip scan over `outbox_unfinished`, or a stored head marker maintained under the ordering key lock. Two cautions. Whatever you pick changes which conditions are re-evaluated on the locked row, so the state, lease and `seq` re-check argument from rounds 1 and 2 must be made again and the five planner settings re-run against it. And a walk in `seq` order still visits every non-head row of a hot key whose head is in backoff, so check the hot-key shape (20 keys x 4,500 versions), not only distinct keys.

author: gablooge

**should-fix** This refusal has no test, and the clamp nine lines below is silent and undocumented. The coverage profile shows this block with a count of 0. No test passes a batch above 10, so `min(batch, 1000)` is never exercised as a clamp either.

**Cost:** the guard is load-bearing. Without it a zero or negative lease reaches `make_interval`, the row is "leased" with a `lease_until` already in the past, stays claimable, and every poll adds 1 to `attempts`: the ladder is used up in seconds with no delivery ever attempted, and the row is parked as dead. A negative batch becomes `LIMIT -1`, an error. Nothing fails if someone removes or loosens the check. Separately, the godoc says "leases up to batch rows": a caller that asks for 5,000 gets at most 1,000 with no way to know, and sizes its goroutine pool on a wrong assumption.

**Suggested direction:** a table test for batch 0, batch -1, lease 0 and a negative lease (each an error, and no row changed), one for a batch above 1000 against more than 1000 claimable keys, and one sentence in the doc comment naming the cap.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** Two properties of `transition` that B10 will lean on are correct today and pinned by nothing.

1. **A database or context error must not read as `ErrLeaseLost`.** The two mean opposite things to the worker: `ErrLeaseLost` says stop working on the row, anything else says the transition may be retried while the lease lasts. Every error path here and in `Claim`, `acceptIn` and `Replay` is uncovered (coverage count 0 at lines 106, 121, 141, 154, 221, 227, 246). A test with a cancelled context would cover most of them: `Claim` returns an error and leases nothing, `MarkDelivered` returns an error that is not `ErrLeaseLost` and leaves the row as it was.
2. **A real `Claimed` aimed at another tenant.** The only forged value tested is one with no token (`outbox_test.go:291`), which is stopped by the `c.token == ""` check before any SQL runs. Take a genuine `Claimed` from `Claim`, set `Tenant` to tenant B, and call `MarkDelivered`: it must return `ErrLeaseLost` and leave the row of tenant A untouched. Reading the code that is what happens, because `TenantTx` binds B and the row-level security policy hides the row (reasoned, not run: see the review body). But that is the isolation property of this function, and today nothing fails if a later change runs transitions under a wider role.

**Suggested direction:** two small tests. Neither needs a new helper.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `Fail` says "cause must never contain token material". `MarkDead` takes the same `cause` plus a free-text `reason`, writes both to plain `text` columns, and says nothing. Neither the column comments in the migration nor architecture 3.2 mention it.

**Cost:** B09 and B11 will fill these from sink and provider errors, and the obvious call is `MarkDead(ctx, c, "sink rejected", err.Error())`. An error from `http.Client.Do` is a `*url.Error` whose text quotes the full request URL. Go redacts a password in the userinfo, but not the query string, so a sink or provider endpoint configured as `https://host/hook?api_key=...` lands in `last_error`, a plain column that the operator API (B14) will display and that every backup carries. `clip` makes the text storable, it does not make it safe, and a reader of `MarkDead` has no hint that it should.

**Suggested direction:** at minimum repeat the duty on `MarkDead` for both parameters and on the two columns in the migration, and say in architecture 3.2 that these columns hold text written by callers and must never hold secret material. Better, for B09 and B10 (please copy to those issues): do not let raw error strings in at all, for example by taking a small cause type built from a classification and a status code instead of a `string`, so the safe call is the easy one.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** An empty ordering key is refused by name, but there is no upper bound, and the real one is an accident of the btree page size. `ordering_key` is a column of `outbox_unfinished`, and a btree tuple cannot exceed 2704 bytes.

**Fails when:** probed on Postgres 17 with the same index definition. A 2,016 byte key is accepted. A poorly compressible 8,000 byte key fails the INSERT with `index row size 8024 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index "o_unfinished"` (SQLSTATE 54000), while 100,000 bytes of one repeated character pass because the index tuple compresses. So whether a delivery can be stored depends on how compressible its key is, and `Accept` reports it as an opaque wrapped database error. The ingress (B06) cannot tell that from Postgres being down, will answer 5xx, and the provider will re-send a delivery that can never be stored, which is the retry storm architecture 3.1 rules out. Keys are derived from provider entity ids, so they are sender-influenced.

**Suggested direction:** refuse a key above a stated length (a few hundred bytes is generous for an entity id) in `acceptIn`, next to the empty check, with an error B06 can recognise and park as poison, and add the boundary to `TestAcceptRefusesBadInput`.

author: gablooge
text:
**Fixed in efcf231.** The claim now costs its batch. Same shapes as yours, Postgres 17.11, 5,000,000 delivered rows present, as `sluiceway_worker`, warm, before (the claim of dfc5af4 on the same database) and after:

| Unfinished | Batch | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 over 90,000 keys | 10 | 265 ms, 386,914 buffers | 0.37 ms, 339 |
| same | 100 | 269 ms, 389,626 | 1.4 ms, 2,856 |
| 1,000,000 over 990,000 keys | 10 | 4,142 ms, 4,382,297 (two Seq Scans of the heap) | 0.28 ms, 344 |
| 1,000,000 all in backoff | 10 | 391 ms, 237,065, returns 0 | 0.02 ms, 3 |
| 20 hot keys x 4,500 plus 10,000 distinct | 10 | 148 ms, 107,234 | 0.22 ms, 285 |
| same, the hot keys' heads in backoff | 10 | 122 ms, 49,268 | 0.19 ms, 303 |

My "before" numbers agree with yours within the difference between two machines. What is left is almost all the UPDATE (about 25 buffers per leased row). Finding the rows costs about one buffer each.

**The design: a stored head marker** (ADR 10, `docs/adr/0010-outbox-head-marker.md`). `is_head` is true for exactly the earliest unfinished row of a key, and the claim is `WHERE is_head AND due_at <= now() ORDER BY due_at, seq LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` over `(due_at, seq) WHERE is_head`. `due_at` is a generated column, the later of `next_attempt_at` and `lease_until`, so the lease is folded into the index order and a poll does not revisit what other workers hold either.

**Why not your probe.** I took your second caution seriously: the walk in `seq` order visits every non-head row it meets. One hot key whose head is backing off puts thousands of rows in front of every poll, and with every head backing off the walk covers the whole backlog to return nothing, which is exactly the sink-outage case. An index on `next_attempt_at` does not cure it, because the rows behind a head are due from the moment they are accepted. The recursive skip scan costs the number of keys with work, 990,000 in your large shape.

**Your first caution, the re-check argument, made again.** The claim is now a single-table scan, so there is no join whose other side can be stale: both conditions (`is_head`, `due_at`) are columns of the locked row and are re-evaluated on its latest version. Safety no longer rests on the lock at all: `UNIQUE (tenant_id, ordering_key) WHERE is_head` plus `CHECK (NOT is_head OR state IN ('pending','prepared'))` plus "an unfinished row keeps the marker until it finishes" means two committed rows of one key can never both be leasable, whatever a writer does. That replaces the snapshot-evaluated `NOT EXISTS`, which you noted in round 1 was not re-checked under the lock. The ADR has the table of everything that can happen to a row between the snapshot and the lock. The five planner settings still run, against a gate row that is now first in line and row-locked (a gate row that is never due is not read by an index walk, so the old one would no longer pause anything). Mutation M1, `is_head` judged through a join instead of on the locked row, fails `TestClaimRechecksARowReplayedAfterItsSnapshot` under all five.

**The new race the marker brings, and its fix.** `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` now take the key's advisory lock too. Without it, `Accept` of v2 sees v1 unfinished and stores v2 as a non-head while the finish of v1 cannot yet see v2 and promotes nothing: v2 is never delivered. Three deterministic tests with two real transactions pin it from both sides and against a replay, and each fails under the mutation with "0 heads among 1 unfinished rows". Lock order stays advisory first, row second, everywhere, and the claim still takes no advisory lock.

**Two things I want you to look at critically.**

1. **The claim has no condition on the state, on purpose.** I first kept `c.state IN (...)` as belt and braces next to `is_head`. Measuring at your scale showed it is harmful: the planner treats the two as independent, expects about 200 heads where there are 10,020, decides a walk would take too long to fill a batch of 100, and ANDs in a bitmap of `outbox_unfinished`: 100,202 index entries read to return 100 rows. O(backlog) again, through the back door. The CHECK already makes every head unfinished on every row version, so `is_head` on the locked row is the state re-check. It also let the worker lose its SELECT on `state`. The guard test pins this by the shape of the plan.
2. **It is O(batch) plus Postgres housekeeping, and I would rather say so than not.** Every lease, retry and finish leaves a dead entry at the front of the index the claim walks. The first poll to pass one marks it, later polls skip it, and the leaf pages (about 260 entries each) stay until a vacuum. Worst case I could build: 990,000 heads moved by ONE statement and no vacuum at all: 116 ms for the first poll, once, then 5.9 ms and 3,844 buffers per poll, against 391 ms and 237,065 for the old claim in the same state. After a vacuum: 0.02 ms and 3 buffers. A long-running transaction holds that cleanup back, as for any queue in Postgres. It is in the ADR under Cost and in architecture section 9.

**The permanent guard**, `TestClaimCostFollowsTheBatchNotTheBacklog` in `outboxdb`, runs the generated claim through `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)` as the worker role and bounds the search and the whole statement separately, for batches of 10, 100 and 1000 and three nothing-is-due phases. It fails against the old claim in every phase (16,694 to 20,948 buffers to find rows against bounds of 150 to 10,000). The whole-statement bound alone would have let the old claim through at batch 100, so the search is bounded on its own.

`Accept` is still O(1): 0.17 ms and 24 buffers onto a new key at 6,000,000 rows, 0.78 ms and 104 onto a key with 4,500 unfinished versions. Section 9's claim about replicas is now true and says why, and what does not scale (one hot entity, by design).

author: gablooge
text:
**Fixed in 4ca4a74**, with the stronger of your two directions: the API no longer takes text.

`Fail(ctx, c, ladder, cause Cause)` and `MarkDead(ctx, c, cause Cause)`. A `Cause` (`internal/outbox/cause.go`) is built from a `Class`, which is one of the outbox's own texts following the failure table in architecture section 11, plus at most two facts about the response: `WithStatus` (kept only if 100 to 599) and `WithCode`, the remote system's error code, kept only if it is at most 64 bytes of ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`, and otherwise recorded as "withheld" so an operator can see there was one. There is no constructor that takes an `error` or a message, so `err.Error()` does not compile. `dead_reason` is one of two fixed texts ("retries exhausted", "not retryable"). `clip` stays in front of both columns as the last line of defense, with a unit test of its own now that no test can reach it with hostile text through the API.

`TestWhateverARemoteSystemSendsTheFailureIsRecordedAndNothingOfItIsStored` passes your exact leak as the code (`Post "https://sink.example/hook?api_key=...": context deadline exceeded`), and a URL, a bearer header, JSON, invalid UTF-8, a NUL and 4,000 bytes, through `Fail`, `Fail` to dead and `MarkDead`, and asserts against the database that the failure IS recorded and that nothing of the key is. It replaces `TestAnyCauseCanBeRecorded`, whose premise (arbitrary text as the cause) is gone, and keeps both of its properties. Mutation: `WithCode` lets anything through: the test finds the URL with the key in `last_error`.

The rule is on the two columns in the migration and in architecture 3.2 ("What a failure leaves behind").

One limit I would rather state than have you find: a bare token looks like a code. The type stops a secret that arrives by accident inside a message, a URL or a header, not a caller that passes the secret itself as the code. The godoc of `WithCode` says so and says what to pass. Worth copying to #9, #10 and #11 with the rest, which the orchestrator handles.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** The argument relies on READ COMMITTED, the code asks for nothing and checks nothing, and under REPEATABLE READ the package's own operations strand a row, silently. This sentence records the dependency. It does not enforce it.

**Fails when:** the server, the database or the role has `default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read'` (one `ALTER DATABASE` or `ALTER ROLE`, and some shops set it as policy). Probe, with the pull request's own helpers: set it on the test database, reopen the pool, accept v1, claim it, hold its `MarkDelivered` open (`deliverAndHold`), start `Accept` of v2. The Accept waits for the key lock as it should. Its snapshot was already taken by the `set_config` that binds the tenant, so when the finish commits and the lock is granted, the `NOT EXISTS` still sees v1 unfinished and stores v2 without the marker. The finish has already promoted nothing. Result: `tenant_a/task:2: 0 heads among 1 unfinished rows, the earliest is not a head`, `Claim` returns nothing, `Accept` returned success. Every Accept that waits for a finish of its entity does this, which is the normal case for an entity that changes often. Safety is unaffected (the database still refuses two heads), and under SERIALIZABLE the same interleaving should abort with a serialization failure instead, which is loud. REPEATABLE READ is the silent one.

Before this redesign the isolation level did not matter for liveness: the claim worked the heads out by itself. The marker made it load-bearing, so this is new with efcf231.

**Suggested direction:** ask for the level instead of inheriting it: `pgx.BeginTxFunc` with `IsoLevel: pgx.ReadCommitted` in `store.begin` is one line and makes the ADR's premise true by construction. Or have the preflight refuse a session whose `default_transaction_isolation` is anything else, in the fail closed spirit of the role checks. Either way, a test like the probe above, so the premise cannot rot. `store` belongs to #31, so say in the reply where you put it.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** Mutant E1 survives the whole suite: return `ErrLeaseLost` instead of `err` here, and also in the `case err != nil` a few lines down. `go test ./internal/outbox/` stays green. Coverage agrees: `finishIn` is at 75 percent, and the two uncovered blocks are exactly these two returns.

Round 3 asked for this property to be pinned (a database or context error must never read as a lost lease, because the two tell a worker opposite things). `TestAnErrorIsNotALostLease` pins it in `transition`, where your mutation S3 was. But it cancels the context before the transaction begins, so `BeginFunc` fails and no statement of `finishIn` ever runs. The redesign moved the decision between the two outcomes into `finishIn` (the `pgx.ErrNoRows` switch is new code), and that is the part no test reaches.

**Cost:** this is the statement where errors will actually happen in production. ADR 10 names it as a cost: finishing a row waits for an open Accept of the same entity, so a finish with a deadline times out right here, on the lock. If a later change turned that into `ErrLeaseLost`, the worker would stop working on a row it still holds and has already delivered to the sink, and leave it to be delivered again after the lease runs out. The code is right today: my probe P7 (hold an Accept of the key open with `acceptAndHold`, call `MarkDelivered` with a 300 ms deadline) gets `outbox: timeout: context deadline exceeded`, not `ErrLeaseLost`, the row unchanged, and the same lease delivers it afterwards.

**Suggested direction:** that probe as a test, for `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead`. It kills E1 at the lock statement. An error from the finishing UPDATE itself needs a different trick (a statement timeout, or a throwaway trigger that raises), if you want the second return covered too.

**should-fix** The contract this sentinel was added for has a hole: a key Postgres cannot store as `text` is not `ErrBadOrderingKey`, it is the opaque database error round 3 was about.

**Fails when:** probed against the head. `OrderingKey: "task:\x001"` returns `outbox: accept: ERROR: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00 (SQLSTATE 22021)`, and so does `"task:\xff\xfe"`. `errors.Is(err, ErrBadOrderingKey)` is false for both. A NUL is reachable from a sender: `encoding/json` decodes the JSON escape for U+0000 inside an entity id into a NUL byte without complaint (invalid UTF-8 it replaces, so that one needs a provider that is not JSON). The key can never be stored however often it is sent, so by the godoc of `ErrBadOrderingKey` it is poison. But B06 sees a wrapped database error, cannot tell it from an outage, answers 5xx, and the provider re-sends it: the retry storm of architecture 3.1, from one crafted entity id. The same is true of `Provider`, but that one is not sender-controlled.

`clip` already knows both rules for the error text. The key does not get them.

**Suggested direction:** refuse a key that is not valid UTF-8 or contains a NUL in the same `if`, under the same sentinel, add both to `TestAcceptRefusesAnOrderingKeyItCannotStore`, and widen the sentinel's text and godoc, which today say "1 to 512 bytes" and nothing else.
