Trust model", `#6-the-record-format-proposed` to "## 6. The record format (proposed)"). author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** This check survives the mutation it exists to catch. I deleted `utf8.Valid` from `decodeStrict` (and the import) and ran `go test ./... -count=1`: **every package green**, including `internal/provider/fake` and `internal/ingress`. The description lists this as M22 "the fake accepts bytes that are not UTF-8", caught by `TestADeliveryThisProviderWouldNotHaveSentIsAnError`. It is not caught.

**Fails when:** the only test that names UTF-8 (`fake_test.go:235`) sends `{0xff, 0xfe, '}'}`, which is not valid JSON, so `json.Decode` refuses it whether or not this line exists. The case the line is actually here for is invalid UTF-8 **inside a JSON string**, where `encoding/json` silently rewrites the bytes to U+FFFD. With the line deleted, `Parse` of a delivery whose `title` is `x\xff` succeeds, and so does `x\xfe` and `x\xc3(`; with the line present all three are refused with `fake: bad delivery: not UTF-8` (I ran both). So the defence works today and nothing keeps it working. That matters beyond this package: `CLAUDE.md` says a test double must reject whatever the real system rejects, the record format refuses a non-UTF-8 document on the bytes before parsing (B05), and B07, B09 and the pipeline tests will all build on this double. A silently lenient double is exactly the failure mode the package comment says it exists to prevent.

**Suggested direction:** add the case the comment describes, a delivery whose string field carries a raw `0xff` (and one carrying a truncated two byte sequence such as `\xc3(`), asserting `Parse` and `DeliveryKeys` both refuse; then re-run with this line deleted to confirm the new case fails.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `Verify` is given the body, the headers and the secret, but not the request method and not the request URI, and `Hub.Accept` does not carry them either, so no implementation can ever reach them. That is enough for ClickUp (body only) and for Slack (`v0:timestamp:body`, timestamp from a header), but not for HubSpot.

**Fails when:** B18 ("HubSpot. Reconcile-only by default; signed webhooks (v3 signature) as an option", `docs/backlog.md:152`) implements the v3 signature, whose base string is the request method, then the full request URI, then the raw body, then the `X-HubSpot-Request-Timestamp` value. With this signature the provider package cannot build it, so B18 has to widen `WebhookSource.Verify` and `Hub.Accept` at a point where B07's hub, B11's ClickUp and B15's Slack already implement them. This item's own description calls the interfaces "the seam the rest of M1 hangs off", which is the argument for getting the arguments right now rather than in three items' time.

**Suggested direction:** hand `Verify` the same thing `Handshake` already gets, the request with `Body` replaced by `http.NoBody`, or add an explicit small struct carrying method, URL and headers. Either way `Hub.Accept` needs it too, since the hub is what calls `Verify`. Note that the URI a provider signs is the public one, so whatever is passed must survive the tunnel (`X-Forwarded-Proto` and `Host`), which is a decision worth making here and not inside a provider.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** This branch is the only one in the file that can drop a real provider's delivery, and it logs nothing at all. The unknown-segment branch above it is right to be silent, because what reaches it is a scanner and the segment is unloggable text. This one is different: it can only be reached by a key that **is** in the registry, so there is a safe, constant string to log (`entry.Key()`), and the thing it reports is a wiring bug in our own program rather than traffic from a stranger.

**Fails when:** a provider is registered but its type stops satisfying `WebhookSource` (a method renamed in a refactor, a value receiver where a pointer receiver was meant, a provider registered as `Provider` by mistake). Every real delivery then answers 404 and is dropped, the sender is told there is no such endpoint, and the only place the loss is visible is the provider's own dashboard. Nothing in the process says a word.

**Suggested direction:** keep the response byte-identical, and log at warn with the registry's key on this branch only. When metrics land (B25) a counter of unknown-segment 404s belongs next to it, so the same mistake spelled in the URL instead of in the wiring is visible too.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** The content type is checked for shape and never for value, so anything printable passes. I drove a handshake returning `ContentType: "text/html"` with the body `<script>alert(1)</script>`: the edge answers 200 `Content-Type: text/html` with that body, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` does not help, because nosniff stops a browser guessing a type, not honouring the one that was sent. A 4096 byte content type is accepted too.

**Fails when:** a provider package echoes part of a challenge (which is what a handshake is for, and a challenge is a stranger's text) with an HTML content type, or with a type it built from something in the request. The result is reflected script execution on the ingress origin. The origin holds no cookie and serves nothing else today, which is why this is not blocking, but the guard immediately above it exists precisely so that "a provider implementation cannot turn the edge into something that serves content", and this is the hole in that guard.

**Suggested direction:** allow the small closed set a handshake can need (`text/plain; charset=utf-8`, `application/json`, maybe `application/xml`), refuse anything else as a provider bug the same way a 3xx is refused. That also bounds the length for free.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** `handshakeStatus` admits every 4xx, so a provider's handshake may answer 401. The contract three files away says 401 is **only** a signature that did not verify, and the architecture 3.1 table this pull request adds says the same in bold.

**Fails when:** a provider package answers a malformed challenge with 401 rather than 400 (an easy and defensible-looking choice, since a challenge is a proof of identity of sorts). From outside, that 401 is indistinguishable from the one the hub's `Unverified` produces, so the one status the contract reserves stops meaning one thing, and whoever debugs a provider's retry storm two milestones from now reads the table and is misled. Nothing produces it today, because the only `WebhookSource` in the tree answers 400, so this is a latent gap rather than a live defect.

**Suggested direction:** refuse 401 from a handshake the way 3xx and 5xx are refused, and say why in the comment, or, if a handshake really may need it, add the exception to the architecture table so the code and the document still agree.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** The status paragraph now says the webhook edge exists and that what is missing is verification and the outbox insert. A reader takes from that that the built binary answers at `/ingress/{provider}`, and it does not: `newMux` in `cmd/lawang/serve.go` mounts `GET /healthz` and nothing else, because `ingress.New` refuses a nil hub and B07 does the wiring.

**Fails when:** someone follows the README, starts `lawang serve`, points the Cloudflare Tunnel at it (the tunnel forwards exactly `^/ingress/[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}$`) and POSTs. They get a 404 from the mux, which is the same status the real edge answers for an unregistered provider, so there is nothing to tell the two apart and no log line either way. The decision itself is right and I agree a 503 stub in `serve` would be worse; it is only the README that leaves it out.

**Suggested direction:** one clause, that the route is not mounted in the binary until the hub lands in B07. The backlog log line and the pull request description both say it already.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 820b08d. You are right, and the mutation score was wrong.

The new `TestBytesThatAreNotUTF8AreRefusedBeforeTheDecoder` puts the bad byte inside a JSON string, in `title`: the one field `parseEvent` does not otherwise constrain, since `workspace`, `subscription`, `version` and `container` are all printable ASCII only and a bad byte in those is refused twice over. Six cases, a lone `0xff`, a lone `0xfe`, a truncated `\xc3(`, a bare continuation byte, a UTF-8-encoded surrogate half and an overlong `\xc0\xaf`, plus the old not-JSON-either case kept as a seventh. Each asserts `json.Valid` first, so the fixture itself fails loudly if it ever stops isolating the check, and each asserts both `Parse` and `DeliveryKeys` refuse. A control case at the end parses the same delivery with a valid title, so the test cannot pass against a `Parse` that refuses everything.

Re-ran your mutation two ways: deleting the `utf8.Valid` line (and the import) and making it never fire. Both fail all six new cases, across `go test ./internal/...`.

**The same shape elsewhere.** I mutated every other check in `internal/provider/fake` and `internal/ingress` that looked like it might be satisfied by a neighbouring layer, and found two more:

- `len(ev.ExternalID) > maxProviderID` survived deletion: no fixture ever had a long external id with the right prefix. Added one.
- `ev.OccurredAt = ev.OccurredAt.UTC()` survived deletion: every `occurred_at` fixture in the tree is already spelled with a `Z`, so nothing could see the conversion. Added `TestAnOffsetTimeIsNormalizedToUTC`, which sends `+07:00` and walks Parse, Hydrate and Normalize to the record.

One more survived and I left the code alone: `len(want) != sha256.Size` in `Verify`. `hmac.Equal` already refuses a digest of the wrong length, so the line changes no answer and no test can tell it from its absence. I kept it (it is the shape of the refusal written down) and said so in a comment, rather than leave a line that looks tested and is not.

Caught, for the record: the trailing-data check, the subscription id check, the empty and over-long `validationToken`, the body-shape challenge length bound, the handshake reply body cap, the early `Content-Length` refusal and the prealloc bound. Coverage stayed at 100% / 99% through all of it, so, as you said, it showed none of this.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/provider/fake/fake.go

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 820b08d, widened now rather than in B18.

**The shape.** A struct, `provider.Request{Method, URL string; Header http.Header; Body []byte}`, not a longer parameter list. The reason is exactly the one you gave for widening now: the schemes disagree about what a signature covers (ClickUp the body, Slack v0 a timestamp header and the body, HubSpot v3 the method, the full URI, the body and a timestamp), so the fifth provider will want a sixth field, and with a struct that costs one field instead of breaking every implementation again.

`Hub.Accept` takes the same value: `Accept(ctx, provider.Entry, provider.Request) (Verdict, error)`. The hub is what calls `Verify` once per candidate, so it hands the value straight through and there is nothing to assemble.

`DeliveryKeys` and `Parse` kept their signatures, and that is a line rather than an oversight: the routing keys are in the delivery's own content (a key read from configuration would select candidates for the wrong delivery), and `Parse` runs in the worker on the stored bytes, where the request is gone. Said so in the doc comments.

**The URL.** Taken from configuration, `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, and never from `Host`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` or `Forwarded`. Your point is the whole argument and I have written it into `internal/ingress`'s package comment and architecture 4: the URL is the one piece of a signature base string the receiver has to supply, so a receiver that read it off a header would let the sender choose part of what it is proving. The edge builds `base + r.URL.RequestURI()`, so only the path and query, which the sender signed too, come from the request.

`config.NormalizePublicBaseURL` owns the rules (absolute, http or https, a host, no credentials, no query, no fragment, a clean unescaped path prefix, no trailing slash) and `ingress.New` **calls** it rather than carrying a copy, for the `record.ValidProviderKey` reason: the two strings meet inside an HMAC, so a value `Load` accepted and the edge spelled differently would fail every signature with nothing to see. Errors never echo the value, since a swapped manifest puts the database URL here.

**Unset.** Your suggestion, and for your reason. The edge still serves, `Request.URL` is empty, and a scheme that signs the URL returns `false`, which is a 401 for every delivery of that provider: loud, and fixed with one variable. The alternative is a signature checked against a URL Lawang invented, which passes or fails for reasons nobody can reconstruct. `provider.Request.URL`'s doc comment says this is what an implementation must do.

Tests: `TestTheSignedURLComesFromConfigurationAndNeverFromTheRequest` sends `Host`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-For` and `Forwarded` all pointing at `attacker.example` and asserts the URL the hub got, over five path and query shapes; `TestWithNoPublicBaseURLTheEdgeServesAndAURLSigningProviderRefuses` runs a HubSpot-shaped verifier (`req.URL != ""`) configured and unconfigured and gets 202 and 401; `TestNewRefusesAPublicBaseURLItCannotUse`; and in config, a normalization table with an idempotence check plus sixteen refusals.

Mutations, all caught: building the URL from `r.Host`; preferring `X-Forwarded-Host` when present; guessing from the request when the base is unset; dropping the query; `ingress.New` not validating; `ingress.New` validating but keeping the raw spelling (caught by the doubled slash); the method not carried; the headers not carried; and in config, accepting a query, accepting credentials, not trimming the trailing slash, not cleaning the path, accepting a percent-encoded prefix, and `Load` ignoring the variable.

Architecture 3.1, 4 and 7 all say this now, and 7 carries the `Request` struct.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 820b08d.

`h.log.Warn("ingress: a registered provider is not a webhook source, so its deliveries are dropped", "provider", entry.Key())`, on this branch only, with the registry's own constant and no path segment. The response is untouched, so the two 404s are still indistinguishable from outside. The comment now says why the branch above stays silent and this one does not, in your words: what reaches the one above is a scanner and the segment is unloggable, and this one can only be our own wiring.

The test that covered this case was one row of `TestAnUnknownProviderIs404AndNothingElseHappens`, whose table asserts the log never quotes the segment, and `"plain"` is both a segment and a provider key, so the new log line broke it. That row moved out into `TestARegisteredProviderThatIsNotAWebhookSourceIsLoggedAndStill404`, which builds the edge with a **warn-level** handler (so the assertion is that an operator at the default level sees it, not that it is somewhere in a debug stream) and compares the body and every response header against the unregistered case for byte identity. While the row was moving I also tightened the table it left: every unknown-segment case now asserts the log is completely empty, not just free of the segment.

Mutations: removing the log line, and demoting it to `Debug`. Both caught.

The B25 counter idea is noted on #7 along with the other forward-looking notes, so it lands next to the metrics work rather than getting lost here.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 820b08d. `handshakeStatus` refuses 401, and 403 with it.

I took the first branch of your suggestion rather than the second: the table stays as it is and the code refuses, because the whole value of "401 means exactly one thing" is that it has no exceptions, and a handshake has nothing to verify in the first place. A provider that cannot read a challenge answers 400.

403 goes with it for the reason you were circling: it is the same claim in a different number, nobody debugging a provider's retries reads them apart, and no handshake shape in the wild needs it. The rest of 4xx stays allowed, so a provider is not boxed in.

The doc comment carries the argument, and architecture 3.1 now spells out the whole handshake reply contract in one place: the 8 KiB body cap, the status rules including this one, and the content type allowlist from the next finding.

Mutations: allowing 401 and 403 again (both cases fail), and allowing 401 alone while keeping 403 refused (the 401 case fails, which is what proves the two are tested separately rather than by one condition).

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in 820b08d. Your `text/html` + `<script>alert(1)</script>` case is in the table and now answers 500 with nothing written.

`validHandshakeContentType` replaces `printableASCII`: length at most 64 bytes, then `mime.ParseMediaType`, then the media type must be `text/plain` or `application/json`, and the only parameter allowed is `charset`, case-insensitively `utf-8`. I left `application/xml` out: nothing in the shapes we know needs it, and the two we do need are what Microsoft Graph and Slack use. It is one entry in a slice when a provider turns up that wants it.

`mime.ParseMediaType` also refuses a control character, so it subsumes the printable-ASCII check outright, which is why the newline case still passes and why the duplicated `printableASCII` (your N6) is gone from `internal/ingress` rather than being shared: the second copy stopped being needed. `internal/provider/fake` keeps its own, which now has one home.

The length cap is separate, and finding it teeth took a second attempt: my first fixture was `text/plain; charset=` + 64 `u`s, which the charset check refuses on its own, so deleting the cap changed nothing. The fixture is now `text/plain;` + 64 spaces + `charset=utf-8`, which `ParseMediaType` accepts and which leaves the media type and the one parameter exactly as the allowlist wants them, so only the cap can refuse it.

Ten new refusal cases (`text/html` bare and with a charset, `image/svg+xml`, `application/octet-stream`, an unknown parameter, a non-utf-8 charset, a type that is not a media type, a lone space, the over-length one, plus the two statuses from the finding below) and ten allowed cases, including an upper-case media type and an upper-case charset, a `text/plain` echo, a JSON challenge echo, a 400, a body exactly at the reply cap, and `nosniff` still asserted on every one.

Mutations: widening the allowlist to include `text/html`, `image/svg+xml` and `application/octet-stream`; dropping the media type check; dropping the parameter check; and dropping the length cap. All four caught.

title: Review comment on PR #47, README.md

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** `NormalizePublicBaseURL` breaks its own documented postcondition, and is not idempotent, for two inputs it accepts. Both end up inside an HMAC base string, which is the one place this function exists to make safe.

**Fails when:**

*Shape one, a doubled slash at the root.* `strings.TrimSuffix` removes exactly one slash, so `https://x//` leaves `p == "/"`, which `path.Clean` says is already clean, and the function returns `https://x/` **with the trailing slash it promises to remove**. I ran it: `ingress.New(reg, hub, Options{PublicBaseURL: "https://lawang.example.test//"})` is accepted and the edge then signs `https://lawang.example.test//ingress/fake`, a doubled slash inside the signature base string. Worse, the composition B07 will write disagrees with itself: `config.Load` of that value stores `https://lawang.example.test/`, and `ingress.New(cfg.PublicBaseURL)` normalizes the stored value a second time to `https://lawang.example.test`. So the value `Load` holds (which is what a `Registrar` in B13 or B18 will build the URL it registers with the provider from) and the value the edge signs are different strings. That is precisely the failure this function's own doc comment says it prevents: "a base URL that Load accepted and the edge spelled differently would make every signature fail with nothing to see." The provider gets 401 on every delivery, and 401 is the status the contract reserves for a forged signature.

*Shape two, an escape Go re-spells to itself.* The `u.RawPath != ""` guard only catches escapes whose canonical re-encoding differs from what was written (`%2F`, `%2e`). `%20`, `%23` and `%3F` re-encode to themselves, so `RawPath` stays empty and they pass. `https://x/a%20b` is accepted and returns `https://x/a b`, a base URL with a literal space in it, and the second pass **refuses** it ("the path prefix must not be percent-encoded"). So `config.Load` accepts the variable, stores `https://x/a b`, and `ingress.New` on that same value refuses to build the handler: in B07 the process fails to start, with an error that deliberately does not quote the value, after `Load` said nothing.

The test has an idempotence assertion, added for exactly this class, and neither shape is in the accepted table, so it never fires. The refused table has `/a//b` but not `//`.

Three documents state the postcondition the code does not keep: this doc comment ("no trailing slash"), architecture 4 ("a clean path prefix, no trailing slash") and the pull request description ("a clean unescaped path prefix, no trailing slash").

**Suggested direction:** stop editing the string and rebuild it from the parsed URL: refuse unless `u.EscapedPath() == u.Path` (which catches `%20` and every other escape, not only the ones Go re-spells), then reduce the path with `path.Clean` and treat a result of `"/"` as empty, then return `(&url.URL{Scheme: u.Scheme, Host: u.Host, Path: p}).String()`. For the tests: put `https://x//` and `https://x/a%20b` in a table, and make the idempotence check a property over every accepted input rather than a line inside one subtest, so a shape nobody thought of still has to survive a second pass.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/config/config.go

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** "The mux has already refused anything that needed cleaning" is not what the mux does. It **redirects**, and with a 307, which preserves the method and the body.

**Fails when:** I sent these over a real TCP connection to a server with this handler mounted: `//ingress/fake`, `/ingress//fake` and `/ingress/fake/../fake` each answer `307 Temporary Redirect` with `Location: /ingress/fake`. A well-behaved provider follows a 307 by re-POSTing the same body to the cleaned path, and the edge then signs the **cleaned** URL while the provider signed the one it was given. Every delivery is 401 and the operator reads that as a forgery, per the contract at the top of this file. This is not hypothetical in combination with the blocking finding on `NormalizePublicBaseURL`: a base of `https://x//` produces exactly a registered URL with a doubled slash in it.

**Suggested direction:** correct the comment to say that the mux cleans and redirects rather than refuses, and say what that costs, so B07 wires the route knowing it. If the behaviour should change too, the choice is between refusing a non-canonical path outright at the edge (the tunnel already does, for what comes through it) and signing what was actually sent; either is defensible, but the comment currently asserts an invariant that does not hold.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** An unset `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is a silent misconfiguration with no signal anywhere, and it spends the one status the contract reserves.

**Fails when:** an operator deploys the HubSpot connector and forgets one variable. The edge serves, `Request.URL` is `""`, `Verify` returns false, and every delivery answers **401**. I checked what tells them: `cfg.PublicBaseURL` has no reader outside `internal/config` itself, nothing logs the config at start (`serve` logs only `listening`), and `ingress.New` says nothing when this field is empty. So the process is completely silent and the provider's dashboard shows 401s, which the architecture table (and any alert built on it) says means a forged signature. The fail-closed decision itself is right, and I am not asking for it to change; what is missing is that the operator is never told which of the two it is.

This is also the same argument the round 1 reply used to refuse 401 from a handshake: "the whole value of '401 means exactly one thing' is that it has no exceptions." A misconfiguration that produces 401 is an exception, and it is the more common one.

**Suggested direction:** the cheap half is one `Warn` in `New` when `PublicBaseURL` is empty, naming the variable and saying that a scheme covering the URL will refuse every delivery. The better half, and the one `CLAUDE.md`'s fail-closed rule points at, is for B07 to refuse to start when a registered provider's scheme needs the URL and none is configured, since a deployment in that state cannot accept a single delivery.

author: gablooge
text: **note** "as the sender spelled it" suggests this varies, and it cannot. `ingress.Pattern` is `POST /ingress/{provider}`, so the mux answers 405 or 404 for every other method and the handler never sees anything but `POST`. Harmless for B18 (HubSpot posts), but a provider author reading this will believe there is something to branch on. One clause saying the edge only routes POST would settle it.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/provider/provider.go

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in b64f6af. Both shapes reproduced first, and the property found two more.

**The strategy: each rule idempotent in itself, not a second pass that has to converge.** The reason is what a second pass would do when it disagreed with the first. Normalizing to a fixed point and refusing if it does not converge turns a bug in this function into a refusal at start, with an error that deliberately does not quote the value, so the operator sees "LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL: could not be normalized" for a value that is perfectly fine and no way to tell which of the two is wrong. A rule that cannot move a value twice has nothing to converge, the failure shows up as a red test instead of a confused operator, and the function stays a straight line to read.

So, concretely:

- **Trailing slashes:** `strings.TrimRight(u.Path, "/")`, every one of them rather than one. That is a rewrite whose output is a fixed point of the rewrite. `https://x//` and `https://x///` are now `https://x`. A doubled slash *inside* the prefix stays a refusal (`/a//b`, and `//a` as well now), because that one is not a spelling with an obvious intent behind it, and quietly rewriting it to `/a/b` would hand a provider a URL the operator never registered.
- **Escapes:** `u.EscapedPath() != u.Path` refuses the lot, which is your suggestion and for your reason. It catches `%20`, `%23`, `%3F` and anything outside ASCII, not only the escapes Go re-spells. `%23` and `%3F` were the same bug wearing different clothes: they came back as a literal `#` and `?`, and the second pass refused them as a fragment and a query.

**Proved as a property, over a corpus.** `TestNormalizingTheResultAgainChangesNothing` feeds every input from both tables plus the product of five schemes, seven hosts and twenty-seven path shapes (the trailing-slash family, the doubled-slash family, `.` and `..`, the escapes, a literal space, a non-ASCII prefix, an IPv6 literal, a default port, an uppercase host) through `f`, then `f(f(x))`, and holds every accepted answer to the whole postcondition: a second pass returns it unchanged, it has no trailing slash, it parses, it has a host and a usable scheme, and its path is its own escaped form. It asserts at least 50 of the corpus was accepted, so the test cannot pass by the corpus quietly becoming all refusals. `FuzzNormalizePublicBaseURL` carries the same property with the corpus as seeds, so `go test` runs the seeds and `go test -fuzz` keeps going.

**The fuzzer found two more shapes inside a minute**, and both are in `testdata/fuzz` as seeds now:

- `http://0/!000000000`. My first version of the fix rebuilt the answer with `(&url.URL{...}).String()`, exactly as you suggested, and `String` escapes a path by its own rules rather than by the ones `url.Parse` accepted: it turned `/!a` into `/%21a`, which the next pass refused. So the answer is concatenated from the three parts that were just checked, with a comment saying why. `url.Parse` reads it back the same way: the host cannot hold a `/`, a `?` or a `#` (parse would have split there), and a path that is not absolute and clean was refused above.
- `http://%25`. `url.Parse` **decodes** percent-escapes in the host, so that parses with a host of `%`, and the answer is a string no second pass can read. There is now a check that the host carries no `%` at all. The only escape a host legitimately carries is an IPv6 zone id (`http://[fe80::1%25eth0]:8080`), which a public base URL has no use for, so the whole shape is refused rather than re-encoded.

Then 95 million executions of `-fuzz` with no counterexample.

**Mutations, all caught:**

| Mutation | What failed |
|---|---|
| `TrimRight` back to `TrimSuffix` | `TestNormalizingTheResultAgainChangesNothing` ("`https://x//` normalizes to `https://x/`, which normalizes to `https://x`") and five rows of the accepted table |
| `EscapedPath() != Path` back to `RawPath != ""` | the property, and the escaped space, hash and question mark rows |
| the answer rebuilt with `url.URL.String` | the property, on the `!` seed |
| the host `%` check deleted | the property, on both `http://%25` and the IPv6 zone id |

**On the host case and the default port:** kept, and the doc comment now carries your argument as the reason, under a heading of its own ("What it deliberately does not touch"), so it reads as a decision rather than an omission. Architecture 4 says it too, since that is where an operator looks first.

**One thing I removed while in there:** the `!strings.HasPrefix(p, "/")` disjunct, your note N8. I could not reach it either, and I now know why: with a host present `url.Parse` only ever yields an empty or an absolute path (`https:/x` and `https:///x` both parse with an empty host, so they are refused by the host check first). Rather than leave a guard nobody can trip, the premise is asserted where it would show: `checkNormalizedFixedPoint` fails if any accepted answer parses to a relative path, with a comment saying the check has to come back if it ever fires.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/config/config.go

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in b64f6af, behaviour and comment both. You are right about what the mux does, and I reproduced all three 307s over a real socket before changing anything (Go 1.26.7: `//ingress/fake`, `/ingress//fake`, `/ingress/fake/../fake` and `/ingress/./fake` all answer `307 Temporary Redirect` with `Location: /ingress/fake`, and the query survives into the Location).

**The decision: refuse, with the 404 an unknown provider gets.** Signing what was actually sent was the alternative and it does not work: the mux redirects before any handler runs, so "what was actually sent" never reaches the edge to be signed. That leaves refusing, and 404 is right for the reason you give, a provider only ever posts to the one URL Lawang gave it, so nothing legitimate needs cleaning. The answer is byte-identical to the unregistered-provider 404 (the test compares the body against a real `/ingress/nosuch` request), so the shape of a path cannot be used to ask which providers are registered.

**Where it lives: in front of the mux, and `Mount` returns it.** `net/http.ServeMux` does the cleaning in `findHandler`, before it dispatches, so a handler cannot see these requests and neither can the pattern. The only place a guard works is in front of the mux, and the only way to make that the default for B07 is for `Mount` to hand back the thing the server must serve:

```go
func (h *Handler) Mount(mux *http.ServeMux) http.Handler {
	mux.Handle(Pattern, h)
	return canonicalPathOnly(mux)
}
```

so B07 writes `srv.Handler = ingressHandler.Mount(mux)` and gets it without knowing any of this. Wrapping the mux rather than the route also means `/healthz`, and whatever B08 adds to the same mux afterwards, are behind the same rule, and this service now answers no redirects at all. `canonicalPath` mirrors `net/http`'s own unexported `cleanPath` (`path.Clean` with a trailing slash put back), so it refuses exactly what the mux would have redirected and nothing more: a pattern that legitimately ends in a slash keeps working, and there is a test route `POST /sub/` that proves it.

**Tested over a real socket**, since as you say `httptest.NewRequest` cannot pose the question: `rawPOST` writes the request line verbatim on a `net.Conn` with a 10 second deadline on both halves (a hang is a failure in seconds, not a stuck test) and reads the response with `http.ReadResponse`. `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected` sends `//ingress/fake`, `/ingress//fake`, `/ingress/fake/../fake`, `/ingress/./fake`, `/ingress/fake/.`, `/ingress/../ingress/fake`, `//healthz` and `/sub//`, and asserts for each: 404, **no `Location` header at all**, the content type, a body identical to the unknown-provider answer, and that the hub was not called once. Then the controls: `/ingress/fake?a=1` is 202 and the hub gets `https://lawang.example.test/ingress/fake?a=1`, and `/sub/` is still the teapot.

`TestPathTraversalNeverReachesTheHandler` was asserting only "not 2xx", which was true of a 307 as well; it now asserts 404 and no `Location`.

**Mutations:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `Mount` returns the bare mux | **caught**: four 307s in the new test with the Location assertion naming the re-POST, plus four rows of `TestPathTraversalNeverReachesTheHandler` |
| `canonicalPath` uses bare `path.Clean` (no trailing slash rule) | **caught**: `/sub/` answers 404 instead of 418, which is the collateral damage this rule exists to avoid |

Architecture 3.1 carries the whole argument now, including the 307 and why the guard cannot be inside the handler, and the 404 row of the status table says "or a path that is not already canonical".

Fixed in b64f6af, and recorded on #7.

`ingress.New` now warns once when `PublicBaseURL` is empty, naming the variable and what it costs:

> ingress: LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL is not set, so a provider whose signature covers the request URL (HubSpot v3) will answer 401 for every delivery

`TestAnUnsetPublicBaseURLIsSaidOutLoudAtStart` builds the edge with a handler at **warn** level, so what it asserts is that an operator at the default level sees it rather than that it is somewhere in a debug stream, and it checks the line names the variable and says 401. It belongs there and not here for one reason, which is now also in architecture 4: the edge does not know which providers a deployment registered or which of their schemes cover the URL. The hub does. `ingress.New` would have to guess, and a guess that refuses to start is worse than a warning.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** A base URL with **no host at all** passes this check, because `u.Host` carries the port. `http://:8080`, `https://:443` and even `http://:` are accepted, normalized to themselves, and handed to the edge.

**Fails when:** an operator sets `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=http://:8080`, which is an easy thing to do with `LAWANG_LISTEN_ADDR` ("host:port or :port") three entries above it in the same usage text. `Load` accepts it. `ingress.New` accepts it and does **not** warn, because the warn only fires on the empty string. The edge then signs `http://:8080/ingress/hubspot`, HubSpot v3 signed the real public URL, and every delivery answers 401 on the provider's dashboard with nothing in the process to say why. That is exactly the silent-401 failure this function exists to prevent, and it is the failure round 2's blocking finding was about, reached by a different door. I ran it: `NormalizePublicBaseURL("http://:8080")` returns `"http://:8080"`, with no error.

Neither the tables nor the new property can see it: `http://:8080` is a perfect fixed point, it parses, it has a non-empty `u.Host`, its path is its own escaped form. The property is doing its job, the postcondition is just silent about whether the answer names a machine. `http://host:` (an empty port) is accepted for the same reason.

The sibling case is the host's character set: a non-ASCII path prefix is refused (`/café`), but a non-ASCII **host** is accepted (`http://例え.jp` and `https://café.example` both come back unchanged). A provider spells a host in punycode, so an operator who pastes an IDN URL gets the same silent 401, and the refusal message that exists for the path never appears for the host.

**Suggested direction:** check `u.Hostname() == ""` rather than `u.Host == ""`, with `http://:8080` and `http://host:` as table rows; and decide explicitly whether a host outside ASCII is refused here or documented as the operator's problem, since the path half already made that choice the other way.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** "refuses exactly the paths the mux would have redirected and nothing else" is not true in either direction, and this comment is what the next person adding a route will read.

**Fails when:**

*It refuses more.* `net/http.ServeMux.findHandler` (Go 1.26.7, `server.go:2662`) cleans `r.URL.EscapedPath()`; this guard checks `r.URL.Path`, which is decoded. So `/ingress/fake%2f%2fx` and `/ingress/%2e%2e` are refused here although the mux would not have redirected them. Today that costs nothing, because both answer 404 anyway, and I verified that: through the guard and through the bare mux they are 404 either way. It costs something the day a pattern has a wildcard segment that can legitimately carry an encoded slash.

*It refuses less.* The clean-path redirect is not the mux's only redirect. `matchOrRedirect` also answers 307 for the subtree case, and that one runs **after** this guard has passed the request. Over a real socket, against a mux with this file's own test route `POST /sub/` on it: `POST /sub` answers **307 with `Location: /sub/`**, through `Mount`'s handler. So "this service answers no redirects at all" is not what was built. It does not touch the ingress route (`POST /ingress/{provider}` has no trailing slash, so nothing redirects to it), but B07 and B08 add routes to this same mux, and an operator API mounted as a subtree (`/api/`) brings a 307 with a path in a `Location` back to a service whose architecture text now says a non-canonical path is refused.

**Suggested direction:** say what the guard covers (the `cleanPath` redirect) and what it does not (the trailing-slash redirect on a subtree pattern), and that it reads the decoded path while the mux cleans the escaped one. If the trailing-slash redirect should also be refused, the cheap version is to answer the same 404 when `next` would produce a 3xx, which also makes the claim self-enforcing rather than a comment.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** Nothing stops B07 dropping this return value, and dropping it silently reintroduces the defect this signature exists to prevent.

**Fails when:** B07 writes the obvious three lines:

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
h.Mount(mux)
srv.Handler = mux
```

I wrote exactly that into this package and built it: **`go build` passes, `go vet` passes, `golangci-lint run` reports nothing about it** (its only complaint was that my probe function had no caller). Go does not require a return value to be used, and `errcheck` only looks at errors. Then I served the bare mux over a real socket on this very commit: `//ingress/fake`, `/ingress//fake` and `/ingress/fake/../fake` answer `307 Temporary Redirect` with `Location: /ingress/fake`, which is round 2's finding, back in full, in a pull request that has no test that could fail because the mistake lives in the other package.

The bold sentence in this comment is the only thing standing between B07 and that, and a comment is not a guard, which is the argument this branch used (rightly) about `Request.Header` one commit ago.

**Suggested direction:** make the unguarded mux unreachable rather than merely discouraged. Either `ingress` owns the mux (`func NewMux(h *Handler, routes ...) http.Handler`, so there is no bare mux for a caller to hold), or `Mount` takes what it must set (`func (h *Handler) Mount(mux *http.ServeMux, srv *http.Server)`, setting `srv.Handler` itself, so there is no return value to drop). Failing either, B07's wiring needs a test that sends `//ingress/{provider}` over a socket to the **server as it is actually configured** and asserts 404 with no `Location`.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** This branch is the only thing stopping one more kind of redirect, and no test reaches it. It is the package's single uncovered statement (`internal/ingress` is at 99.2%, and `go tool cover` shows `ingress.go:313.28,315.3` with a count of 0).

**Fails when:** a sender uses an absolute-form request line with no path, `POST http://host HTTP/1.1`, or the asterisk form, `POST * HTTP/1.1`. Both are legal on the wire and both arrive with `r.URL.Path == ""`. I sent them over a real socket: through the guard they answer 404, and through the bare mux `POST http://attacker.example` answers **307 with `Location: /`**. I confirmed by coverage that these request lines are what reaches this branch (`313.28,315.3` goes from 0 to 1 when I send them). `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected` sends eight paths and every one of them starts with a slash, so the branch is unpinned: deleting it, or turning it into `if p[0] != '/'`, leaves the suite green and reintroduces a redirect (and, for the second spelling, an index out of range on the empty string).

**Suggested direction:** add `POST http://host HTTP/1.1` (absolute form, no path) to the refused list in that socket test, since it also documents that an absolute-form request line cannot smuggle a host past the edge, which is a property this branch happens to be defending.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** "there is nothing an implementation can write to" is not true of `Request`, and the field it is not true of is the one a signature is actually over.

**Fails when:** a provider implementation writes through `Request.Body`. It is a `[]byte` handed out by value, aliasing the edge's own buffer, and I checked that it is writable and that the write is visible to the next reader and in the edge's buffer. So a `Verify` or a `DeliveryKeys` that normalizes bytes in place (trimming a BOM, lowercasing, zeroing a field before hashing) changes what every later candidate verifies **and** what B07 then stores in the outbox, which is the same intermittent, second-candidate-only failure this bullet was written to close, only now it changes a stored record and not just a verdict.

The struct comment above says "never modified", which is an instruction to implementations. This bullet upgrades it to a guarantee the type does not give, and a provider author reading architecture 7 will believe nothing in `Request` is mutable and that nothing in review needs to check for it.

**Suggested direction:** the sentence should say that nothing in the **header** can be written to, and that `Body` is the one field an implementation can still corrupt, so it stays a documented rule rather than a guarantee. Whether to make it a guarantee is B07's call and belongs on #7: copying a megabyte per candidate is not obviously worth it, and the cheaper option is for the hub to compare a hash of the body before and after each candidate in tests.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `cc03b72`, both directions, and I read Go 1.26.7's `net/http` for both mechanisms rather than inferring them.

**It refused more.** `findHandler` cleans `r.URL.EscapedPath()` (server.go:2662 and 2680), so the guard now reads that string. `canonicalPath` is net/http's own `cleanPath` inlined and compared against its input. `/ingress/fake%2f%2fx` and `/ingress/%2e%2e` reach the handler now, exactly as the mux would have routed them, and are refused by the registry lookup instead. The socket test has a `POST /echo/{seg}` route and asserts that `/echo/a%2f%2fb` answers 418 with a wildcard value of `a//b`, which is a case that only passes with the escaped path: mutating the guard back to `r.URL.Path` fails it.

**It refused less.** The trailing-slash redirect is a second mechanism, and a guard in front of the mux cannot see it coming, because `matchOrRedirect` (server.go:2731) decides it from the routing table and not from the request. So it is taken away from the mux instead of guarded against: `ingress.New` now owns the table, takes every other route as an `ingress.Route`, and registers the slash-less path itself with the same 404. Reading `exactMatch` (server.go:2772) and then checking each spelling over a real socket, exactly three can match a path ending in a slash and so enable the redirect: a trailing slash, `/{name...}`, and `/{$}`. A literal or a `{name}` segment cannot, which is why `POST /ingress/{provider}` never had a root to redirect from. `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect` covers all three plus a wildcard segment before the slash, a rooted subtree, two spellings of the same subtree, and the case where the caller already answers the slash-less path.

Mutations: deleting the shadow registration reproduces `307 Location: /sub/` in all four redirect-enabling cases; deleting the `{$}` spelling from `subtreeRoot` reproduces it for that one; deleting the multi-wildcard spelling reproduces it for that one.

One over-refusal is left and is deliberate: `findHandler` exempts CONNECT from cleaning, and this guard does not. The edge answers POST only, and the doc comment says so.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `cc03b72`. You are right that a comment is not a guard, and your probe is the argument: the mistake lives in the other package, so no test here could have failed.

**The shape I chose is stronger than either suggestion: `Mount` is gone and `New` returns `http.Handler`.** Other routes go in `Options.Routes` as `ingress.Route{Method, Path, Handler}`, so `/healthz` and the `/v1` operator API still sit on one mux behind one guard.

Why this rather than `NewMux(h, routes...)`: with `New` returning `*Handler`, the type still implements `http.Handler` and `Pattern` was still exported, so a caller could write `mux.Handle(ingress.Pattern, h); srv.Handler = mux` and get the bug back by a different door. Now there is no exported handler type, no exported pattern, and no `ServeHTTP` on the edge at all (`serveHTTP` is unexported, and `newMux` wraps it in an `http.HandlerFunc` itself). The mux is built inside `New` and never leaves it.

So dropping it is impossible rather than loud: there is no bare mux to serve, the only value that can reach `http.Server.Handler` is the guarded one, and a caller who drops it has nothing to serve and a server that answers nothing. The error return is checked by `errcheck`, which is on in `.golangci.yml`'s default set.

Two things came with it, both because `New` now owns the table:

- Every route is validated (nil handler, a path that does not start with a slash, a host or a pattern written into `Path`, a space, a lower case method, a duplicate pattern, a route that would take over the webhook endpoint) and a `net/http` pattern panic is turned into an error. A wiring mistake is now a start-up error with a message rather than a panic in a request goroutine. `TestARouteNewCannotServeIsRefusedAtStart` covers it.
- `Route` carries `Method` and `Path` separately rather than one pattern string, which is what lets `New` derive the slash-less path safely instead of parsing `net/http`'s pattern grammar back out of a string.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `cc03b72`. The check is `u.Hostname() == ""` now, so `http://:8080`, `https://:443` and `http://:` are refused, and `http://host:` is refused by a second check on a trailing colon, since `Hostname()` reads that one as a host with no port. All four are table rows, with the note that the property cannot see them because each is its own normal form.

**On the host's character set, I went the way the path half already went: a host outside ASCII is refused.** A provider's dashboard holds the punycode form, which is what DNS carries and what ends up in a HubSpot v3 base string, so `https://café.example` in this variable is the same silent 401 as an unescaped path prefix, only harder to see. Refusing it at start costs an operator one edit and tells them exactly what to write; accepting it costs them a day on a dashboard. `xn--80ak6aa92e.com` and `xn--caf-dma.example` are accepted and are now rows in the accepted table, so IDN is usable, in the one spelling that works. The usage text and architecture 4 say so.

text:
Fixed in `cc03b72`. Both spellings are in the refused list of the socket test now, and both disjuncts are pinned separately:

It is worth a correction to the finding: `net/http` does not answer this one itself, it reaches the handler (I printed the path from a handler in front of the mux), and the 400 you saw came from the mux's own redirect handler after `cleanPath("*")` produced `/*`. Through the guard it is the ordinary 404. Deleting the `escaped[0] != '/'` disjunct makes that case answer 400 with an empty body, and the test fails on the status, the body and the content type.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `cc03b72` by stating the truth, which is your suggested direction, and I measured the other option before choosing.

Architecture 7 now says the header is a guarantee (no mutating method, nothing copied) and that `Request.Body` is a **rule and not a guarantee**: it aliases the edge's own buffer, an implementation that normalizes it in place changes what every later candidate verifies and what B07 stores in the outbox, and only a review of the provider package catches that. The doc comment on the field says the same thing, so the document and the code agree.

**The measurement, because it changes the argument you and I would both have made.** Copying the slice costs 0.9 us for an 8 KiB delivery and 57 us at the 1 MiB cap on this machine (Apple M5 Pro, 18 GB/s), against an accept path that targets 200 ms with no provider I/O. Ten candidates at the cap is 0.6 ms, which is 0.3% of the budget. So "a megabyte per candidate is not obviously worth it" turns out to be worth it, and the reason not to do it here is not cost: the edge builds one `Request` and has no candidate loop to copy in. The copy belongs in the loop, which is B07's.

Recorded on #7 with the numbers, together with N1 (`provider.Header` is a live view of the request's map, not a snapshot), which matters for the same reason: B07 is the next thing to build a `Request`.
title: Review comment on PR #47, docs/architecture.md

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** `coveredBy` decides by comparing path **strings**, but the thing it has to decide is whether the mux would redirect, and that is a property of the whole routing table. When some other route already answers the slash-less path through a wildcard, `coveredBy` says "not covered", the shadow route is registered anyway, and it is **more specific than the wildcard**, so it wins. The caller's route stops answering.

**Fails when:** a caller passes a collection route and a subtree under it, which is the ordinary shape of the `/v1` operator API this whole mechanism exists for. I ran exactly this, over a real socket, both ways:

```go
{Method: "POST", Path: "/v1/{resource}", Handler: byResource},
{Method: "POST", Path: "/v1/tenants/",  Handler: tenants},
```

- through a bare `net/http.ServeMux`: `POST /v1/tenants` answers **418 from `byResource`, with no `Location` and no redirect**, because `/v1/{resource}` is an exact match for it and `matchOrRedirect` stops at an exact match;
- through `ingress.New` with the same two routes: `POST /v1/tenants` answers **404 `no such provider`**.

So the shadow is registered where there was never a redirect to prevent, and it buries a live route. Nothing warns, nothing logs, and the 404 body talks about providers. `POST /v1/other`, `/v1/tenants/` and `/v1/tenants/x` are all unaffected, so it is one path out of a family: exactly the shape that survives a smoke test and is found in production.

The same wrong rule also refuses a table `net/http` accepts. With

```go
{Method: "GET", Path: "/v1/{id}/",  Handler: h},
{Method: "GET", Path: "/v1/{name}", Handler: h},
```

`net/http` registers both happily (I checked), while `New` fails at start with `ingress: net/http.ServeMux refused a route: pattern "GET /v1/{id}" (registered at ingress.go:393) conflicts with pattern "GET /v1/{name}"`, quoting a pattern the caller never wrote and a line inside this file. Loud rather than silent, but it is the same root cause and it blocks a legal wiring.

`TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect` cannot see either case: every route table in it has at most one route per path depth, so `coveredBy`'s string comparison is always the right answer there. Mutating `coveredBy` to return false always is caught, which pins that it is consulted, not that its rule is right.

**Suggested direction:** stop predicting the mux and ask it. The table is fully built before this loop runs, so for each candidate root you can put a synthetic request for that method and root through `mux.Handler(req)` (or through a `ResponseRecorder`) and register the 404 only when the answer is a 3xx. That is exact by construction for every present and future pattern spelling, it fixes finding 2 for free, and it turns the three-spellings argument from something a reader has to re-derive from `net/http`'s source into something the code checks.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** "only in three spellings" is not true, and `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect` asserts a universal that has a counterexample.

**Fails when:** a route's last segment is written `%2F`. `parsePattern` (pattern.go:158, Go 1.26.7) stores `{$}` as `segment{s: "/"}`, and it stores a literal segment as `pathUnescape(seg)`, so `/a/%2F` produces the **identical** segment. `exactMatch` then returns true for `/a/` on the non-multi branch, and `matchOrRedirect` redirects. I ran it: `ingress.New` accepts `Route{Method: "POST", Path: "/a/%2F"}`, and `POST /a` through the handler `New` returns answers **307 with `Location: /a/`**. That is a redirect escaping from a package whose test for this is called `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`, and a 307 is exactly what turns a delivery into a 401 that reads as a forgery.

The operational cost today is near zero: nobody writes `%2F` as a route segment on purpose. The cost that is not zero is the comment. It is the argument a reader has to trust when they add the fourth route, it is stated as a closed enumeration checked over a socket, and one of the two spellings it says "never matches" (a literal) does match when it decodes to a slash.

**Suggested direction:** the fix suggested on `coveredBy` covers this one too, because asking the mux needs no enumeration. If the enumeration stays, say that it holds for a last segment that does not percent-decode to a slash, and add `/a/%2F` as a case so the claim is pinned rather than asserted.

author: gablooge
text:
**should-fix** A route can take the webhook endpoint over, and the description says it cannot. The refusal that exists catches only the pattern `POST /ingress/{provider}` spelled exactly, via the duplicate-pattern check; a literal path under `/ingress/` is more specific than the wildcard and simply wins.

**Fails when:** a caller passes `Route{Method: "POST", Path: "/ingress/fake", Handler: h}`. `New` accepts it with no error and no log, and `POST /ingress/fake` answers that handler instead of the edge: I ran it and got 418 with my own body where 202 `stored` belongs. Every delivery for that provider is answered by the wrong handler, the provider sees a 2xx and retries nothing, and nothing is stored. It is a wiring mistake rather than sender input, which is why this is not blocking, but it is the exact class of mistake `New` took ownership of this round, and the description lists "a route that would take over the webhook endpoint" among what is "a start-up error with a message".

I checked the neighbours, and they are all fine: `/ingress/{p}` is refused as a conflict, and `/ingress/{p...}`, `/ingress/`, `/`, `/ingress/{provider}` with no method and `/ingress/{provider}/` all leave the edge answering 202. It is the literal that gets through.

**Suggested direction:** refuse in `check` any path under the edge's own route, which is one `strings.HasPrefix(r.Path, "/ingress/")` away and costs a caller nothing (no legitimate route lives there), and add a test whose route path is a literal provider key rather than the wildcard pattern, since that is the case the current test cannot see. If the refusal is meant to stay narrow, the description should say that only the exact pattern is refused.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `581b862`. You are right, and both reproductions are in the test table now, driven over a real socket.

**What it does now.** `newMux` builds a second `http.ServeMux` next to the real one, carrying the same patterns and a handler that does nothing, and asks that one: `redirects(probe, rt.Method, root)` serves a synthetic request into it and reports whether the status is 3xx. Nothing a caller wrote can run, so the probe cannot have a side effect by construction rather than by argument. I took that route rather than `mux.Handler(req)` for exactly that reason: `findHandler` returns `RedirectHandler(...)`, whose type is unexported, so classifying its answer means either `reflect.TypeOf` against `http.RedirectHandler("/", 307)`, which fails **open** if `net/http` ever changes shape, or running the handler, which for a non-redirect is the caller's own. The second mux costs one extra registration pass at start and is thrown away when `newMux` returns.

**Your two probes, as test cases.** `a wildcard at the same depth as a subtree` is P1 (`POST /v1/{resource}` + `POST /v1/tenants/`): `/v1/tenants` and `/v1/other` are 418 from the wildcard, `/v1/tenants/` and `/v1/tenants/x` are 200. `two wildcards at the same depth` is P2 (`/v1/{id}/` + `/v1/{name}`): `New` accepts it and `/v1/a` is 200. I also added the case where the redirect is **real** at the same depth, the same two patterns under different methods, where `GET /v1/a` must be 404 and `POST /v1/a` must be 200: that pins that the guard route still carries the method of the route that needs it.

**The deduplication came out in the wash.** `probe` learns each guard route as it is registered, so a second route with the same root finds an exact match and asks for nothing. The explicit `registered[shadow]` branch is gone; deleting `probe.Handle(guarding, nothing)` fails `two_spellings_of_the_same_subtree`.

**Mutations.** The previous implementation, in full, against the new tables: `a_wildcard_at_the_same_depth_as_a_subtree`, `two_wildcards_at_the_same_depth` and `a_last_segment_that_percent-decodes_to_a_slash` all fail. `redirects` always false: eight cases fail. Always true: five, including both of yours. `redirectRoot`'s `i <= 0` to `i < 0`: four. `internal/ingress` is still at 100.0% of statements.

**One shape is still refused, and I think correctly.** A methodless route plus a method-ful one at the same depth (`Route{Path: "/v1/tenants/"}` + `Route{Method: "GET", Path: "/v1/{name}"}`) is a table `net/http` accepts and that genuinely redirects for every method but GET, and the route that would stop it conflicts with the caller's. There is no table that both stops the redirect and keeps both routes, so `New` refuses. What I changed is the message: while a route of this package's own is being registered, `guarding` holds its pattern, and the refusal says the pattern is needed so the mux cannot answer that path with a redirect, instead of leaving `net/http` to name a pattern the caller never wrote. There is a case for it, and deleting the branch fails it.
title: Review comment on PR #47, internal/ingress/ingress.go

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `581b862`, and the enumeration is gone rather than extended, as you suggested.

`redirectRoot` now returns `p` without its last segment and reads nothing about how that segment is written:

```go
i := strings.LastIndex(p, "/")
if i <= 0 {
	return "", false
}
return p[:i], true
```

The argument is that the redirect fires from `X` when `X + "/"` exactly matches some pattern `P`, and `X + "/"` has one slash more than `X`, so the only candidate for `P` is `P` minus its last segment. Whether that candidate really redirects is the mux's to answer now, so there is nothing left to enumerate and nothing for a reader to re-derive from `net/http`'s source when they add the fourth route.

It is pinned, not asserted. `a last segment that percent-decodes to a slash` is your P5: `Route{POST, "/a/%2F"}`, `POST /a` must be 404 with no `Location` and `POST /a/` must reach the handler. Running the previous implementation against that case fails it with the 307 you saw.

Your finding also turned up a second escaping bug in the probe itself, which the socket test now covers as `a subtree whose root carries a percent-escape` (`Route{POST, "/a%2Fb/"}`). The mux matches on `EscapedPath` and unescapes one segment at a time, so the question has to be put in the spelling a sender would use: `&url.URL{Path: root}` alone re-escapes the `%` to `%25` and the probe answers "no redirect" for a route that does redirect. `redirects` sets `Path` and `RawPath` together when `url.PathUnescape` succeeds, and falls back to `Path` alone when it does not, which is what `net/http`'s own pattern parser does with an undecodable segment. Replacing that assignment with a no-op fails that case and only that case.

text:
**should-fix (finding 1)** The probe asks about **one path per pattern**, and that path is the pattern string, so a wildcard segment is asked about as the literal text `{x}`. Nothing says the answer is then generalised to the whole family of paths the pattern matches, and it is not always sound: `net/http` unescapes a literal segment when it parses a pattern, so a percent-escaped brace produces a literal segment that collides with the representative and makes `redirects` report "no redirect" for a family where every real path still redirects.

**Fails when:** the table is `POST /a/{x}/` plus `POST /a/%7Bx%7D`. `redirectRoot` gives the root `/a/{x}`; the probe request's `EscapedPath()` is `/a/%7Bx%7D`, whose segment unescapes to `{x}`, which the literal pattern matches exactly, so no guard is registered. Over a real socket `POST /a/b` then answers **307 `Location: /a/b/`** through the handler `New` returns, which is the one thing this package promises cannot happen. Reproduced for 17 of the 560 tables in my sweep, and every one of them contains the escaped-brace literal. It is not reachable from anything in this repository today, which is why it is should-fix and not blocking.

**Suggested direction:** the cheap and complete fix is to refuse the input rather than to widen the probe: `Route.check` can refuse a `Path` whose `url.PathUnescape` differs from itself (no route this program writes needs a percent-escape, and the same rule closes finding 2). If you would rather keep escaped paths, then say in the comment here that the answer is generalised from one representative, and state the condition under which that is sound. Either way the backlog log line's "exact by construction for every pattern spelling" needs softening to match.

**note (1).** The comment above says "When it cannot be decoded, Path alone is right: net/http's own pattern parser leaves an undecodable segment as it is written, and so does EscapedPath." The second half is not what `EscapedPath` does. With `Path = "/a/%zz"` and `RawPath = ""` it returns **`/a/%25zz`**, because `%` is escaped under `encodePath` (`/a/%` gives `/a/%25`, `/a/%2F%zz` gives `/a/%252F%25zz`).

No behaviour change is needed; the sentence should say why it works rather than assert something `net/url` does not do. Worth fixing in the same pass as finding 1, since it is the same paragraph.

Fixed in `1c9129e`, together with finding 2, by taking the refusal you suggested.

`Route.check` now refuses a `Path` containing a percent-escape at all, rather than comparing it to its decoded form. I chose the blunter rule for three reasons: a `Route` is a Go string literal in this repository's own source and none of them needs an escape; refusing only the paths whose decode differs would have left exactly the malformed ones (`/a/%zz`, `/a/%2`) accepted while refusing the well-formed ones, which is the wrong way round; and with no escape possible anywhere in a path, the representative argument becomes provable rather than conditional. A literal segment equal to the text `{x}` can only be written with an escape, since the parser reads a bare `{` as a wildcard, so no pattern in a table can single the representative out.

That also made the `RawPath` handling in `redirects` unreachable, so it is gone. With no escape in the path, `EscapedPath()` yields the same segments whether or not `RawPath` is set, which I checked over `/a/b`, `/a/{x}`, `/a/~b` and a non-ASCII path. Deleting it also deletes the comment note 1 is about.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** The candidate lookup is an either/or, so a subscription whose `workspace_id` is empty is never a candidate for any delivery that carries a workspace key, even when the delivery names that subscription's `external_id` exactly. `CandidatesBySubscription` runs only when `keys.Workspace == ""`, and the by-workspace query has `AND workspace_id = @workspace`, which such a row cannot satisfy.

**Fails when:** two tenants share a signing secret and registered with different key shapes.

```go
e.register(tenantA, "mailbox-1", "", "S1", shared) // workspace_id = ''
e.register(tenantB, "W1", "W1", "", shared)        // external_id  = ''
e.accept(h, entry, signed(delivery("W1", "S1", "1"), shared))
```

I ran this against `da05a1c`: the verdict is `stored` and the outbox holds one row owned by `tenant_b`. Both tenants' secrets verify these exact bytes, so acceptance criterion 3 says it must be a parked row and never a routed one. Only tenant B's row was ever asked, so the hub never learned there was a second tenant to be ambiguous about. The delivery may well be tenant A's.

There is a second, more ordinary cost that needs no shared secret. `Register` accepts `(workspace "", external "S1")`, and the table's CHECK accepts it (the migration comment says a row is refused only when it has *neither* key, so that it does not "sit in the table unreachable"). But once a delivery of that provider carries a workspace key, the row *is* unreachable: I registered it alone and the matching delivery came back `unattributable: no owner`. `Register`'s own doc comment says it "refuses anything that could not resolve a delivery", and this is something it accepts that cannot.

**Suggested direction:** make the candidate set the union of what either key could select rather than picking one query, for example one statement whose WHERE is `provider = $1 AND ((workspace_id = $2 AND (external_id = '' OR $3 = '' OR external_id = $3)) OR (external_id <> '' AND external_id = $3))`, which a BitmapOr can still serve from the two existing indexes. Whatever the shape, the test that fixes it wants to be the pair above: the shared-secret case must park, and the single-tenant case must store.

author: gablooge
text:
**blocking** This test EXPLAINs a hand-copied SQL string, not the query the hub sends, so it cannot fail for anything that happens to `internal/hub/queries.sql`. It is the test that exists to keep the accept path off a table scan, and it has no teeth against the only query that runs on the accept path.

**Fails when:** the checked-in query stops being indexable. I changed `AND workspace_id = @workspace::text` to `AND workspace_id || '' = @workspace::text` in the generated query and ran the whole suite: **green**, this test included. The measured cost of that change, on 50,000 rows, as a prepared statement under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`:

```
as checked in:  Index Scan using subscriptions_by_workspace, Buffers: shared hit=3,   0.055 ms
mutated:        Seq Scan on subscriptions,                    Buffers: shared hit=515, 3.33 ms
```

That is 515 buffers on a path that runs once per delivery, growing linearly with the table, and nothing in the suite says a word about it. (Dropping the index itself is caught, so the fix from the first round works; it is the query the test cannot see.)

While you are here: the literal also differs from the real query in a way that changes the plan. The test writes `'S42' = ''`, which the planner constant-folds away, whereas the real query has `$3 = ''`, which it cannot. The two are not the same question.

**Suggested direction:** ask the database about the statement the hub actually sends, rather than a copy of it. `PREPARE` the text from `queries.sql` (or drive `hubdb.CandidatesByWorkspace` once and read the plan from `pg_stat_statements` / an `auto_explain` capture), with `SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan` so the parameterized plan is the one under test, and keep the index-by-name and buffer assertions you already have.

text:
**should-fix** A delivery the provider cannot read is parked with its **whole body**, and `ParkUnreadable` is the one reason no sweep can ever settle: ADR 11's own table says the first two reasons are what B25 re-resolves, and this is the third. So the bytes are stored forever, for nothing, at the sender's choosing.

**Fails when:** anyone who knows the URL posts garbage. I ran 20 unauthenticated POSTs with distinct unparseable bodies and got 20 outbox rows. The dedupe is on `blake3(provider, raw_body)`, so distinct bodies are trivially free, and the edge's cap is 1 MiB, so that is up to 1 MiB of database per request from a stranger with no credential, with retention not built yet. It is not reachable today only because no provider is registered; B11 makes it reachable.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `1cdc490`. You were right, and the reproduction is now a test.

**The shape.** The lookup is no longer a choice between two queries. Each key the delivery carries runs its own equality probe on its own index, and the candidate set is the union, deduplicated by subscription id and re-sorted by it (each query orders by id, the union of two does not, and the order decides which candidate is verified first). `CandidatesBySubscription` gained the mirror of the filter `CandidatesByWorkspace` already had, so the two are symmetric: a key that both the delivery and the row carry must agree, and a key either of them left empty says nothing either way.

I went with two probes rather than your single statement with an `OR` for one reason. Under the generic plan, `external_id = $3` with `$3` empty is an index probe that matches every row that recorded no registration id, which for a ClickUp-shaped deployment is every row. Guarding it with `external_id <> ''` does not save it, because the planner cannot fold that either. Running the by-subscription probe only when the delivery actually carries a registration id has no such case. The cost is two round trips inside the one resolver transaction instead of one, and no extra transaction, lock or loop.

**The table.** Rows are registered `(workspace, external)`, and a row must have at least one key (the table's CHECK).

| delivery keys | row `(W1, "")` | row `("", S1)` | row `(W1, S1)` | row `(W1, S2)` | row `(W2, S1)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `W1` only | candidate | no | candidate | candidate | no |
| `S1` only | no | candidate | candidate | no | candidate |
| `W1` and `S1` | candidate | candidate | candidate | no | no |
| neither | refused before the lookup: `deliveryKeys` parks it | | | | |

The two "no"s in the last row are what the filters are for: a row that names another registration in this workspace, or the same registration in another workspace, contradicts the delivery and is not a candidate. `TestEveryRowTheKeysCouldBelongToIsACandidate` is that table, one subtest per cell that matters, with **one secret shared by every row in a case**, so the verdict counts the rows the lookup actually asked: none parks as unowned, one stores for its tenant, two park as ambiguous. With a secret per row, a lookup that skipped a row would still store the right delivery for the right tenant and the test would prove nothing about which rows were asked.

Your P1 is `TestARowFoundOnlyByItsRegistrationIdIsStillACandidate`, spelled exactly as you wrote it. Before the fix it stored for `tenant_b`; it now parks as ambiguous. Three cells of the table failed before the fix and pass after: the P2 row, and the two two-tenant cases.

**The plan.** 50,000 rows, prepared statements under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`, explained through the statement pgx actually prepared (see my reply on the plan test):

```
CandidatesByWorkspace     Index Scan using subscriptions_by_workspace
                          Index Cond: (provider = $1) AND (workspace_id = $2)
                          shared hit=3, 0.017 ms
CandidatesBySubscription  Index Scan using subscriptions_by_external
                          Index Cond: (provider = $1) AND (external_id = $2)
                          shared hit=3, 0.020 ms
```

The second is 3 buffers whether the delivery carries a workspace or not (the workspace consistency is a Filter on the rows the index prefix found, exactly as the subscription filter already was). So a delivery with both keys costs 6 buffers rather than 3, and neither probe can degrade with the table. `TestTheCandidateLookupUsesAnIndex` asserts both by index name, the absence of `Seq Scan`, 1 to 100 buffers, and that the probe returned the row it went looking for.

**`Register`.** The lookup now serves every shape, so `Register` refuses nothing new, and I do not think it should: which keys a provider puts on a delivery is the provider's business and `Register` cannot know it. What was false was the doc comment, and that is what I changed. It now says it refuses what could resolve **no** delivery at all, and spells out that a row with one key is found by a delivery that carries that key. ADR 11 has a new decision 4 with the whole argument, and architecture 3.1 step 2 is rewritten.

**Mutations.** Restoring the either/or (`keys.Subscription != "" && keys.Workspace == ""`) fails `TestARowFoundOnlyByItsRegistrationIdIsStillACandidate` and three cells of the table. Removing the deduplication fails six existing tests plus the "both keys on both sides" cell, because a row returned by both probes would verify twice and look like two tenants.

author: gablooge
text:
Fixed in `1cdc490`. This was the bad one: a test whose whole job is to keep a per-delivery path off a table scan, unable to see the query that runs on it.

**How it reaches the generated query now.** `explainAsSent` (in `subscriptions_test.go`) takes the sqlc query name, the generated method, and arguments:

1. Run the method the hub itself calls, `hubdb.Queries.CandidatesByWorkspace`, inside the resolver transaction. pgx's default exec mode is `QueryExecModeCacheStatement`, so this prepares the statement on that connection.
2. `SELECT name FROM pg_prepared_statements WHERE statement LIKE '%-- name: CandidatesByWorkspace :%'`. Protocol-prepared statements appear there, and sqlc writes `-- name: <Name> :many` as the first line of every query text it generates, so the statement is found by something sqlc put there rather than by a copy of the SQL. Nothing in the test file contains any of the query.
3. `SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`, then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT) EXECUTE <that name>(...)`.

The difference from the old test shows up in the plan itself. Your point about `'S42' = ''` versus `$3 = ''` was exactly right, and it is visible: the plan now reads `Index Cond: ((provider = $1) AND (workspace_id = $2))` and `Filter: ((external_id = ''::text) OR ($3 = ''::text) OR (external_id = $3))`, parameters and not folded constants. Explaining the same text with literals passed as pgx parameters gives `Index Cond: ((provider = 'fake') AND (workspace_id = 'W42'))` and a filter with the `$3 = ''` disjunct folded away, which is the wrong question as you said.

**Your mutation.** I rewrote the checked-in `workspace_id = @workspace::text` to `workspace_id || '' = @workspace::text`, ran `make sqlc`, and ran the test:

```
--- FAIL: TestTheCandidateLookupUsesAnIndex
    by workspace does not use subscriptions_by_workspace, on a path that runs once per delivery
    by workspace has a sequential scan in its plan
    by workspace read 1545 buffers for at most 33 rows, which is not an index probe
        ->  Seq Scan on subscriptions  (cost=0.00..1765.00 rows=1 ...) (actual time=0.006..3.207 rows=1 loops=1)
```

All three assertions fire. Restored and regenerated afterwards; `sqlc diff` is clean in `make check`.

I also added a fourth assertion that the old test did not have: the plan's outermost `(actual ... rows=N)` must be 1. The `EXECUTE` arguments are positional, so without it they could sit in the wrong parameters, match nothing, and still descend the right index in two buffers. With it, an argument in the wrong place fails the test.

**"Anything else asserting against a copy."** I went through the tests this change adds. Two things are copies, and I kept both deliberately:

- `reasonNoOwner` and friends in `hub_test.go` are the five `dead_reason` texts spelled out rather than taken from `outbox.ParkReason.String()`. That is a golden value, not a stale copy: B25 re-resolves rows by that column, so a change to one of the texts should fail a test rather than pass silently, and it can only do that if the expected value is written down independently. `TestEveryParkReasonHasItsOwnText` pins the other side.
- The `granted` column list in `TestTheResolverRoleReadsNoMoreThanItNeeds` is the specification of the grant, and it is checked by actually reading each column as `lawang_resolver` and by proving the two ungranted ones are refused, so it cannot drift from the database.

Everything else in the new tests goes through the real thing: `hub.MaxDeliveryKeyLen` against the table's own CHECK, the outbox read as the superuser, the delivery keys through the provider double rather than a struct literal in the hub.
